source_case_name: Sachith Prabath Wijeratna v. Police Inspector B.S. Chandrasiri and Others

intake.incident_location: Yakalla and Anuradhapura Police Station
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Crime Branch of Anuradhapura Police Station
intake.what_happened: I was taken to the Anuradhapura Police Station by police officers to give a statement about a shop burglary, questioned, hung with my hands and legs tied, beaten for hours, denied food and water, forced to sign and put fingerprints on a blank paper, and later produced on a heroin allegation that I say was false.
intake.harm_suffered: Physical injuries including contusions, rope marks and neuropathy, mental shock and trauma, hospital treatment, police custody, remand custody, and a false criminal allegation.
intake.user_narrative: I was taken from Yakalla by police officers attached to the Anuradhapura Police Station because they said they wanted a statement about a shop burglary. At the police station I was questioned even though I said I knew nothing about it. I was tied up, suspended and beaten for a long time by officers who wanted me to admit to the theft. I was not given proper food or water, and I was forced to sign and place fingerprints on a blank paper. Later I was taken to hospital with injuries and then produced in court on a heroin allegation which I say was made up to justify what happened to me.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The judgment held that police officers unlawfully arrested the petitioner without reasonable suspicion, subjected him to torture while in custody, and fabricated or relied on a false heroin charge to justify the arrest and remand. The Court declared violations of Articles 11, 12(1) and 13(1) by the 1st to 3rd respondents.
gold.gold_remedy: The 2nd and 3rd respondents were ordered to each pay Rs. 100,000 as compensation and Rs. 25,000 as costs to the petitioner within one month, for a total of Rs. 250,000. The Registrar was also directed to send a copy of the judgment to the Chairman of the National Police Commission.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Existing written law and unwritten law
retrieved_articles.text: Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

cases.case_name:
Ediriweera Arukpatabandige Sugath Rohan Jayasuriya v. Manikkaratnam and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was brutally assaulted by three police officers near a boutique on December 29, 2007, and claimed that one officer struck his head with a firearm, causing unconsciousness. The Respondents denied the allegations and asserted that the Petitioner had been riding a motorcycle while intoxicated, ignored police orders to stop at a roadblock, and fell from the motorcycle twice while attempting to escape. Upon arrest, police officers allegedly discovered two packets of heroin in his possession. The Petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest. Medical evidence before the Court included an initial medico-legal report recording that the Petitioner himself admitted he had fallen due to drunkenness. The injuries documented, including scalp lacerations and scratches, together with the damaged condition of the motorcycle, were found consistent with a fall rather than a police assault. The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the Petitioner failed to satisfy the high standard of proof necessary to establish a violation of Article 11. The Court also noted inconsistencies in the Petitioner's subsequent claims of hearing and vision loss, which medical examinations failed to substantiate. The Court concluded that the arrest was lawful because the Petitioner was allegedly committing cognizable offences involving heroin possession and intoxicated driving. The Petitioner's credibility was further undermined by inconsistent accounts and undisclosed prior criminal convictions relating to substance abuse.

cases.case_name: M.D. Nandapala v. Sergeant Sunil and Others
cases.summary: On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name:
Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and Others concerned allegations of custodial torture and illegal detention following an arrest on 20 September 2017 by Anuradhapura police officers. The petitioner alleged that he was arrested without explanation, taken to a secluded teak forest near Thisa Wewa, suspended from a tree, and brutally assaulted for two hours before being detained at the police station for four days without medical care or production before a Magistrate. The respondents claimed that he was a drug user who sustained injuries while attempting to flee during questioning related to a stolen motorcycle. Medical evidence, however, confirmed six grievous injuries including a brachial plexus rupture consistent with forceful suspension. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2). The Supreme Court found the respondents' explanation wholly implausible and held that the injuries could only have resulted from deliberate custodial violence. It further held that failure to maintain proper arrest records and failure to produce the petitioner before a Magistrate constituted unlawful detention. The Court concluded that both torture and arbitrary detention were established and held the responsible officers personally liable, awarding compensation and costs from their personal funds.

cases.case_name: Gamlath v Neville Silva and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested by officers attached to the Padukka Police Station on suspicion of receiving a stolen water pump belonging to the wife of a senior police officer. He was not informed of the reasons for his arrest and was taken into police custody where he was brutally assaulted with clubs, suspended by his wrists from a beam, and had water mixed with chili powder thrown into his face. Medical evidence later confirmed seventeen injuries, including abrasions and contusions consistent with being tied and beaten while suspended. The respondents denied the allegations and claimed that the petitioner sustained the injuries by falling on rocks while assisting police investigations. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation against the State together with personal liability for costs against the individual officers. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion because it was based solely upon an unsupported allegation from another suspect claiming to have sold the stolen property to the petitioner. It further observed that the medical evidence conclusively disproved the police version of events and established custodial torture. The Court emphasized that the intentional infliction of violence upon suspects held in police custody is barbaric and incompatible with constitutional guarantees of dignity and liberty. The State bears primary responsibility for preventing abuses committed by officers exercising coercive powers over individuals deprived of their liberty.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and
Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner in Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and Others concerned allegations of custodial torture and illegal detention following an arrest on 20 September 2017 by Anuradhapura police officers. The petitioner alleged that he was arrested without explanation, taken to a secluded teak forest near Thisa Wewa, suspended from a tree, and brutally assaulted for two hours before being detained at the police station for four days without medical care or production before a Magistrate. The respondents claimed that he was a drug user who sustained injuries while attempting to flee during questioning related to a stolen motorcycle. Medical evidence, however, confirmed six grievous injuries including a brachial plexus rupture consistent with forceful suspension. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2). The Supreme Court found the respondents' explanation wholly implausible and held that the injuries could only have resulted from deliberate custodial violence. It further held that failure to maintain proper arrest records and failure to produce the petitioner before a Magistrate constituted unlawful detention. The Court concluded that both torture and arbitrary detention were established and held the responsible officers personally liable, awarding compensation and costs from their personal funds.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
Ediriweera Arukpatabandige Sugath Rohan Jayasuriya v. Manikkaratnam and
Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was brutally assaulted by three police officers near a boutique on December 29, 2007, and claimed that one officer struck his head with a firearm, causing unconsciousness. The Respondents denied the allegations and asserted that the Petitioner had been riding a motorcycle while intoxicated, ignored police orders to stop at a roadblock, and fell from the motorcycle twice while attempting to escape. Upon arrest, police officers allegedly discovered two packets of heroin in his possession. The Petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest. Medical evidence before the Court included an initial medico-legal report recording that the Petitioner himself admitted he had fallen due to drunkenness. The injuries documented, including scalp lacerations and scratches, together with the damaged condition of the motorcycle, were found consistent with a fall rather than a police assault. The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the Petitioner failed to satisfy the high standard of proof necessary to establish a violation of Article 11. The Court also noted inconsistencies in the Petitioner's subsequent claims of hearing and vision loss, which medical examinations failed to substantiate. The Court concluded that the arrest was lawful because the Petitioner was allegedly committing cognizable offences involving heroin possession and intoxicated driving. The Petitioner's credibility was further undermined by inconsistent accounts and undisclosed prior criminal convictions relating to substance abuse.

retrieved_cases.case_name: M.D. Nandapala v. Sergeant Sunil and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. cases.case_name: Gamlath v Neville Silva and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested by officers attached to the Padukka Police Station on suspicion of receiving a stolen water pump belonging to the wife of a senior police officer. He was not informed of the reasons for his arrest and was taken into police custody where he was brutally assaulted with clubs, suspended by his wrists from a beam, and had water mixed with chili powder thrown into his face. Medical evidence later confirmed seventeen injuries, including abrasions and contusions consistent with being tied and beaten while suspended. The respondents denied the allegations and claimed that the petitioner sustained the injuries by falling on rocks while assisting police investigations. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation against the State together with personal liability for costs against the individual officers. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion because it was based solely upon an unsupported allegation from another suspect claiming to have sold the stolen property to the petitioner. It further observed that the medical evidence conclusively disproved the police version of events and established custodial torture. The Court emphasized that the intentional infliction of violence upon suspects held in police custody is barbaric and incompatible with constitutional guarantees of dignity and liberty. The State bears primary responsibility for preventing abuses committed by officers exercising coercive powers over individuals deprived of their liberty.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name:
Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and Others concerned allegations of custodial torture and illegal detention following an arrest on 20 September 2017 by Anuradhapura police officers. The petitioner alleged that he was arrested without explanation, taken to a secluded teak forest near Thisa Wewa, suspended from a tree, and brutally assaulted for two hours before being detained at the police station for four days without medical care or production before a Magistrate. The respondents claimed that he was a drug user who sustained injuries while attempting to flee during questioning related to a stolen motorcycle. Medical evidence, however, confirmed six grievous injuries including a brachial plexus rupture consistent with forceful suspension. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2). The Supreme Court found the respondents' explanation wholly implausible and held that the injuries could only have resulted from deliberate custodial violence. It further held that failure to maintain proper arrest records and failure to produce the petitioner before a Magistrate constituted unlawful detention. The Court concluded that both torture and arbitrary detention were established and held the responsible officers personally liable, awarding compensation and costs from their personal funds.

cases.case_name: M.D. Nandapala v. Sergeant Sunil and Others
cases.summary: On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

cases.case_name: Hapugodage Jagath Perera v. Gothami Ranasinghe and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested following a land dispute and alleged that while in police custody he was subjected to severe assault resulting in permanent injuries, including loss of teeth. The case raised issues under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), particularly concerning torture and arbitrary treatment by State officials. The Court found that medical evidence strongly supported the Petitioner's claim, confirming serious physical harm consistent with brutal assault rather than lawful use of force. It held that the level of injury satisfied the high evidentiary threshold required for establishing violations of Article 11. The Court further ruled that State liability arises where police officers act in their official capacity, even if the individual officer is no longer available to answer proceedings. It emphasized that protection against torture is absolute and cannot be justified under investigative or custodial authority. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation for the severe and permanent injuries sustained.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Velmurugu v Attorney-General and Another
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner, a member of the District Development Council, was arrested by army personnel on 9 August 1981 during communal disturbances under the orders of the 2nd respondent, an Assistant Superintendent of Police. He alleged that after the arrest the 2nd respondent instructed the army personnel to "do as they like with him," following which he was brutally assaulted inside an army truck, kicked with booted feet, had his beard burnt, and sustained a fractured jaw. The petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13 of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest by State officers. The respondents denied responsibility for the alleged torture and disputed that any constitutional violation had occurred. The Supreme Court, by a majority of three to two, dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established. The Court applied a high degree of probability because of the gravity of allegations involving torture by State authorities. It emphasized that the petitioner failed to complain before the Magistrate, medical officer, or police at the earliest opportunity. The Court further reasoned that State liability arises only where wrongful acts are committed under colour of office or pursuant to administrative practice. The alleged conduct was characterized as a private criminal aberration rather than official executive action attributable to the State.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Velmurugu v Attorney-General and Another
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, a member of the District Development Council, was arrested by army personnel on 9 August 1981 during communal disturbances under the orders of the 2nd respondent, an Assistant Superintendent of Police. He alleged that after the arrest the 2nd respondent instructed the army personnel to "do as they like with him," following which he was brutally assaulted inside an army truck, kicked with booted feet, had his beard burnt, and sustained a fractured jaw. The petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13 of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest by State officers. The respondents denied responsibility for the alleged torture and disputed that any constitutional violation had occurred. The Supreme Court, by a majority of three to two, dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established. The Court applied a high degree of probability because of the gravity of allegations involving torture by State authorities. It emphasized that the petitioner failed to complain before the Magistrate, medical officer, or police at the earliest opportunity. The Court further reasoned that State liability arises only where wrongful acts are committed under colour of office or pursuant to administrative practice. The alleged conduct was characterized as a private criminal aberration rather than official executive action attributable to the State.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Gamlath v Neville Silva and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested by officers attached to the Padukka Police Station on suspicion of receiving a stolen water pump belonging to the wife of a senior police officer. He was not informed of the reasons for his arrest and was taken into police custody where he was brutally assaulted with clubs, suspended by his wrists from a beam, and had water mixed with chili powder thrown into his face. Medical evidence later confirmed seventeen injuries, including abrasions and contusions consistent with being tied and beaten while suspended. The respondents denied the allegations and claimed that the petitioner sustained the injuries by falling on rocks while assisting police investigations. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation against the State together with personal liability for costs against the individual officers. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion because it was based solely upon an unsupported allegation from another suspect claiming to have sold the stolen property to the petitioner. It further observed that the medical evidence conclusively disproved the police version of events and established custodial torture. The Court emphasized that the intentional infliction of violence upon suspects held in police custody is barbaric and incompatible with constitutional guarantees of dignity and liberty. The State bears primary responsibility for preventing abuses committed by officers exercising coercive powers over individuals deprived of their liberty.

retrieved_cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

intake.actor_name: Cabinet of Ministers and public authorities responsible for police appointments
intake.what_happened: I am a senior police officer and another senior police officer who was due to retire was given re-employment on a contract basis beyond the compulsory retirement age. I believe this decision was made by the wrong authority and affected the vacancy and promotion opportunity that would otherwise have arisen in the police service.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of a promotional opportunity, adverse effect on career advancement, and unfair treatment in public service employment.
intake.user_narrative: I am a senior officer in the police service. Another senior officer above me was due to retire when he reached the compulsory retirement age, and I expected that a vacancy would arise for the next senior officer to be considered. Instead, government authorities approved his re-employment on a contract basis for another year. I believe the decision was not made by the legally proper authority and that it unfairly affected my chance of promotion and my ability to progress in my profession.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner challenged the Cabinet decision to re-employ the 41st respondent on contract basis after retirement age. The Court held that after the 19th Amendment, the National Police Commission, not the Cabinet of Ministers, had the relevant authority over police officers. The Cabinet decision was therefore ab initio void, and the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) were declared violated.
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) were violated, declared that the 41st respondent stood retired on 21 July 2015, and declared that the 41st respondent was not entitled to be re-employed, granted an extension, or appointed after reaching the age of sixty. No costs were ordered.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear public employment and promotion-related violation case involving state actors and unlawful executive decision-making. No internal corpus case ID was provided, so source_case_id is null and gold_relevant_case_ids is empty.

final_answer:
SECTION 1 — RIGHTS ASSESSMENT:
Based on the structured reasoning chain, the following article(s) appear to remain supported as potentially violated:
- Article 12(1): The user's complaint about being unfairly affected in promotion opportunities due to a re-employment decision by government authorities aligns with the principles of equality before the law. The precedent case, Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others, found a violation of Article 12(1) where arbitrary actions and inconsistent application of promotion criteria in the police service led to an officer being unfairly bypassed, directly impacting their right to equality in career progression.
- Article 14(1)(g): The user's belief that the re-employment decision unfairly affected their 'ability to progress in my profession' directly relates to the right to engage in a lawful profession. The precedent case, Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others, also found a violation of Article 14(1)(g) because arbitrary actions in promotion decisions within the police service directly impacted the petitioner's career progression and ability to advance in their chosen profession.

SECTION 2 — PRECEDENT:
The precedent alignment was classified as: supports.

SECTION 3 — STRENGTHS OF THE CASE:
- The incident occurred within the 30-day filing period, making the petition timely.
- The alleged infringement was committed by state actors (Cabinet of Ministers and public authorities responsible for police appointments).
- There is strong factual similarity to the precedent case Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others, which found violations of both Article 12(1) and 14(1)(g) in similar circumstances involving unfair promotion practices and arbitrary decisions affecting police officers' career progression.

cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name:
Y.G. Gnanathilaka v. D. Dissanayake, Chairman, Public Service Commission
and Others
cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 240/2020 and connected applications, the petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Survey, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision to deduct his authorized no-pay overseas leave period from seniority, resulting in delayed promotion. At the time of his leave in 2001–2003, applicable circulars did not provide for such deduction, but a later 2004 amendment was applied retrospectively to his disadvantage. Despite an Administrative Appeals Tribunal ruling in his favor, the PSC refused to implement it. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). It held that applying retrospective administrative rules to deprive vested rights was unlawful and contrary to the presumption against retrospectivity. The Court further held that the petitioner had a legitimate expectation based on the 2001 circular that his career progression would not be adversely affected. It emphasized that disregard of binding appellate decisions undermines the rule of law and administrative hierarchy. The Court concluded that the PSC's actions were arbitrary and amounted to unjustified interference with his occupational progression and equality rights. It ordered restoration of seniority and awarded compensation, reaffirming that administrative authorities must act consistently with legal certainty and fairness.

cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

cases.case_name:
Wasantha Dissanayake and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public
Administration
cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

cases.case_name:
Dola Mullage Gunarathna and Another v. K. W. E. Karalliyadda, Chairman,
National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. stage_b_cases.case_name:
Y.G. Gnanathilaka v. D. Dissanayake, Chairman, Public Service Commission
and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 240/2020 and connected applications, the petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Survey, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision to deduct his authorized no-pay overseas leave period from seniority, resulting in delayed promotion. At the time of his leave in 2001–2003, applicable circulars did not provide for such deduction, but a later 2004 amendment was applied retrospectively to his disadvantage. Despite an Administrative Appeals Tribunal ruling in his favor, the PSC refused to implement it. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). It held that applying retrospective administrative rules to deprive vested rights was unlawful and contrary to the presumption against retrospectivity. The Court further held that the petitioner had a legitimate expectation based on the 2001 circular that his career progression would not be adversely affected. It emphasized that disregard of binding appellate decisions undermines the rule of law and administrative hierarchy. The Court concluded that the PSC's actions were arbitrary and amounted to unjustified interference with his occupational progression and equality rights. It ordered restoration of seniority and awarded compensation, reaffirming that administrative authorities must act consistently with legal certainty and fairness.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

cases.case_name: Seetha Weerakoon v. Mahendra, OIC, Police Station, Galagedera and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner and her sister were arrested and initially detained under an Emergency Regulations detention order valid for ninety days, which expired on 12 November 1989. Despite expiration of legal authority, the petitioner remained in police custody for approximately one year without being produced before a Magistrate, and only later was remanded to fiscal custody. The State failed to justify continued detention or provide evidence supporting prolonged custody, raising issues under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning arbitrary arrest and detention and failure to produce a detainee before judicial authority within a reasonable time. The Supreme Court held that once the lawful detention order expired, any continued confinement without fresh valid authority was unconstitutional and amounted to unlawful detention. The Court emphasized that investigative convenience cannot override constitutional safeguards protecting personal liberty, and that prolonged detention without evidence of culpability is impermissible. It further noted that executive officers bear responsibility to ensure strict compliance with legal requirements governing deprivation of liberty. The Court declared the detention illegal, quashed relevant orders, and granted relief including compensation against the State and personal costs against the officer in charge. The decision reaffirmed strict judicial protection against arbitrary executive detention and reinforced the requirement of timely judicial oversight over custodial deprivation of liberty.

cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

cases.case_name: Shanthi Chandrasekeram v. D. B. Wijetunga and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, political and trade union leaders, were arrested following a bomb blast investigation and detained initially under time-bound orders, later converted into indefinite detention orders under Emergency Regulations. They alleged arbitrary arrest, illegal detention, and torture while in custody. The State justified detention based on suspected links to a suicide bomber. The Supreme Court held that arrests lacked credible supporting material and were not backed by contemporaneous records demonstrating reasonable suspicion. It further held that continued detention without disclosure of factual basis for executive satisfaction was arbitrary and contrary to constitutional safeguards. Although allegations of torture were raised, the Court found insufficient evidence to establish a violation of Article 11. It concluded that detention orders were unlawful and that Articles 13(1) and 13(2) were violated due to lack of objective justification and failure of evidentiary support. The Court ordered compensation and costs.

cases.case_name: Dhammika Yapa v. Bandaranayake and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested following a complaint by a government minister alleging involvement in a mob attack on his residence. He was detained under Emergency Regulations on suspicion of committing an offence involving public disorder. The petitioner challenged the arrest and detention as mala fide and violative of Articles 13(1), 13(2), 14(1)(g), and 14(1)(h) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court examined whether the arrest was supported by reasonable suspicion under emergency legal frameworks. It held that an arrest is valid if the officer has objective material amounting to reasonable suspicion at the time of arrest, and that a direct complaint from a responsible authority may constitute sufficient basis. The Court further held that in a state of emergency, authorities are entitled to broader discretion in restricting liberty, provided procedural requirements are substantially complied with. It found insufficient evidence to prove mala fides or political victimization and accepted the respondents' affidavits denying improper motive. The Court also held that incidental restrictions on profession and movement were justified consequences of lawful detention under emergency powers. Accordingly, it concluded that the petitioner's fundamental rights were not violated and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Gamini Perera, Attorney-at-Law v. W. B. Rajaguru, Inspector-General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a soldier, was arrested on suspicion of involvement in murders and detained under Emergency Regulation 17(1) based on a detention order that did not specify the precise ground relied upon among multiple available statutory grounds. He challenged the arrest and detention under Articles 13(1) and 13(2). The State argued that detention was authorized under emergency powers. The Supreme Court held that lawful arrest requires reasonable suspicion based on objective facts, which was absent as the officer acted on a mere hunch. It further held that a detention order must demonstrate application of mind by specifying the exact statutory ground relied upon; failure to do so renders the order vague and illegal. The Court emphasized strict compliance with legal safeguards governing deprivation of liberty even during emergencies. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, violating Articles 13(1) and 13(2), and awarded compensation.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

intake.incident_location: Negombo Police Station and Ragama
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Negombo Police Station and Ragama Police Station
intake.what_happened: I am an Attorney-at-Law who represented people complaining of police abuse. After visiting the Negombo Police Station for professional work, I had a confrontation with officers and say I was threatened and struck. A few days later, my office next to my home was destroyed by fire. I complained to the police, but I believe the police did not properly investigate the burning of my office.
intake.harm_suffered: Alleged assault and threats at a police station, destruction of office premises by fire, loss of valuables and work materials, lack of proper police investigation, and disruption to professional work.
intake.user_narrative: I work as an Attorney-at-Law and have represented people who complained about unlawful arrest and torture by police officers. I went to the Negombo Police Station to obtain a copy of a complaint for a client-related matter. There was an argument about where I could park, and later I say a police officer threatened me and hit me. I complained about that incident. A few days later, my office beside my house in Ragama caught fire and was destroyed along with valuables and documents. I made a complaint to the Ragama Police, but I believe they failed to properly investigate what happened or try to find the people responsible.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Court rejected the Article 11 complaint arising from the alleged police station assault because the conflicting versions and nature of the complaint did not satisfy the required threshold for torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment. The Court also rejected the Article 14(1)(g) claim because the petitioners did not substantiate that the failure to investigate prevented them from engaging in their professional duties. However, the Court held that the inaction of the Officer-in-Charge of Ragama Police Station in failing to properly investigate the complaint about the office being set on fire violated the petitioners' rights under Article 12(1), and the State was responsible for that inaction.
gold.gold_remedy: The State was directed to pay Rs. 50,000 as compensation to each petitioner within three months. No order was made as to costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Partial-violation case useful for rejected-article overclaiming control: Article 12(1) was finally accepted based on police inaction, while Articles 11 and 14(1)(g) were rejected. cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name: De Silva v. Manoj and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was allegedly assaulted by a traffic police constable during a routine stop in Mount Lavinia after a brief exchange regarding vehicle documentation. The officer punched and kicked the petitioner without provocation, prompting a complaint and medical treatment. Although an internal inquiry resulted in a minor disciplinary warning, the petitioner filed a fundamental rights application alleging violation of Article 11. The respondent denied the assault, but evidence including medical records, prompt complaint, and inconsistent police documentation supported the petitioner's version. The Supreme Court found the denial not credible and held that corroborating evidence established the occurrence of physical violence. It concluded that law enforcement officers must act within constitutional limits and that unprovoked assault constitutes cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered compensation against the officer personally as well as partial payment by the State. The decision emphasized accountability of police officers and the constitutional prohibition against unnecessary use of force.

cases.case_name: Bandula Samarasekera v. Vijitha Alwis, OIC Ginigathhena and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a former employee of Brown and Company, was returning from an exorcism ritual performed for his son on February 28, 2007 when his vehicle encountered that of the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Ginigathhena Police Station, on a narrow road. Following a dispute over reversing the vehicles, the 1st Respondent assaulted the Petitioner and accused him of being a treasure hunter after observing ritual items inside the jeep. The Petitioner was arrested, transported to Kandy Police Station while bleeding and injured, and detained for approximately eighteen hours before being produced before a Magistrate, who observed that no offence appeared to have been committed. Medical evidence established grievous injuries including a fractured nasal bone and perforated ear drum caused by a blunt weapon. The Respondents attempted to justify the arrest by alleging treasure hunting activities and claimed the injuries were caused by a crowd. The Court rejected these explanations after the Archaeological Department confirmed that the location possessed no archaeological significance. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion and that detention for eighteen hours without promptly recording a statement or producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate was arbitrary. The Court further ruled that the severe assault constituted cruel and degrading treatment contrary to Article 11. The Supreme Court found violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), ordered compensation against the 1st Respondent and the State, and condemned the use of barbarous police methods undermining public confidence.

cases.case_name: Sri Thaminda, Dharshane and Mahalekam v. Inspector of Police and Others
cases.summary: During a festival on August 11, 2003, the three Petitioners, who were intoxicated, became involved in a confrontation with police officers regarding the parking of a three-wheeler. A scuffle followed during which a Police Constable was injured and hospitalized. The Petitioners were arrested and later sustained multiple injuries. They alleged that police officers and members of the Rapid Deployment Force assaulted them while in custody, amounting to cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11. The Respondents contended that the injuries resulted from an angry crowd attempting to rescue the injured constable and denied responsibility for the assaults. The Supreme Court held that the arrests themselves were justified because the Petitioners had behaved aggressively and police intervention was necessary to prevent escalation of violence and maintain public order. Consequently, no violation of Article 13(1) was established. However, the Court found sufficient material to conclude that the Petitioners were assaulted by state officers acting under colour of office. The Court reaffirmed that constitutional protection against torture and cruel or degrading treatment applies irrespective of the victim's conduct. Nevertheless, the Court declined to award compensation because the Petitioners had themselves behaved in a disorderly and disgraceful manner and contributed to the circumstances leading to the incident. Declaratory relief alone was therefore granted for the infringement of Article 11.

cases.case_name:
Hondamuni Chandima Samanmalee de Zoysa Siriwardena and Another v.
Inspector Malaweera and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, two Attorneys-at-Law, visited Ambalangoda Police Station on February 28, 2010, to represent a client whose relatives had allegedly been detained in connection with a child custody dispute following the death of the child's mother. The Petitioners alleged that the police had summoned the grieving family to the station and thereby prevented them from attending funeral arrangements. At the police station, the 1st and 2nd Respondents verbally abused the Petitioners, accused lawyers of earning money unfairly, threatened to arrest them for providing "wrong advice," and ordered them to switch off their mobile phones while coercing the family to surrender the child to the estranged father. The Petitioners contended that these acts violated Articles 11, 12(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court held that Article 11 protects against severe mental suffering intentionally inflicted by public officials and that humiliating and threatening legal practitioners in front of a bereaved family amounted to degrading treatment. The Court further held that lawyers possess a constitutional right to represent clients and that intimidation aimed at obstructing legal representation violated the freedom to engage in a lawful profession guaranteed by Article 14(1)(g). The Court rejected any justification for the conduct of the officers and observed that the Petitioners had acted professionally while the Respondents acted under colour of office in an arbitrary and abusive manner. Accordingly, the Court found violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 14(1)(g) and ordered the Respondents to personally pay compensation and litigation costs to the Petitioners.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment under existing written law
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Existing written law and unwritten law
retrieved_articles.text: Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to a fair trial
retrieved_articles.text: Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.
