intake.what_happened: We are Chief Inspectors of Police who were in the same batch and promoted to Chief Inspector along with another officer. Later, based on a political victimization relief process, that officer's promotion was backdated several years, placing him above us in seniority and making him eligible for consideration for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police ahead of us.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of equal treatment in police promotions, prejudice to seniority, reduced promotional prospects, and unfair disadvantage in consideration for the rank of Assistant Superintendent of Police.
intake.user_narrative: We are Chief Inspectors of Police who joined the police service around the same time as another officer and were promoted to Chief Inspector on the same date. Later, government and police authorities treated that officer as if he had been promoted to Chief Inspector several years earlier, based on a political victimization relief recommendation. This moved him above us in seniority and allowed him to be considered for the next promotion before us. We believe this unfairly affected our career progression and our chance to be considered equally for promotion.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners challenged the backdating of the 48th respondent's promotion to Chief Inspector of Police from 08 February 2020 to 01 January 2014 based on a political victimization relief process. The Court held that the Cabinet decision was not a valid policy decision applicable generally, but an ad hoc decision benefiting an individual, and that the backdating unfairly altered seniority and prejudiced the petitioners' promotional prospects. The Court found violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioners' rights under Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) had been infringed, nullified the directives marked X13, X16 and X17, declared the backdating of the 48th respondent's appointment to Chief Inspector effective from 01 January 2014 illegal and of no force or effect, and declared that the 48th respondent was ineligible at the relevant time to be appointed Assistant Superintendent of Police.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear public-sector promotion and seniority violation case involving state actors and unlawful individual relief through a political victimization process. No internal corpus case ID was provided, so source_case_id is null and gold_relevant_case_ids is empty.

cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name:
Dola Mullage Gunarathna and Another v. K. W. E. Karalliyadda, Chairman,
National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. The Supreme Court found that the impugned backdating conferred an impermissible double benefit on the 11th Respondent for the same period of service, disrupting established seniority principles. It further held that such arbitrary restructuring of promotions without transparent criteria was inconsistent with the rule of law and equal treatment in public employment. The Court also emphasised that the process undermined institutional discipline and fairness within the police service. Accordingly, it quashed the impugned communication and held that the Petitioners' constitutional rights had been violated.

cases.case_name: Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others, comprising serving and retired police officers, alleged discriminatory treatment in the implementation of recommendations made by a committee addressing political victimisation claims between 1994 and 2014. They contended that while some officers were promoted under Cabinet-approved recommendations following the Basnayake Committee report, their own promotions were withheld, and that another officer (the 17th respondent) was unfairly favoured. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police argued that implementing retrospective promotions would adversely affect the seniority of a large number of serving officers and would contravene conditions imposed by the President in the Cabinet decision, which required protection of existing seniority structures. The petitioners invoked Article 12(1) alleging unequal treatment. The Supreme Court examined whether differential treatment existed in comparable circumstances and whether executive implementation of a policy decision could override statutory recruitment principles. It held that the 17th respondent's circumstances were distinguishable, particularly as his promotion did not disrupt existing seniority due to his impending retirement. The Court further held that Cabinet decisions under Articles 55 and 155G must operate within the framework of law and cannot confer enforceable individual entitlements contrary to service regulations. It concluded that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been proven and dismissed the application for failure to establish a violation of Article 12(1).

cases.case_name: Chandra Jayasinghe v. Mahendran and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, was denied promotion to the rank of Deputy Inspector General despite greater seniority and a comparatively cleaner disciplinary record than several officers who were promoted. The authorities relied on evaluations by a Selection Board that applied subjective assessment criteria. The petitioner alleged that the promotion process was arbitrary and inconsistent with established standards governing seniority and merit, thereby violating Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court examined whether the selection procedure had been administered fairly and rationally. It held that while the State possesses discretion to formulate and apply promotion schemes, such discretion must be exercised transparently, consistently, and on objective grounds. The Court found that subjective scoring had been used to override objective seniority without adequate justification or documented reasoning. It further held that seniority in public service constitutes a significant factor that cannot be disregarded absent clear evidence of unsuitability or exceptional merit in junior candidates. The failure of the Selection Board to explain the petitioner's exclusion rendered the process arbitrary and discriminatory. The Court concluded that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed. Accordingly, it directed the authorities to promote the petitioner with retrospective effect and awarded compensation.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination

retrieved_cases.case_name:
Dola Mullage Gunarathna and Another v. K. W. E. Karalliyadda, Chairman,
National Police Commission and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. The Supreme Court found that the impugned backdating conferred an impermissible double benefit on the 11th Respondent for the same period of service, disrupting established seniority principles. It further held that such arbitrary restructuring of promotions without transparent criteria was inconsistent with the rule of law and equal treatment in public employment. The Court also emphasised that the process undermined institutional discipline and fairness within the police service. Accordingly, it quashed the impugned communication and held that the Petitioners' constitutional rights had been violated.

intake.what_happened: We are Chief Inspectors of Police who joined the police service and received promotions on the same dates as another officer. A political victimization relief process recommended backdating that officer's promotion to Chief Inspector several years earlier, and government and police authorities implemented it, making him much senior to us and eligible for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police ahead of us.
intake.harm_suffered: Unequal treatment in police promotion and seniority, prejudice to career progression, and risk of losing fair consideration for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police.
intake.user_narrative: We are Chief Inspectors of Police. We joined the police service on the same date as another officer, were promoted to Inspector on the same date, and became eligible for promotion to Chief Inspector on the same date. Later, a committee dealing with alleged political victimization recommended that this other officer's promotion be treated as if it had taken effect several years earlier. The Cabinet, Public Service Commission, Ministry of Public Security and Inspector-General of Police acted on that recommendation. This made him about six years senior to us and allowed him to be considered for promotion ahead of us. We believe this is unfair because he was in the same position as us and there was no proper basis to treat him differently.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners challenged the executive action backdating the 48th respondent's promotion to Chief Inspector of Police to 01 January 2014. The Court found that the petitioners and the 48th respondent were similarly circumstanced, having joined the police service on the same date, been promoted to Inspector on the same date, and become eligible for promotion to Chief Inspector on the same date. The sole basis for the political victimization recommendation was that the 48th respondent had served at Kalkuda Police Station, which the Court held could not justify treating him as politically victimized or backdating his promotion. The executive action therefore infringed the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were infringed, quashed the Political Victimization Committee recommendation to backdate the 48th respondent's promotion to 01 January 2014, quashed the Cabinet approval, quashed the Public Service Commission decision to implement it, and quashed its implementation by the Inspector-General of Police. The judgment was also directed to apply to SC FR 159/2022.

cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name: Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Saman Ratnayake and Others v. National Police Commission and Others, comprising serving and retired police officers, alleged discriminatory treatment in the implementation of recommendations made by a committee addressing political victimisation claims between 1994 and 2014. They contended that while some officers were promoted under Cabinet-approved recommendations following the Basnayake Committee report, their own promotions were withheld, and that another officer (the 17th respondent) was unfairly favoured. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police argued that implementing retrospective promotions would adversely affect the seniority of a large number of serving officers and would contravene conditions imposed by the President in the Cabinet decision, which required protection of existing seniority structures. The petitioners invoked Article 12(1) alleging unequal treatment. The Supreme Court examined whether differential treatment existed in comparable circumstances and whether executive implementation of a policy decision could override statutory recruitment principles. It held that the 17th respondent's circumstances were distinguishable, particularly as his promotion did not disrupt existing seniority due to his impending retirement. The Court further held that Cabinet decisions under Articles 55 and 155G must operate within the framework of law and cannot confer enforceable individual entitlements contrary to service regulations. It concluded that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been proven and dismissed the application for failure to establish a violation of Article 12(1).

cases.case_name: Gunawardana v. National Police Commission
cases.summary: The petitioners, Police Inspectors, challenged the cancellation of a completed recruitment process for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police, despite having successfully passed examinations and being placed on a merit list. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police cancelled the process based on a Cabinet decision to restructure the police service. The petitioners alleged violations of Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g), claiming deprivation of earned promotional rights. The Supreme Court held that once a competitive recruitment process is completed and a merit list is finalized, candidates acquire a legitimate expectation of promotion. It found that the retrospective cancellation of a valid selection process was arbitrary and irrational. The Court further held that while restructuring of public services is permissible, it cannot be used to nullify completed lawful processes without justification. It emphasized that administrative discretion must be exercised consistently with the rule of law and fairness. Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and quashed the impugned cancellation decisions.

cases.case_name:
Dola Mullage Gunarathna and Another v. K. W. E. Karalliyadda, Chairman,
National Police Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, Inspectors of Police, challenged the retrospective backdating of promotions granted to the 11th Respondent, which altered his seniority by backdating his promotion to Sub-Inspector and subsequently to Inspector of Police. They contended that such administrative action unlawfully elevated a junior officer above them, thereby violating Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) relating to equality and freedom of occupation in public service. The Respondents raised a limitation objection, but the Court held that the time bar was inapplicable because the Petitioners had promptly invoked the Human Rights Commission, thereby suspending limitation. The Supreme Court found that the impugned backdating conferred an impermissible double benefit on the 11th Respondent for the same period of service, disrupting established seniority principles. It further held that such arbitrary restructuring of promotions without transparent criteria was inconsistent with the rule of law and equal treatment in public employment. The Court also emphasised that the process undermined institutional discipline and fairness within the police service. Accordingly, it quashed the impugned communication and held that the Petitioners' constitutional rights had been violated.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination

intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation and its Chairman
intake.what_happened: I applied for internal promotion to the post of Technical Administrator at Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation. After interviews, a waiting list showed that I had higher marks than some employees who were later promoted to that post, but I was not promoted while they were appointed.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of fair consideration for internal promotion, adverse impact on career progression, and unequal treatment compared with lower-ranked candidates.
intake.user_narrative: I am an employee of Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation. I applied for internal promotion to the post of Technical Administrator. According to the waiting list, I had obtained higher interview marks than some employees who were later promoted. Even though I was placed above them on the list, they were appointed and I was left out. I believe this was unfair and affected my career progression within the corporation.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g) arising from appointments to the post of Technical Administrator. The Court held that it was unjustifiable to promote the 16th, 17th and 18th respondents over the 1st petitioner because the 1st petitioner had obtained higher marks on the waiting list. cases.case_name:
Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

cases.case_name: Weerasuriya Arachchige Leela Weerasuriya v. People's Bank and Others
cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 419/2015, the petitioner, a senior officer at People's Bank, alleged that she was unfairly denied promotion to Deputy Head of Finance despite being qualified and repeatedly applying between 2009 and 2013. She contended that the Bank deliberately delayed recruitment processes, cancelled interviews without justification, and ultimately promoted a junior officer after ensuring he became eligible. The Supreme Court considered whether this conduct violated Article 12(1). It found that the repeated postponement and cancellation of recruitment processes lacked valid justification and demonstrated arbitrariness and lack of transparency. The Bank's explanation of restructuring was rejected as a pretext. The Court held that failure to disclose criteria or marks and the manipulation of timing in recruitment undermined fair competition. It emphasized that when a public institution undertakes selection for promotion, it must act reasonably, transparently, and consistently with equal treatment principles. The Court concluded that the petitioner's legitimate promotional expectations were frustrated through discriminatory administrative conduct. Accordingly, it held that her fundamental rights were violated and declared the actions of the Bank and officials unconstitutional under Article 12(1).

cases.case_name: Wickramasinghe and Others v. Attorney General
cases.summary: The petitioners, public sector technical officers, challenged a decision altering their salary placement after appointment. Although initial recruitment documents guaranteed higher salary steps to preserve prior seniority and pay, the respondents later unilaterally placed them at lower initial salary levels. The petitioners alleged violation of Article 12(1), arguing breach of legitimate expectation and unfair administrative action. The respondents contended that revised administrative decisions justified the salary adjustment. The Supreme Court held that the salary terms formed part of binding employment conditions and could not be altered unilaterally after acceptance of appointment. It found that the respondents acted arbitrarily and contrary to principles of fairness and consistency in administrative law. The Court further held that legitimate expectation arising from official appointment letters must be honoured unless a rational basis exists for deviation. It concluded that failure to implement agreed salary steps constituted unequal and unreasonable treatment under Article 12(1). Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and directed restoration of the originally promised salary structure.

cases.case_name:
Wasantha Dissanayake and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public
Administration
cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to form and join trade unions
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to form and join trade unions. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to form and join a trade union.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and
Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

retrieved_cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Weerasuriya Arachchige Leela Weerasuriya v. People's Bank and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 419/2015, the petitioner, a senior officer at People's Bank, alleged that she was unfairly denied promotion to Deputy Head of Finance despite being qualified and repeatedly applying between 2009 and 2013. She contended that the Bank deliberately delayed recruitment processes, cancelled interviews without justification, and ultimately promoted a junior officer after ensuring he became eligible. The Supreme Court considered whether this conduct violated Article 12(1). It found that the repeated postponement and cancellation of recruitment processes lacked valid justification and demonstrated arbitrariness and lack of transparency. The Bank's explanation of restructuring was rejected as a pretext. The Court held that failure to disclose criteria or marks and the manipulation of timing in recruitment undermined fair competition. It emphasized that when a public institution undertakes selection for promotion, it must act reasonably, transparently, and consistently with equal treatment principles. The Court concluded that the petitioner's legitimate promotional expectations were frustrated through discriminatory administrative conduct. Accordingly, it held that her fundamental rights were violated and declared the actions of the Bank and officials unconstitutional under Article 12(1).

retrieved_cases.case_name: Wickramasinghe and Others v. Attorney General
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioners, public sector technical officers, challenged a decision altering their salary placement after appointment. Although initial recruitment documents guaranteed higher salary steps to preserve prior seniority and pay, the respondents later unilaterally placed them at lower initial salary levels. The petitioners alleged violation of Article 12(1), arguing breach of legitimate expectation and unfair administrative action. The respondents contended that revised administrative decisions justified the salary adjustment. The Supreme Court held that the salary terms formed part of binding employment conditions and could not be altered unilaterally after acceptance of appointment. It found that the respondents acted arbitrarily and contrary to principles of fairness and consistency in administrative law. The Court further held that legitimate expectation arising from official appointment letters must be honoured unless a rational basis exists for deviation. It concluded that failure to implement agreed salary steps constituted unequal and unreasonable treatment under Article 12(1). Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and directed restoration of the originally promised salary structure.

intake.incident_location: Department of Technical Education and Training, Colombo
intake.actor_name: Department of Technical Education and Training, Ministry of Public Administration, Department of Pensions and Treasury
intake.actor_role: government officials responsible for salaries and pensions
intake.what_happened: We are serving and retired officers connected to the Sri Lanka Technical Education Service. After a public administration salary circular, our salaries and pensions were enhanced through three salary increments and we received those payments for several years. Later, officials said the payments were erroneous, reduced our salaries and pensions, and moved to recover alleged overpayments from us.
intake.harm_suffered: Reduction of salary and pension benefits, threatened recovery of past payments, financial loss, uncertainty over retirement income, and unfair treatment after relying on payments made for several years.
intake.user_narrative: I work, or previously worked, in the Sri Lanka Technical Education Service. After a government salary circular, my salary or pension was increased with three increments, and this continued for several years. Later, the authorities suddenly said the increments had been given by mistake and decided to reduce my salary or pension and recover the amounts already paid. I had relied on those payments, especially for retirement and family expenses, and I believe it is unfair for the authorities to change their position after many years and recover money from us when the issue arose from their own circulars and decisions.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners challenged the reduction of salaries and pensions and the recovery of alleged overpayments after they had received three increments for several years under PA Circular 06/2006(VII). The Court held that the relevant circulars lacked clarity, that the respondents failed to justify the legal basis for recovering amounts paid from 2008 to 2012, and that the delay and arbitrary withdrawal of the increments violated the petitioners' right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioners' fundamental rights under Article 12(1) were infringed, declared the decisions to recover the increments null and void, directed that those decisions be cancelled forthwith, refrained from awarding compensation because interim relief had restrained deductions, allowed both applications, and ordered parties to bear their own costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear Article 12(1) salary and pension recovery violation case involving government salary and pension authorities. Useful for testing public employment benefit reduction, legitimate expectation, delay, and arbitrary administrative action. final_answer:
SECTION 1 — RIGHTS ASSESSMENT:
Based on the structured reasoning chain, the following article(s) appear to remain supported as potentially violated:
- Article 12(1): The facts describe a situation where state authorities, after years of providing enhanced salaries and pensions based on their own circular, suddenly declared these payments erroneous and moved to reduce benefits and recover past payments. This sudden reversal and recovery of funds due to an administrative error originating with the authorities, after a long period of reliance by the petitioner, appears to constitute an arbitrary or unfair exercise of state power. cases.case_name:
F. A. Azeez v. H. M. Gunasekera, Secretary, Ministry of Education & Higher
Education and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, appointed in 1999 to the Sri Lanka Education Administrative Service Class III, challenged the 2009 cancellation of her appointment and the State's attempt to recover approximately Rs. 1.9 million as alleged overpaid salary. The Respondents relied on a prior Supreme Court judgment invalidating the recruitment batch due to non-compliance with the national ethnic ratio requirement, asserting that the appointment was void ab initio. The Petitioner invoked Article 12(1), alleging arbitrary deprivation of employment benefits after years of service. The Supreme Court held that the cancellation was not arbitrary but a necessary consequence of compliance with a binding judicial determination affecting the entire recruitment scheme. However, it found that the Petitioner had acted in good faith and performed duties for a decade without knowledge of illegality. The Court accepted that although the matter arose long prior, filing before the Human Rights Commission activated statutory protection under Section 13(1) regarding limitation. While upholding the cancellation, the Court exercised equitable jurisdiction to prevent recovery of salaries already paid, considering it unjust to penalise the Petitioner for administrative error not attributable to her. Accordingly, the application was dismissed with partial relief.

cases.case_name:
Padma Maithrilatha Akarawita and Others v. Dr. Nanda Wickramasinghe and
Others (Supra Grade Librarians Case)
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Supra Grade Librarians in the public service, challenged the salary structure introduced through Public Administration Circular No. 6/2006 revising public service salaries. They contended that Supra Grade Librarians had historically enjoyed salary parity with officers in the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Class II Grade II and alleged that the revised circular created discrimination by granting SLAS officers a more favourable salary conversion. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) of the Constitution, asserting unequal treatment and arbitrary discrimination. The Court examined whether the Petitioners and SLAS officers constituted similarly situated categories capable of comparison for constitutional equality purposes. It held that the two services belonged to entirely distinct categories within the public service and therefore could not automatically be treated as equals for salary determination. The Court further considered evidence demonstrating that, following recommendations by the National Salaries and Cadre Commission, the Petitioners had in fact been placed on a salary step enabling them to draw higher remuneration than the SLAS officers with whom they compared themselves. In light of this evidence, the Court found no actual financial disadvantage or discriminatory treatment suffered by the Petitioners. It further held that the salary revisions formed part of a broader policy decision concerning restructuring of the public service and that there was no evidence of arbitrariness or irrationality in the implementation of the circular. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Wasantha Dissanayake and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public
Administration
cases.summary: The petitioners, officers of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged Cabinet decisions granting retrospective promotions to another group of officers, arguing that such backdating adversely affected their seniority and career progression. The respondents justified the decision as part of a broader policy to correct historical administrative anomalies and recruitment delays. The Supreme Court held that seniority within public service is not an absolute vested right and may be adjusted through lawful policy decisions aimed at administrative reform. It found that the affected officers constituted a distinct category appointed under different recruitment schemes, thereby justifying differential treatment. The Court further held that the executive enjoys broad discretion in restructuring public services, provided decisions are not arbitrary or mala fide. It concluded that the policy was rationally connected to legitimate administrative objectives and did not amount to discriminatory treatment under Article 12(1). The Court emphasized that equality does not prohibit reasonable classification based on different service conditions or recruitment frameworks. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, reaffirming judicial restraint in reviewing complex administrative restructuring decisions.

cases.case_name:
Abdul Razak Mohamed Hussain v. M.M.N.D. Bandara, Secretary, Ministry of
Education and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a retired Principal of a Government School, challenged the calculation of his pension and salary-related benefits under Public Administration Circular No. 9/2004, which introduced a revised salary structure for public officers. The dispute concerned whether the Petitioner fell within Clause 10.1, applicable to pensioners retiring on or before December 1, 2004, or Clause 10.2, applicable to officers who worked on December 1, 2004 and retired thereafter. The Petitioner argued that because he had worked on his final day of service, he should receive the more advantageous benefits available under Clause 10.2. The Respondents maintained that the Petitioner's retirement legally took effect on December 1, 2004 and therefore fell squarely within Clause 10.1. The Court relied on prior judicial precedent establishing that where an officer's retirement becomes effective from a specified date, the officer is deemed to have retired on that date itself. Applying this interpretation, the Court held that the Petitioner retired on December 1, 2004 and therefore did not qualify for benefits reserved for officers retiring after that date. The Court further emphasized the necessity of strictly construing the language of administrative circulars governing pension entitlements and held that the Petitioner had received all benefits applicable to his proper category. Since the classification was based on objective criteria applicable uniformly to all similarly situated officers, the Court found no arbitrariness or unequal treatment. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

Here is an analysis of each case based on the provided materials:

**Case 1: F. A. Azeez v. H. M. Gunasekera, Secretary, Ministry of Education & Higher Education and Others (SC/FR/06/2011) [2011]**

1.  **KEY SIMILAR FACTS**:
    *   The current situation involves authorities stating that salary/pension increments were given by mistake and moving to recover alleged overpayments after several years of receipt.
    *   In F. A. Azeez, the State sought to recover alleged overpaid salary (approximately Rs. 1.9 million) after the Petitioner's appointment was cancelled a decade later, with the error (non-compliance with ethnic ratio) not attributable to the Petitioner. The Petitioner had acted in good faith and performed duties for a decade.

2.  **COURT DECISION**:
    *   NOT_VIOLATED.
    *   The Court upheld the cancellation of the appointment but exercised equitable jurisdiction to prevent the recovery of salaries already paid.

3.  **RATIO DECIDENDI**:
    *   The cancellation of the appointment was deemed a necessary consequence of complying with a binding judicial determination, not an arbitrary act.
    *   However, the Court found it unjust to penalise the Petitioner by recovering salaries already paid, given that she had acted in good faith, performed duties for a decade, and the error was an administrative one not attributable to her.

4.  **RELEVANCE TO CURRENT SITUATION**:
    *   This case suggests that while authorities might have a basis to correct an administrative error that led to "erroneous" payments (similar to the cancellation of the appointment), a court might be inclined to prevent the recovery of amounts already paid. This could apply if the recipients of the increments acted in good faith, the error originated from the administration's own circulars or decisions, and the payments were received for several years. The exercise of equitable jurisdiction to prevent recovery appears to be a significant precedent.

Based on the structured reasoning chain, the following article(s) appear to remain supported as potentially violated:
- Article 12(1): The facts describe a situation where state authorities, after years of providing enhanced salaries and pensions based on their own circular, suddenly declared these payments erroneous and moved to reduce benefits and recover past payments. This sudden reversal and recovery of funds due to an administrative error originating with the authorities, after a long period of reliance by the petitioner, appears to constitute an arbitrary or unfair exercise of state power. The principle that public authorities must act fairly and consistently, and that recovering payments made due to their own administrative errors, especially after reliance, would be arbitrary and unjust, aligns with the concept of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1). The case of F. A. Azeez v. H. M. Gunasekera, while not explicitly finding a 12(1) violation for the recovery, exercised equitable jurisdiction to prevent such recovery, emphasizing that it would be unjust to penalize a petitioner for an administrative error not attributable to them, and that public authorities should not act arbitrarily.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of association
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of association. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of association.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

intake.incident_location: Sir John Kothalawala Maha Vidyalaya, Kurunegala
intake.actor_name: Sir John Kothalawala Maha Vidyalaya, Kurunegala
intake.what_happened: I was a Grade 11 student at a public school. My class teacher suspected me of being involved in a petition against her and often harassed me. One day before a term test, another teacher took me to her, and instead of only advising me about my haircut, she became angry and hit me hard on the head. I was sent to sit for the exam but left because of the pain. My father took me to hospital, where I was treated for an injury to my ear. When we complained to the principal, he did not conduct a proper and independent inquiry.
intake.harm_suffered: Physical assault at school, perforated left ear drum, temporary impairment of hearing, hospital treatment, pain, distress, and denial of a proper school-level inquiry.
intake.user_narrative: I am a Grade 11 student at a public school in Kurunegala. My English teacher had been treating me badly because she suspected that I had complained about her. On the day of a term test, another teacher stopped me and took me to her about my haircut. She became angry and hit me hard on the side of my head. I tried to sit for the exam but I was in too much pain and went home. My father took me to hospital, and doctors found that my ear drum had been injured. We complained to the principal, but he did not properly investigate what happened and seemed to protect the teacher.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the 1st respondent, a teacher at a public school acting under colour of office, assaulted the 1st petitioner student and caused a traumatic perforation of the left ear drum with temporary impairment of hearing. The Court found that the assault amounted to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment and infringed Article 11. The Court also held that the 2nd respondent principal failed to conduct an impartial and comprehensive inquiry and acted to shield the teacher, thereby depriving the petitioners of equal protection of the law under Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The application was allowed. The Court declared that the 1st respondent infringed the 1st petitioner's Article 11 right and that the 2nd respondent infringed the 1st and 2nd petitioners' Article 12(1) rights. No heavy compensation was imposed because the 1st respondent had been in remand custody for seven months and had complied with a Court of Appeal compensation order. The petitioners were entitled to recover costs from the 1st respondent. The Secretary to the Ministry of Education was directed to issue a circular within nine months stating zero tolerance for physical or psychological harm to children as punishment, with the Attorney General to advise, and copies of the judgment were to be sent to the Attorney General and the Secretary to the Ministry of Education.

cases.case_name: Bandara v Wickremasinghe
cases.summary: The petitioner, a minor studying at Sri Subhuthi Vidyalaya, was summoned to the principal's office where he was assaulted by the Principal, Deputy Principal, Vice Principal, and a teacher. The assault included slapping and repeated blows with a cane, causing injuries to the petitioner's ear and face. The respondents claimed that the incident either constituted lawful disciplinary action or was a private act arising from tensions created by the petitioner's father regarding matters connected to a school sports meet. The petitioner alleged that the conduct violated Article 11 of the Constitution prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and awarded compensation and costs against both the State and the individual respondents. The Court rejected the argument that the assault was a private act and held that the respondents, being public officers acting during school hours within the school environment, were engaged in executive or administrative action. Although school authorities possess disciplinary powers, the Court held that savage corporal punishment causing physical injury exceeded the limits of reasonable chastisement and amounted to unconstitutional treatment prohibited by Article 11. The Court relied on medical evidence confirming injuries consistent with the allegations and emphasized the personal responsibility of educators to avoid abuse of authority while exercising disciplinary functions within public educational institutions.

cases.case_name:
Mahapitiya Gedera Shanuka Gihan Karunaratne and Another v. Lory Koswatte
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, two schoolchildren, alleged that they were subjected to severe corporal punishment by the Deputy Principal after being wrongly accused of damaging school property. They were caned repeatedly, resulting in physical injuries and psychological trauma confirmed by medical evidence. They invoked Article 11 and Article 12(1), alleging cruel treatment and unequal protection of the law. The Supreme Court held that the conduct amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of constitutional guarantees. It further found that the Respondent acted in breach of Ministry of Education circulars prohibiting corporal punishment, and that such unlawful exercise of authority constituted arbitrary treatment under Article 12(1). The Court rejected the justification of disciplinary necessity, holding that teachers act under colour of office and remain subject to constitutional constraints. It also held that the State bears vicarious liability where there is a sufficient nexus between official duties and abusive conduct. Emphasising the heightened protection owed to children under domestic and international standards including the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Court declared that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name: Sudath and Others v. E.P.T.K. Ekanayake and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Sudath and Others v. E.P.T.K. Ekanayake and Others alleged that following objections raised by the first petitioner regarding a school administrative appointment, his two children were subjected to harassment and assault by a teacher and school staff, and that the school authorities failed to take adequate action. They contended that this inaction forced the children to leave the school and constituted a violation of Article 12(1). The respondents demonstrated that prompt disciplinary measures were taken, including removal of the teacher from classroom duties, initiation of formal disciplinary proceedings, salary increment delays, and punitive transfer following findings of misconduct. An alternative school placement was also offered by education authorities. The Supreme Court examined whether there was arbitrary state inaction or discriminatory failure to protect the petitioners. It held that the authorities had acted with due diligence and that multiple corrective measures were taken in response to complaints. The Court further found that the alternative school offered was of comparable status and that the petitioners' refusal to accept it undermined the allegation of denial of educational access. It concluded that allegations of assault were not substantiated by independent evidence such as medical or police records. Accordingly, the Court held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: Wijayasiriwardene v. Kumara, Inspector of Police, Kandy and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a sixteen-year-old student, was involved in a student demonstration during a period of civil unrest and was apprehended by police while attempting to join the gathering. He alleged that he was assaulted, resulting in injuries, including a slit lip and cheek injury. The respondent officer admitted to using a single blow but justified it as necessary to effect arrest in a volatile situation. The case involved Article 11 concerning freedom from torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Supreme Court assessed whether the use of force met the constitutional threshold of severity required to constitute Article 11 violation. It held that while police use of force must be reasonable and proportionate, not all instances of physical force amount to constitutional torture or degrading treatment. It found that the circumstances justified limited force in a chaotic environment and that there was no evidence of intentional humiliation or brutality. The Court concluded that although the force might have been excessive in a technical sense, it did not reach the constitutional standard of inhuman or degrading treatment. Accordingly, the application was dismissed and no violation was found.

cases.case_name: Kankanige v. Senadheera and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner visited the BMICH on March 1, 2014, to purchase books and while searching for his motorbike in the parking area was confronted by police officers identified as the first to third respondents. Despite identifying himself as a medical student and producing identification documents, the officers verbally abused him, accused him of theft, and physically assaulted him. He was slapped, kicked, dragged by his hair, and suffered injuries including a perforated eardrum together with psychological trauma. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 12(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered personal compensation against each officer. The Court reasoned that Article 11 protects individuals not only from physical injury but also from psychological suffering and degrading treatment. Public humiliation, abusive language, and unjustified violence against a cooperative citizen constituted degrading and inhuman treatment prohibited by the Constitution. The Court further held that the medical evidence provided by the Judicial Medical Officer strongly corroborated the petitioner's account and rendered the respondents' explanation that the injuries resulted from a fall implausible. Emphasizing that police officers are required to exercise restraint and lawful authority, the Court concluded that the assault represented an arbitrary abuse of power incompatible with equal protection of the law and constitutional guarantees against cruel treatment.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Bandara v Wickremasinghe
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner, a minor studying at Sri Subhuthi Vidyalaya, was summoned to the principal's office where he was assaulted by the Principal, Deputy Principal, Vice Principal, and a teacher. The assault included slapping and repeated blows with a cane, causing injuries to the petitioner's ear and face. The respondents claimed that the incident either constituted lawful disciplinary action or was a private act arising from tensions created by the petitioner's father regarding matters connected to a school sports meet. The petitioner alleged that the conduct violated Article 11 of the Constitution prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. The Supreme Court held that the respondents had infringed the petitioner's fundamental rights and awarded compensation and costs against both the State and the individual respondents. The Court rejected the argument that the assault was a private act and held that the respondents, being public officers acting during school hours within the school environment, were engaged in executive or administrative action. Although school authorities possess disciplinary powers, the Court held that savage corporal punishment causing physical injury exceeded the limits of reasonable chastisement and amounted to unconstitutional treatment prohibited by Article 11. The Court relied on medical evidence confirming injuries consistent with the allegations and emphasized the personal responsibility of educators to avoid abuse of authority while exercising disciplinary functions within public educational institutions.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Mahapitiya Gedera Shanuka Gihan Karunaratne and Another v. Lory Koswatte
and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, two schoolchildren, alleged that they were subjected to severe corporal punishment by the Deputy Principal after being wrongly accused of damaging school property. They were caned repeatedly, resulting in physical injuries and psychological trauma confirmed by medical evidence. They invoked Article 11 and Article 12(1), alleging cruel treatment and unequal protection of the law. The Supreme Court held that the conduct amounted to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment in violation of constitutional guarantees. It further found that the Respondent acted in breach of Ministry of Education circulars prohibiting corporal punishment, and that such unlawful exercise of authority constituted arbitrary treatment under Article 12(1). The Court rejected the justification of disciplinary necessity, holding that teachers act under colour of office and remain subject to constitutional constraints. It also held that the State bears vicarious liability where there is a sufficient nexus between official duties and abusive conduct. Emphasising the heightened protection owed to children under domestic and international standards including the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Court declared that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered compensation.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Sudath and Others v. E.P.T.K. Ekanayake and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioners in Sudath and Others v. E.P.T.K. Ekanayake and Others alleged that following objections raised by the first petitioner regarding a school administrative appointment, his two children were subjected to harassment and assault by a teacher and school staff, and that the school authorities failed to take adequate action. They contended that this inaction forced the children to leave the school and constituted a violation of Article 12(1). The respondents demonstrated that prompt disciplinary measures were taken, including removal of the teacher from classroom duties, initiation of formal disciplinary proceedings, salary increment delays, and punitive transfer following findings of misconduct. An alternative school placement was also offered by education authorities. The Supreme Court examined whether there was arbitrary state inaction or discriminatory failure to protect the petitioners. It held that the authorities had acted with due diligence and that multiple corrective measures were taken in response to complaints. The Court further found that the alternative school offered was of comparable status and that the petitioners' refusal to accept it undermined the allegation of denial of educational access. It concluded that allegations of assault were not substantiated by independent evidence such as medical or police records. Accordingly, the Court held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established and dismissed the application.
