cases.case_name:
W.K.B. Seneviratne and 5 Others v. Justice P.R.P. Perera, Chairman, Public
Service Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Class II Jailors in the Department of Prisons, challenged the promotion of the 15th to 23rd Respondents to the rank of Class I Jailors. The promotions were conducted under a 2004 marking scheme allocating marks for seniority, experience, performance, and presentation at an interview. The Petitioners alleged that the promotions violated Article 12(1) because several selected officers were junior to them in service and because the marking scheme introduced subjectivity. They also contended that an inquiry was pending against the 17th Respondent, making that promotion improper. The Respondents maintained that the governing recruitment scheme lawfully permitted promotions based on both seniority and merit. The Court held that seniority alone was not the exclusive criterion in public service promotions and that the applicable recruitment framework authorized the consideration of efficiency and performance. Although the Court acknowledged that interview presentation marks introduced some degree of subjectivity, it found this acceptable because such marks represented only a limited portion of the total evaluation and were assessed by a balanced panel. The Court further determined that the Petitioners had failed to provide any specific evidence regarding the alleged inquiry against the 17th Respondent. The Supreme Court concluded that the marking scheme constituted an objective method of appraisal ensuring fairness among eligible candidates and held that the Petitioners failed to establish any infringement of the right to equality and equal protection of the law.

cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name: W.S. Nissanka and Others v. Inspector General of Police and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, police officers and unsuccessful candidates for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police, challenged a complex series of promotional decisions arising from inconsistent use of two different examination mark sheets (raw and converted scores). Over time, conflicting administrative actions resulted in multiple competing promotions far exceeding the original vacancies. The Petitioners specifically challenged the promotion of officers with lower raw scores based on converted marks. The Supreme Court considered Article 12(1) and held that although the system was irregular, the impugned decision could not be struck down due to limitation under Article 126(2), as the underlying mark-sheet structure had been publicly known for years. The Court further held that the National Police Commission's later standardisation of a minimum cut-off constituted a reasonable attempt to restore order and uniformity in a previously chaotic recruitment process. It found that once dual systems had been officially recognised, candidates were not in comparable circumstances for equality analysis. The Court also emphasised cadre limitations and administrative necessity in preventing further expansion of promotions. Accordingly, the application was dismissed and no violation was found.

cases.case_name: N.C. Gajaweera v. National Police Commission
cases.summary: The petitioners, Chief Inspectors of the Special Task Force, challenged the National Police Commission's decision to promote certain officers to Assistant Superintendent of Police without following the established competitive procedure. They alleged that senior and more qualified officers were bypassed in violation of merit-based selection and Article 12(1). The respondents argued administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that once a formal recruitment and promotion scheme with marking criteria is established, it cannot be arbitrarily abandoned. It found that appointments made through letters rather than competitive evaluation were unlawful and inconsistent with administrative fairness. The Court recognized the petitioners' legitimate expectation that promotions would be based on published criteria. It further held that failure to provide rational justification for deviation from procedure constituted arbitrariness. The Court declared the impugned appointments null and void and ordered adherence to proper selection processes. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated due to unequal and non-transparent treatment in public service recruitment.

cases.case_name: Dayaratne v National Savings Bank
cases.summary: The petitioners were employees of the National Savings Bank who applied for promotion from Grade III to Grade II of the Executive Service. Following an interview-based selection process conducted in 2001, forty-one officers were promoted, including several candidates junior to the petitioners. The petitioners challenged the promotions under Article 12(1) of the Constitution, alleging that the interview procedure was arbitrary, rushed, and manipulated. Evidence before the Court showed that interviews lasted only a few minutes and that assessment marks had been altered or overwritten without explanation. The petitioners further argued that certain promoted officers received evaluation scores inconsistent with their actual service records. The respondents raised a preliminary objection that the petition was time-barred, contending that the challenge should have been filed from the date of interview. The Supreme Court rejected this objection, holding that the relevant time period commenced when the promotions were officially announced. Examining the merits, the Court concluded that the interview process lacked transparency and fairness, making it impossible to properly evaluate the candidates' suitability. Although seniority alone did not guarantee promotion, the Court emphasized that departures from seniority required a rational and merit-based justification supported by a valid process. The arbitrary conduct of the interviews and unexplained alterations to marks constituted unequal treatment and violated the petitioners' right to equal protection of the law under Article 12(1). The Court therefore quashed the promotions of fourteen junior officers and directed that a fresh selection process be conducted for all eligible candidates.

article_assessments.reason: The alleged irregularities in the competitive examination and promotion process, including potential leakage of question papers or marking schemes, improper marking, and the promotion of a candidate with marks below the pass mark while others with equal or higher marks were denied promotion, appear to directly implicate the right to equality before the law and equal protection. Based on the materials provided, precedent cases with highly similar facts involving arbitrary and unfair public service examination and promotion processes have consistently found violations of Article 12(1).

While the denial of promotion could impact career progression, the core alleged infringement appears to be about the fairness and equality of the promotion process rather than the fundamental freedom to engage in an occupation itself. The provided precedent cases, which are factually similar regarding examination irregularities and denial of promotion, primarily focus on violations of Article 12(1) and do not explicitly analyze or support a claim under Article 14(1)(g) in this specific context. Therefore, its applicability appears weak or uncertain based on the materials provided.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment under existing written law
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment under existing written law. The subjection of any person on the order of a competent court to any form of punishment recognized by any existing written law shall not be a contravention of the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
W.K.B. Seneviratne and 5 Others v. Justice P.R.P. Perera, Chairman, Public
Service Commission and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Class II Jailors in the Department of Prisons, challenged the promotion of the 15th to 23rd Respondents to the rank of Class I Jailors. The promotions were conducted under a 2004 marking scheme allocating marks for seniority, experience, performance, and presentation at an interview. The Petitioners alleged that the promotions violated Article 12(1) because several selected officers were junior to them in service and because the marking scheme introduced subjectivity. They also contended that an inquiry was pending against the 17th Respondent, making that promotion improper. The Respondents maintained that the governing recruitment scheme lawfully permitted promotions based on both seniority and merit. The Court held that seniority alone was not the exclusive criterion in public service promotions and that the applicable recruitment framework authorized the consideration of efficiency and performance. Although the Court acknowledged that interview presentation marks introduced some degree of subjectivity, it found this acceptable because such marks represented only a limited portion of the total evaluation and were assessed by a balanced panel. The Court further determined that the Petitioners had failed to provide any specific evidence regarding the alleged inquiry against the 17th Respondent. The Supreme Court concluded that the marking scheme constituted an objective method of appraisal ensuring fairness among eligible candidates and held that the Petitioners failed to establish any infringement of the right to equality and equal protection of the law.

retrieved_cases.case_name: W.S. Nissanka and Others v. Inspector General of Police and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioners, police officers and unsuccessful candidates for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police, challenged a complex series of promotional decisions arising from inconsistent use of two different examination mark sheets (raw and converted scores). Over time, conflicting administrative actions resulted in multiple competing promotions far exceeding the original vacancies. The Petitioners specifically challenged the promotion of officers with lower raw scores based on converted marks. The Supreme Court considered Article 12(1) and held that although the system was irregular, the impugned decision could not be struck down due to limitation under Article 126(2), as the underlying mark-sheet structure had been publicly known for years. The Court further held that the National Police Commission's later standardisation of a minimum cut-off constituted a reasonable attempt to restore order and uniformity in a previously chaotic recruitment process. It found that once dual systems had been officially recognised, candidates were not in comparable circumstances for equality analysis. The Court also emphasised cadre limitations and administrative necessity in preventing further expansion of promotions. Accordingly, the application was dismissed and no violation was found.

intake.incident_location: Galapallahena land in Hindurangala Grama Niladhari division and Kiriella Police Station
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Kiriella Police Station
intake.what_happened: I am a police officer. My wife owns a land where some villagers had built a shrine without proper authority, and there had already been disputes about that land. When I went there with others to conduct a Bhairava Poojawa, villagers accused us of trying to excavate antiquities and assaulted us. Police from Kiriella arrived, took us to the police station, put us in a cell, refused to properly record my complaint against the villagers, and produced us in court under the Antiquities Ordinance even though I say we were not excavating and the land was outside the Kiriella Police area.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, police detention, remand custody, criminal proceedings under the Antiquities Ordinance, reputational damage, adverse publicity, career impact, and failure to properly investigate the assault complaint against the villagers.
intake.user_narrative: I am an Inspector of Police. My wife owns land in the Kiriella area, but there has been a dispute with villagers who had built a shrine on part of the land. We had earlier objected to further unauthorized construction. One day I went to the land with others to conduct a Bhairava Poojawa. Villagers accused us of searching for treasure, verbally abused and assaulted us, and called the police. I also called the police because the situation was getting dangerous. Officers from the Kiriella Police Station came, but instead of properly protecting us or recording my complaint, they took us to the police station, placed us in a cell and later produced us in court for allegedly trying to excavate antiquities. I believe the officer-in-charge acted unfairly and maliciously because he already knew about the land dispute and the area was not even under his police division.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that although a Bhairava Poojawa may in some circumstances give rise to suspicion of treasure excavation, the surrounding facts showed that the 1st respondent acted maliciously and unlawfully. The 1st respondent knew of the prior land dispute, knew the incident was outside his police area, failed to place the petitioner's version and summary of statements before the Magistrate, and widely reported the petitioner's arrest to superior officers but did not similarly report his discharge. The Court found that the 1st respondent infringed Article 13(1), and that this also resulted in infringement of Article 12(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The 1st respondent had died pending determination, so no compensation was awarded against him. The Court directed the State to pay the petitioner Rs. 50,000 as compensation and Rs. 25,000 as costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Police unlawful arrest and equal protection case arising from an alleged Antiquities Ordinance offence and a private land dispute. Useful for testing cases where some initial suspicion exists but the final finding turns on malicious and unlawful police action. No internal corpus case ID was provided, so source_case_id is null and gold_relevant_case_ids is empty.

final_answer:
SECTION 1 — RIGHTS ASSESSMENT:
Based on the structured reasoning chain, the following article(s) appear to remain supported as potentially violated:
- Article 13(1): The user's account suggests a potential arbitrary arrest, as police officers reportedly took them to the station, placed them in a cell, and produced them in court for allegedly trying to excavate antiquities, while allegedly refusing to record the user's complaint. This sequence of events, especially with the user's belief of malicious intent by the officer-in-charge, aligns with the concept of arrest without reasonable suspicion or proper legal basis. Precedent cases like Bandula Samarasekera v. Vijitha Alwis and S.M.D. Bandara v. OIC, Police Station, Kandy found violations of Article 13(1) where arrests were made without reasonable suspicion.
- Article 13(2): The user was reportedly taken to the police station, placed in a cell, and 'later produced us in court.' This suggests a period of detention and subsequent production. The precedent cases, Bandula Samarasekera v. Vijitha Alwis and S.M.D. Bandara v. OIC, Police Station, Kandy, found violations of Article 13(2) for failures to inform the arrested person of the reason for arrest and/or failure to produce them before a judge promptly. The facts provided suggest a potential failure in adhering to the procedural safeguards required under Article 13(2) following an arrest.

Weak or uncertain article(s):
- Article 12(1): The user believes the officer-in-charge acted unfairly and maliciously, knowing about a land dispute and operating outside his police division, and that the police 'instead of properly protecting us or recording my complaint, they took us to the police station.' This suggests a potential for unequal treatment or discrimination in the application of the law, particularly in the alleged refusal to record the user's complaint while acting on the villagers' accusations. However, the selected precedent cases primarily focus on arbitrary arrest and detention (Article 13) and do not directly address Article 12(1) in the context of police bias or failure to record complaints under similar circumstances, making the support for this article less direct and more fact-dependent.
- Article 11: The facts describe the user being verbally abused and assaulted by villagers, and subsequently taken to the police station and placed in a cell by police officers. However, there is no information provided in the user narrative or extracted facts to suggest that the police officers themselves subjected the user to torture or cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment. Being placed in a cell, while a deprivation of liberty, does not, by itself, constitute torture under Article 11 without further specific allegations of such treatment by state actors. No-Step-9 Fix 2 guard converted rejection to weak_or_uncertain because selected negative precedent was not article-specific.

SECTION 2 — PRECEDENT:
The precedent alignment was classified as: supports.

SECTION 3 — STRENGTHS OF THE CASE:

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of access to public places and worship

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court

cases.case_name: Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

cases.case_name:
Ven. Aturupalayagama Pragna Surinda Thero and Another v. Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station, Minneriya and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

cases.case_name: Bandula Samarasekera v. Vijitha Alwis, OIC Ginigathhena and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a former employee of Brown and Company, was returning from an exorcism ritual performed for his son on February 28, 2007 when his vehicle encountered that of the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Ginigathhena Police Station, on a narrow road. Following a dispute over reversing the vehicles, the 1st Respondent assaulted the Petitioner and accused him of being a treasure hunter after observing ritual items inside the jeep. The Petitioner was arrested, transported to Kandy Police Station while bleeding and injured, and detained for approximately eighteen hours before being produced before a Magistrate, who observed that no offence appeared to have been committed. Medical evidence established grievous injuries including a fractured nasal bone and perforated ear drum caused by a blunt weapon. The Respondents attempted to justify the arrest by alleging treasure hunting activities and claimed the injuries were caused by a crowd. The Court rejected these explanations after the Archaeological Department confirmed that the location possessed no archaeological significance. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion and that detention for eighteen hours without promptly recording a statement or producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate was arbitrary. The Court further ruled that the severe assault constituted cruel and degrading treatment contrary to Article 11. The Supreme Court found violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), ordered compensation against the 1st Respondent and the State, and condemned the use of barbarous police methods undermining public confidence.

cases.case_name:
Hondamuni Chandima Samanmalee de Zoysa Siriwardena and Another v.
Inspector Malaweera and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, two Attorneys-at-Law, visited Ambalangoda Police Station on February 28, 2010, to represent a client whose relatives had allegedly been detained in connection with a child custody dispute following the death of the child's mother. The Petitioners alleged that the police had summoned the grieving family to the station and thereby prevented them from attending funeral arrangements. At the police station, the 1st and 2nd Respondents verbally abused the Petitioners, accused lawyers of earning money unfairly, threatened to arrest them for providing "wrong advice," and ordered them to switch off their mobile phones while coercing the family to surrender the child to the estranged father. The Petitioners contended that these acts violated Articles 11, 12(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court held that Article 11 protects against severe mental suffering intentionally inflicted by public officials and that humiliating and threatening legal practitioners in front of a bereaved family amounted to degrading treatment. The Court further held that lawyers possess a constitutional right to represent clients and that intimidation aimed at obstructing legal representation violated the freedom to engage in a lawful profession guaranteed by Article 14(1)(g). The Court rejected any justification for the conduct of the officers and observed that the Petitioners had acted professionally while the Respondents acted under colour of office in an arbitrary and abusive manner. Accordingly, the Court found violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 14(1)(g) and ordered the Respondents to personally pay compensation and litigation costs to the Petitioners.

cases.case_name:
Hettiarachchige Srimathi Devika Tissera and Others v. Police Constable
Jayasekara and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Hettiarachchige Srimathi Devika Tissera and Others v. Police Constable Jayasekara and Others arose from an incident on Christmas Eve 2012 in Ja-Ela where a family dispute over a parked vehicle escalated into police intervention. The petitioners alleged that police officers verbally abused them, forcibly removed the daughter from the vehicle, and assaulted the minor son. They were taken to the police station and detained for several hours without explanation, effectively amounting to an unlawful deprivation of liberty, and were later formally arrested and remanded on allegations of assaulting police officers. A Special Investigations Unit later found procedural irregularities, including false entries in official records and misconduct by the officer-in-charge. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1) and 13(1), alleging unequal treatment and arbitrary arrest. The Court held that keeping individuals confined at a police station without lawful justification constituted an implicit arrest, even in the absence of formal declaration. It further found that failure to inform the petitioners of reasons for arrest at the earliest opportunity violated mandatory procedural safeguards under Article 13(1). The Court also found the arrest to be arbitrary and supported by falsified documentation, rendering the State action unconstitutional. Accordingly, the Court held that Article 13(1) had been violated, affirmed the infringement of personal liberty, and awarded compensation against both the responsible officers and the State for unlawful arrest and detention.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Bandula Samarasekera v. Vijitha Alwis, OIC Ginigathhena and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a former employee of Brown and Company, was returning from an exorcism ritual performed for his son on February 28, 2007 when his vehicle encountered that of the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Ginigathhena Police Station, on a narrow road. Following a dispute over reversing the vehicles, the 1st Respondent assaulted the Petitioner and accused him of being a treasure hunter after observing ritual items inside the jeep. The Petitioner was arrested, transported to Kandy Police Station while bleeding and injured, and detained for approximately eighteen hours before being produced before a Magistrate, who observed that no offence appeared to have been committed. Medical evidence established grievous injuries including a fractured nasal bone and perforated ear drum caused by a blunt weapon. The Respondents attempted to justify the arrest by alleging treasure hunting activities and claimed the injuries were caused by a crowd. The Court rejected these explanations after the Archaeological Department confirmed that the location possessed no archaeological significance. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion and that detention for eighteen hours without promptly recording a statement or producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate was arbitrary. The Court further ruled that the severe assault constituted cruel and degrading treatment contrary to Article 11. The Supreme Court found violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), ordered compensation against the 1st Respondent and the State, and condemned the use of barbarous police methods undermining public confidence.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

The Petitioner, a former employee of Brown and Company, was returning from an exorcism ritual performed for his son on February 28, 2007 when his vehicle encountered that of the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Ginigathhena Police Station, on a narrow road. Following a dispute over reversing the vehicles, the 1st Respondent assaulted the Petitioner and accused him of being a treasure hunter after observing ritual items inside the jeep. The Petitioner was arrested, transported to Kandy Police Station while bleeding and injured, and detained for approximately eighteen hours before being produced before a Magistrate, who observed that no offence appeared to have been committed. Medical evidence established grievous injuries including a fractured nasal bone and perforated ear drum caused by a blunt weapon. The Respondents attempted to justify the arrest by alleging treasure hunting activities and claimed the injuries were caused by a crowd. The Court rejected these explanations after the Archaeological Department confirmed that the location possessed no archaeological significance. The Court held that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion and that detention for eighteen hours without promptly recording a statement or producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate was arbitrary. The Court further ruled that the severe assault constituted cruel and degrading treatment contrary to Article 11. The Supreme Court found violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), ordered compensation against the 1st Respondent and the State, and condemned the use of barbarous police methods undermining public confidence.

The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

cases.case_name:
Chaminda Sampath Kumara Wickremapathirana v. Sub Inspector Salwatura and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a labourer, was arrested on May 20, 2009, by police officers while returning home carrying chicken meat. Police officers searched his residence without a warrant and seized pawning receipts belonging to third parties. He was detained at the Bandaragama Police Station for seven days before being produced before a Magistrate. During custody, the Petitioner was stripped, beaten with clubs and hose pipes, and forced to consume bird's eye chilies. Crushed chilies were also poured into his eyes and nose while he was restrained in painful positions. The Officer-in-Charge later falsely recorded the date of arrest as May 26 in an attempt to conceal the unlawful delay in producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate. The Petitioner was eventually acquitted of theft charges because of absence of evidence. Alleging violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), the Petitioner challenged the conduct of the Respondents. The Supreme Court accepted the Petitioner's testimony and observed that methods such as the use of chilies and hose pipes are specifically intended to inflict suffering while minimizing visible physical marks. Hospital records corroborated injuries to the wrists and ankles consistent with suspension and assault. The Court held that the torture inflicted caused both physical and enduring psychological harm and that the Officer-in-Charge bore responsibility for permitting the police station to be used for unlawful acts. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's constitutional rights had been violated and awarded compensation against both the officers and the State.

cases.case_name: CH.A. Manoj Talis v. Inspector Hiriyadeniya and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested at his residence on September 24, 2005, by several police officers without being informed of the reasons for the arrest. He was thereafter taken to the Gokarella Police Station where he was subjected to severe physical and sexual torture. The officers assaulted him, struck him on the face and ears, and suspended him in a squatting position by passing an iron bar through his tied hands and legs. During the assault, a PVC pipe was inserted through the Petitioner's rectum. Medical reports produced before Court confirmed a ruptured eardrum and injuries consistent with the Petitioner's account of torture. Prior to the fundamental rights proceedings, the High Court had convicted several of the Respondents under the Convention Against Torture Act for the same conduct. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the failure of the officers to provide any lawful reason for the arrest rendered both the arrest and subsequent detention illegal. The Court further treated the medical reports and prior criminal convictions as compelling corroborative evidence establishing the occurrence of brutal torture and sexual abuse while in police custody. Given the gravity of the misconduct, the Court directed the responsible officers to pay compensation personally rather than through the State. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights guaranteed under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2).

cases.case_name:
Herath Mudiyanselage Podi Kumarihami v. Officer-in-Charge, Mahiyanganaya
Police Station and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Podi Kumarihami v. Officer-in-Charge, Mahiyanganaya Police Station and Others arose from an incident on 17 August 2017 during the arrest of the petitioner's daughter by police officers. The petitioner alleged that she intervened and was subjected to severe assault including slapping, kicking, trampling, and threats of being shot, resulting in humiliation and physical harm. The respondents contended that she obstructed a lawful arrest and sustained no assault, claiming any injury was self-inflicted during resistance. Medical evidence from Kandy Teaching Hospital recorded no injuries, with scans and X-rays showing normal results. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 12(1). The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture require proof to a high degree of probability supported by credible medical evidence. It found the absence of injuries in medical reports inconsistent with the alleged severe assault. The Court also considered inconsistencies in witness statements and noted that the petitioner sought legal advice before medical treatment, which undermined her account of severe trauma. It further observed that internal police inquiries had been conducted into the complaint. Accordingly, the Court held that the petitioner failed to establish any constitutional violation and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name: Roshan Mahesh Ukwatta v Sub Inspector Marasinghe and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner was arrested at his residence on 22 February 2006 by officers attached to the Welikada Police Station. While in police custody he was subjected to severe torture. His hands and legs were tied together, an iron rod was inserted between his elbows and knees, and he was suspended and beaten with batons and poles. He was produced before a Magistrate only on 28 February 2006, six days after the arrest. Medical evidence confirmed nineteen injuries including a fractured jaw, a perforated eardrum, and a dislocated joint. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(2) of the Constitution. The respondents denied the allegations and claimed that the petitioner had been arrested on 27 February 2006 and injured after falling from a wall. The Supreme Court rejected the police version and found that official records had been falsified. A complaint made to the Human Rights Commission on 24 February established that the petitioner had already been detained by that date. The Court further held that the severity of the injuries was inconsistent with the explanation offered by the police. The 2nd respondent, as Officer-in-Charge, was found liable for culpable inaction and complicity because he failed to supervise subordinates and facilitated falsification of official records. The Court declared that Articles 11 and 13(2) had been violated and awarded compensation and costs against the State.

cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
Chaminda Sampath Kumara Wickremapathirana v. Sub Inspector Salwatura and
Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a labourer, was arrested on May 20, 2009, by police officers while returning home carrying chicken meat. Police officers searched his residence without a warrant and seized pawning receipts belonging to third parties. He was detained at the Bandaragama Police Station for seven days before being produced before a Magistrate. During custody, the Petitioner was stripped, beaten with clubs and hose pipes, and forced to consume bird's eye chilies. Crushed chilies were also poured into his eyes and nose while he was restrained in painful positions. The Officer-in-Charge later falsely recorded the date of arrest as May 26 in an attempt to conceal the unlawful delay in producing the Petitioner before a Magistrate. The Petitioner was eventually acquitted of theft charges because of absence of evidence. Alleging violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2), the Petitioner challenged the conduct of the Respondents. The Supreme Court accepted the Petitioner's testimony and observed that methods such as the use of chilies and hose pipes are specifically intended to inflict suffering while minimizing visible physical marks. Hospital records corroborated injuries to the wrists and ankles consistent with suspension and assault. The Court held that the torture inflicted caused both physical and enduring psychological harm and that the Officer-in-Charge bore responsibility for permitting the police station to be used for unlawful acts. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's constitutional rights had been violated and awarded compensation against both the officers and the State.

retrieved_cases.case_name: CH.A. Manoj Talis v. Inspector Hiriyadeniya and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested at his residence on September 24, 2005, by several police officers without being informed of the reasons for the arrest. He was thereafter taken to the Gokarella Police Station where he was subjected to severe physical and sexual torture. The officers assaulted him, struck him on the face and ears, and suspended him in a squatting position by passing an iron bar through his tied hands and legs. During the assault, a PVC pipe was inserted through the Petitioner's rectum. Medical reports produced before Court confirmed a ruptured eardrum and injuries consistent with the Petitioner's account of torture. Prior to the fundamental rights proceedings, the High Court had convicted several of the Respondents under the Convention Against Torture Act for the same conduct. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the failure of the officers to provide any lawful reason for the arrest rendered both the arrest and subsequent detention illegal. The Court further treated the medical reports and prior criminal convictions as compelling corroborative evidence establishing the occurrence of brutal torture and sexual abuse while in police custody. Given the gravity of the misconduct, the Court directed the responsible officers to pay compensation personally rather than through the State. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights guaranteed under Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2).

retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Podi Kumarihami v. Officer-in-Charge, Mahiyanganaya Police Station and Others arose from an incident on 17 August 2017 during the arrest of the petitioner's daughter by police officers. The petitioner alleged that she intervened and was subjected to severe assault including slapping, kicking, trampling, and threats of being shot, resulting in humiliation and physical harm. The respondents contended that she obstructed a lawful arrest and sustained no assault, claiming any injury was self-inflicted during resistance. Medical evidence from Kandy Teaching Hospital recorded no injuries, with scans and X-rays showing normal results. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11 and 12(1). The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture require proof to a high degree of probability supported by credible medical evidence. It found the absence of injuries in medical reports inconsistent with the alleged severe assault. The Court also considered inconsistencies in witness statements and noted that the petitioner sought legal advice before medical treatment, which undermined her account of severe trauma. It further observed that internal police inquiries had been conducted into the complaint. Accordingly, the Court held that the petitioner failed to establish any constitutional violation and dismissed the application.

intake.incident_location: Kottawa and Kottawa Police Station
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Kottawa Police Station
intake.what_happened: I am an omnibus operator. One night after returning home, I saw my buses parked after the day's running and encountered police officers near them. A police officer abused me, pointed a pistol at my head, threatened to kill me, and other officers assaulted me, made me kneel, beat me inside my bus while I was handcuffed, and then took me to Kottawa Police Station where I was placed in a cell. I was later produced in court on a heroin possession allegation which I deny, and I say the police failed to properly produce me before the judicial medical officer after the assault.
intake.harm_suffered: Physical assault, bleeding injuries to the face, mouth, chest, hands and legs, humiliation, arrest, detention, false or disputed heroin allegation, remand custody, failure to be properly examined by a judicial medical officer, and distress to family members who witnessed the assault.
intake.user_narrative: I operate buses between Colombo and Kottawa. One night I was returning home when I saw my two buses parked after the day's running. A police officer abused me, pointed a pistol at my head and threatened to kill me. Other officers came, slapped me, made me kneel and beat me inside my own bus while I was handcuffed. My wife, mother and others pleaded with them to stop, but they continued. I was taken to the Kottawa Police Station, assaulted again, and placed in a cell. The next day I was produced before court on a heroin possession allegation, which I completely deny. My lawyer told court about my injuries, but I was not properly taken before the judicial medical officer at first. Later a medical report recorded injuries to my face, chest, forearms and wrist. I believe the police assaulted me and then made a false drug case to cover it up.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court found that the petitioner was assaulted by police officers while handcuffed, with multiple affidavits and the second judicial medical report corroborating injuries to his face, chest, forearms and wrist. The assault by the 2nd and 3rd respondents amounted to torture or cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment under Article 11, while the other police officers bore responsibility for failing to prevent or rectify the violations. The failure to properly produce the petitioner before a judicial medical officer violated Article 12(1), and the arrest and detention without properly informing him of the reasons for arrest violated Article 13(1).
gold.gold_remedy: The Court declared that the petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 11, 12(1) and 13(1) were violated by the 1st to 6th respondents. Compensation of Rs. 1,000,000 was awarded to the petitioner, to be paid jointly by the 1st to 6th respondents from their personal funds.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear police assault, false or disputed drug-charge, failure-to-produce-before-JMO, and unlawful arrest case. Useful for testing Articles 11, 12(1) and 13(1) together, and for assessing whether the system recognizes police inaction by other officers as responsibility for constitutional violations. retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

cases.case_name:
Ediriweera Arukpatabandige Sugath Rohan Jayasuriya v. Manikkaratnam and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was brutally assaulted by three police officers near a boutique on December 29, 2007, and claimed that one officer struck his head with a firearm, causing unconsciousness. The Respondents denied the allegations and asserted that the Petitioner had been riding a motorcycle while intoxicated, ignored police orders to stop at a roadblock, and fell from the motorcycle twice while attempting to escape. Upon arrest, police officers allegedly discovered two packets of heroin in his possession. The Petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest. Medical evidence before the Court included an initial medico-legal report recording that the Petitioner himself admitted he had fallen due to drunkenness. The injuries documented, including scalp lacerations and scratches, together with the damaged condition of the motorcycle, were found consistent with a fall rather than a police assault. The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the Petitioner failed to satisfy the high standard of proof necessary to establish a violation of Article 11. The Court also noted inconsistencies in the Petitioner's subsequent claims of hearing and vision loss, which medical examinations failed to substantiate. The Court concluded that the arrest was lawful because the Petitioner was allegedly committing cognizable offences involving heroin possession and intoxicated driving. The Petitioner's credibility was further undermined by inconsistent accounts and undisclosed prior criminal convictions relating to substance abuse.

cases.case_name: M.D. Nandapala v. Sergeant Sunil and Others
cases.summary: On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

cases.case_name:
K.H.G. Kushan Indika v. Christy Leonard Ranjan Wijesekera, OIC Pitigala and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, employed as a driver for the Sri Lanka State Plantation Corporation, was waiting at a bus halt on April 2, 2007 when a police jeep arrived and the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Pitigala Police Station, questioned him. Although the Petitioner produced his driving licence as identification, the 1st Respondent assaulted him by slapping him repeatedly and compelled him to load a heavy motorbike into a truck. When the Petitioner requested assistance, the 1st Respondent assaulted him with a club several times. The Petitioner was then taken to the police station, detained in a cell for nearly two hours, and released without any statement being recorded or charges being filed. The Respondent attempted to justify the arrest on the basis of suspicious conduct. The Court held that no reasonable suspicion existed to support the arrest and clarified that a driving licence constituted valid identification. The Court determined that the public assault, forced labour, and unlawful detention subjected the Petitioner to degrading treatment within the meaning of Article 11, notwithstanding the non-grievous nature of the injuries. The Court further held that the failure to provide reasons for arrest or record a statement constituted a serious procedural lapse. The Supreme Court concluded that Articles 11 and 13(1) had been violated and directed the 1st Respondent to personally compensate the Petitioner.

cases.case_name: Sri Thaminda, Dharshane and Mahalekam v. Inspector of Police and Others
cases.summary: During a festival on August 11, 2003, the three Petitioners, who were intoxicated, became involved in a confrontation with police officers regarding the parking of a three-wheeler. A scuffle followed during which a Police Constable was injured and hospitalized. The Petitioners were arrested and later sustained multiple injuries. They alleged that police officers and members of the Rapid Deployment Force assaulted them while in custody, amounting to cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11. The Respondents contended that the injuries resulted from an angry crowd attempting to rescue the injured constable and denied responsibility for the assaults. The Supreme Court held that the arrests themselves were justified because the Petitioners had behaved aggressively and police intervention was necessary to prevent escalation of violence and maintain public order. Consequently, no violation of Article 13(1) was established. However, the Court found sufficient material to conclude that the Petitioners were assaulted by state officers acting under colour of office. The Court reaffirmed that constitutional protection against torture and cruel or degrading treatment applies irrespective of the victim's conduct. Nevertheless, the Court declined to award compensation because the Petitioners had themselves behaved in a disorderly and disgraceful manner and contributed to the circumstances leading to the incident. Declaratory relief alone was therefore granted for the infringement of Article 11.

retrieved_cases.case_name: M.D. Nandapala v. Sergeant Sunil and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: On May 24, 2006, the Petitioner's van was stopped at a police checkpoint by the 1st Respondent. Although the Petitioner produced valid documents, he was slapped and taken into custody along with other occupants at Homagama Police Station. While detained, the Petitioner was taken outside the station and assaulted by the 1st and 2nd Respondents using a hose pipe and wooden club, causing injuries to his back, abdomen, and buttocks. The 1st Respondent retained the Petitioner's driving license and later the 3rd Respondent knowingly recorded a false statement that the license had been lost in order to conceal police misconduct. The officers also falsely accused the Petitioner of possessing a knife, robbery, and attempting bribery in order to justify the arrest. The Petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 12(1), and 13(1). The Supreme Court held that there was no reasonable suspicion supporting the arrest and described the police conduct as a "voyage of discovery" intended to fabricate justification for arbitrary action. Medical evidence from hospital and medico-legal reports corroborated the Petitioner's account of custodial assault. The Court concluded that the physical abuse constituted cruel and inhuman treatment contrary to Article 11 and that the arbitrary arrest and fabricated allegations violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1). Compensation and costs were ordered against the responsible officers, with the primary wrongdoer bearing the greater share of liability.

retrieved_cases.case_name: W.N.L.K. Fernando v. Police Inspector Ranjith and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that police officers assaulted him during an investigation into a theft complaint, using excessive force including beating, dragging, and use of rifle butts. He was subsequently taken into custody and treated in a manner that caused physical illness and distress. The Respondents claimed minimal force was used during a lawful arrest due to resistance. The case involved alleged violations of Articles 11 and 13(1). The Court accepted medical evidence showing injuries consistent with assault rather than accidental force or resistance. It held that custodial violence and degrading treatment by police officers constituted a violation of Article 11, which protects individuals from cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The Court found that while the arrest itself was based on a valid investigation into theft and therefore not unlawful, the manner of execution was unconstitutional. It emphasized that State agents must use proportionate force and maintain humane treatment even during lawful arrests. Accordingly, the Court held the relevant officers personally liable for violating the Petitioner's fundamental rights and ordered compensation.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
Ediriweera Arukpatabandige Sugath Rohan Jayasuriya v. Manikkaratnam and
Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was brutally assaulted by three police officers near a boutique on December 29, 2007, and claimed that one officer struck his head with a firearm, causing unconsciousness. The Respondents denied the allegations and asserted that the Petitioner had been riding a motorcycle while intoxicated, ignored police orders to stop at a roadblock, and fell from the motorcycle twice while attempting to escape. Upon arrest, police officers allegedly discovered two packets of heroin in his possession. The Petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13(1) of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest. Medical evidence before the Court included an initial medico-legal report recording that the Petitioner himself admitted he had fallen due to drunkenness. The injuries documented, including scalp lacerations and scratches, together with the damaged condition of the motorcycle, were found consistent with a fall rather than a police assault. The Supreme Court dismissed the application, holding that the Petitioner failed to satisfy the high standard of proof necessary to establish a violation of Article 11. The Court also noted inconsistencies in the Petitioner's subsequent claims of hearing and vision loss, which medical examinations failed to substantiate. The Court concluded that the arrest was lawful because the Petitioner was allegedly committing cognizable offences involving heroin possession and intoxicated driving. The Petitioner's credibility was further undermined by inconsistent accounts and undisclosed prior criminal convictions relating to substance abuse.

source_case_name: S. Malavipathirana v. Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka and Others

intake.incident_location: Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka, Belihul Oya
intake.actor_name: Sabaragamuwa University of Sri Lanka and University Grants Commission
intake.actor_role: public university officials and higher education authorities
intake.what_happened: I applied for an advertised Senior Lecturer Grade I/II post at Sabaragamuwa University and was appointed as a Lecturer (Probationary) on the understanding that I would be placed as Senior Lecturer Grade II after the necessary approval. I accepted the appointment and joined the university, but the authorities failed for years to regularize me into the advertised post despite my qualifications, internal committee recommendations, Council consideration, and an order of the University Services Appeals Board.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of proper academic designation, delayed career progression, loss of salary entitlements, increments, sabbatical leave, professional recognition and academic opportunities.
intake.user_narrative: I applied for an advertised Senior Lecturer Grade I/II post at Sabaragamuwa University. Instead, I was appointed as a Lecturer (Probationary), but the appointment letter indicated that I would later be placed as Senior Lecturer Grade II after the required approval. I accepted the post and moved from another senior public research position because I expected better academic career prospects. For many years, I repeatedly asked the university and the University Grants Commission to correct my appointment. Internal university bodies later recognized that a mistake had been made, and the University Services Appeals Board also recommended that I be placed as Senior Lecturer Grade II from my initial appointment date. Even after that, the authorities did not implement the recommendation, causing loss of salary benefits, sabbatical leave and professional opportunities.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the petitioner had applied for the advertised Senior Lecturer Grade I/II post but was appointed to a non-advertised Lecturer (Probationary) post with an assurance of later placement as Senior Lecturer Grade II. Internal university committees, the University Council and the University Services Appeals Board recognized the administrative error and recommended rectification, but the university and UGC failed to implement those recommendations. This administrative inaction, procedural irregularity and denial of the petitioner's proper academic position and entitlements violated Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g).

retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds.
