retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

cases.case_name:
Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Sriyanee Dhammika Kumari Semasinghe v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others, a Sri Lanka Foreign Service officer, challenged the Public Service Commission's decision fixing her promotion to Grade I from 13 October 2015 rather than the requested retrospective date of 3 September 2013. She contended that this affected her seniority relative to her 1996 recruitment batch. The State argued that no Grade I vacancies existed in 2013 and that retrospective creation of posts would violate Financial Regulation 70, which prohibits creation of supernumerary posts in closed financial years. The petitioner also faced delays in earlier career progression due to failure to pass Efficiency Bar examinations within the stipulated period. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) or Article 14(1)(g) required retrospective promotion despite statutory financial constraints. It held that equality under Article 12(1) applies only to lawful entitlements and cannot compel the State to act in breach of binding financial regulations. The Court further noted that administrative delay partly arose from the petitioner's own failure to meet qualification requirements in time. It also observed that necessary parties whose seniority would be affected had not been joined. The Court concluded that the Public Service Commission acted within legal limits under the applicable service minute and financial framework. Finding no arbitrariness or illegality, the Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights violation had been established.

cases.case_name: Ananda Dharmadasa and Others v. Ariyaratne Hewage and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, former educational officers, challenged their exclusion from appointment to the Sri Lanka Educational Administrative Service despite earlier Cabinet decisions permitting absorption of officers performing in scheduled posts. They alleged unequal treatment under Article 12(1), arguing that similarly situated officers were appointed while they were excluded without justification. The State raised preliminary objections including delay and ineligibility based on qualification criteria. The Supreme Court held that constitutional relief under Article 126 must be sought within one month of the alleged infringement and that prolonged delay rendered the application time-barred. On merits, the Court found that equality requires comparability of circumstances, and the Petitioners failed to demonstrate that they satisfied the mandatory qualifications required for appointment. It further held that valid administrative classification based on objective criteria does not amount to discrimination. The Court emphasized that unequal treatment must be shown in identical circumstances without rational basis, which was not established in this case. It concluded that there was no violation of Article 12(1) and dismissed the application on both procedural and substantive grounds.

cases.case_name:
Dr. C.L. Illesinghe and Others v. Secretary, Ministry of Public Administration and
Home Affairs and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who were Ayurvedic Medical Officers employed on a contractual basis in the public service, sought absorption into the Sri Lanka Administrative Service or alternatively requested seniority and permanency equivalent to other public officers. The dispute arose from the operation of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Minute and the Establishments Code governing recruitment, appointment, and seniority in the public sector. The Petitioners alleged that despite their qualifications and years of service, they were unfairly denied appointment opportunities within the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, amounting to a violation of their right to equality under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Respondents maintained that recruitment and seniority decisions were governed strictly by the applicable service regulations and that the Public Service Commission had acted lawfully within those established criteria. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had occurred. The Court reasoned that the Petitioners failed to establish discriminatory treatment in comparison with similarly situated officers. It emphasized that seniority must be determined according to the date of appointment to the relevant post and that disturbing established seniority structures without legal basis would be improper. The Court also observed that some contractual claims had become moot because the relevant contracts had already expired.

cases.case_name:
Harshani S. Siriwardana v. Malsiri J. Seneviratne, Secretary, Ministry of Health
(Western Province) and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner applied for the post of Social Service Officer in the Western Province pursuant to a Gazette notification issued in 2007. She attended an interview, produced her academic certificates, and was subsequently selected and issued with an appointment letter. Thereafter, the 1st Respondent informed her that her Bachelor of Arts General Degree did not satisfy the recruitment requirement specifying qualifications in Sociology or Economics. Consequently, the authorities cancelled her appointment. The Petitioner challenged the cancellation under Article 12(1), relying primarily on the doctrine of legitimate expectation and contending that the authorities could not revoke an appointment after formally selecting her. The Court examined the recruitment criteria contained in the Gazette notification and held that the prescribed qualifications expressly required a degree specializing in Sociology or Economics. Since the Petitioner possessed only a general arts degree, the Court found that she did not satisfy the mandatory eligibility criteria for the post. The Court further held that the doctrine of legitimate expectation cannot compel a public authority to perpetuate an illegality or act contrary to lawfully established recruitment requirements. It reasoned that the initial appointment resulted from an administrative error which the State was entitled to correct in the interests of legality and proper administration. The Court concluded that the cancellation was based upon an objective evaluation of qualifications and did not constitute arbitrary or discriminatory treatment. The Supreme Court therefore held that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application without costs.

cases.case_name: M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others challenged the denial of admission to the Faculty of Law despite having obtained three A passes and a competitive Z-score in the GCE Advanced Level examination. The University Grants Commission rejected his application on the basis that he was allegedly registered for a Higher National Diploma at an Advanced Technological Institute, which under admission rules disqualified him from university entry unless formally withdrawn. The petitioner contended that he was never validly registered due to failure to submit mandatory documents and absence of attendance, and that the registration entry was a clerical error. The respondents relied on institutional records indicating active registration status. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court examined whether administrative error could lawfully be used to deny merit-based university admission. It held that the petitioner was not validly registered under the applicable procedural requirements and that the State institution's clerical mistake could not prejudice his educational rights. The Court further held that denial of admission to a qualified student on the basis of erroneous data constituted arbitrary state action contrary to equality principles. It emphasised the State's obligation to ensure fair and non-arbitrary access to higher education. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 12(1), set aside the decision, and granted relief restoring the petitioner's eligibility.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. retrieved_cases.case_name: M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner in M.D. Malik Sachinthana v. University Grants Commission and Others challenged the denial of admission to the Faculty of Law despite having obtained three A passes and a competitive Z-score in the GCE Advanced Level examination. The University Grants Commission rejected his application on the basis that he was allegedly registered for a Higher National Diploma at an Advanced Technological Institute, which under admission rules disqualified him from university entry unless formally withdrawn. The petitioner contended that he was never validly registered due to failure to submit mandatory documents and absence of attendance, and that the registration entry was a clerical error. The respondents relied on institutional records indicating active registration status. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court examined whether administrative error could lawfully be used to deny merit-based university admission. It held that the petitioner was not validly registered under the applicable procedural requirements and that the State institution's clerical mistake could not prejudice his educational rights. The Court further held that denial of admission to a qualified student on the basis of erroneous data constituted arbitrary state action contrary to equality principles. It emphasised the State's obligation to ensure fair and non-arbitrary access to higher education. Accordingly, the Court found a violation of Article 12(1), set aside the decision, and granted relief restoring the petitioner's eligibility.

intake.actor_name: Criminal Investigation Department and Sri Lanka Police
intake.what_happened: I am a Police Sergeant attached to the Police Narcotics Bureau. CID officers arrested me in connection with allegations that some officers were involved in drug trafficking, weapons dealings and other serious unlawful activities. I say I was arrested without being given proper reasons and was then detained under several detention orders under the Prevention of Terrorism Act for many months.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, prolonged detention under terrorism-related detention orders, deprivation of liberty, interdiction from service, impact on occupation and movement, reputational harm, and uncertainty over serious criminal allegations.
intake.user_narrative: I am a Police Sergeant attached to the Police Narcotics Bureau. CID officers took me into custody after allegations were made that some PNB officers were involved in drug trafficking, weapons and other serious unlawful activities. I say I was arrested while at work and was not properly told the reason for my arrest. After that, I was detained under the Prevention of Terrorism Act through several detention orders for long periods. My house was searched and items such as pen drives, an external hard drive and SIM cards were taken. I believe my arrest and detention were unfair and affected my police career, liberty and reputation.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged unlawful arrest and detention under the PTA and claimed violations of several constitutional rights. The Court held that he failed to establish his version that he was arrested inside the Police Narcotics Bureau premises, particularly because no relevant PNB officers responsible for the premises were made parties. The Court accepted the CID's version that he was summoned to the CID and arrested there. It found sufficient material for reasonable suspicion under the PTA, including a complaint by a PNB officer alleging involvement of PNB officers in drug trafficking and weapons dealings, investigation notes, written authorization, an arrest receipt, items seized from the petitioner's residence, and further investigative material. The Court also held that the detention orders were valid, that non-production before a Magistrate was excused where a detention order was obtained within the PTA time frame, and that the orders signed by the President were not invalid because the President was also the Minister of Defence. Therefore no fundamental rights infringement was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The petition was dismissed with costs. The Court also directed the Inspector General of Police to look into the legality or suitability of allowing the petitioner to continue employment as a police officer, and directed the Attorney General to examine the relevant facts and consider giving necessary advice to the Inspector General of Police.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation PTA arrest and detention case involving serious allegations against a police officer. Useful for false-violation control because many articles were granted leave and initially appeared plausible, but the Court rejected all alleged infringements after accepting the legality of the CID arrest, reasonable suspicion and detention orders. cases.case_name: Gunasekera v. De Fonseka
cases.summary: The petitioner's husband was arrested late at night by an Assistant Superintendent of Police acting under Emergency Regulations. The arresting officer acted solely on instructions from a superior officer and possessed no personal knowledge or factual basis regarding the alleged offence. The detainee was not informed of the reasons for arrest. A Habeas Corpus application challenged the legality of the arrest and detention, raising principles now reflected in Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning arbitrary arrest and detention. The Court held that the legality of an arrest without warrant depends on the arresting officer personally possessing reasonable grounds for suspicion at the time of arrest. It reasoned that reasonable suspicion is a condition precedent to lawful exercise of arrest powers and cannot be delegated or mechanically adopted from a superior's instructions. The Court further emphasized that a person deprived of liberty has the right to know the grounds of arrest, and an officer unaware of those grounds cannot lawfully communicate them. Since the arresting officer lacked personal suspicion and failed to inform the detainee of the basis for arrest, the detention was held unlawful. Accordingly, the Court allowed the application and declared the arrest and subsequent detention unauthorized in law.

cases.case_name: P. D. A. Panapitiya and Another v. Mangala De Soyza Amarasekara
cases.summary: The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

cases.case_name: Wickramage Stanley Perera v. P.H. Manatunga and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, an Inspector of Police with twenty-six years of service and numerous commendations, alleged that following successful heroin raids he became the target of arbitrary transfers and fabricated disciplinary proceedings initiated by superior officers. Despite an undertaking given by the State to the Supreme Court that the Petitioner would neither be transferred nor deprived of his personal firearm because of threats posed by underworld figures, the weapon was subsequently withdrawn. The Petitioner asserted that he received threats to his life from criminal elements and was followed by associates linked to a senior police officer. Fearing for his safety, he ceased reporting for duty on March 16, 2017, after which a Vacation of Post notice was issued against him. The Petitioner challenged the notice as arbitrary and malicious, alleging a violation of Article 12(1). The Court held that vacation of post required not only physical absence but also animus deserendi, namely an intention to abandon employment permanently. The Court found that the Petitioner's absence arose from a genuine and grave apprehension regarding his personal safety rather than any intention to desert his office. The Court further held that the State and the Inspector General of Police had breached the undertaking previously given to Court concerning the Petitioner's protection, which directly contributed to his absence from work. The conduct of the superior officers in initiating contradictory transfers and fabricated disciplinary measures was held to be mala fide and arbitrary. The Court quashed the Vacation of Post notice, ordered reinstatement with full benefits, and directed individual Respondents to personally pay compensation.

cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

cases.case_name: Piyasiri and Others v. Nimal Fernando, A.S.P. and Others
cases.summary: Fourteen Customs Officers at Katunayake Airport were stopped, questioned, and taken to a police station by officers investigating alleged bribery. They were searched and money was found in their possession, but they were not informed of specific charges or reasons for arrest. The Petitioners challenged their detention under Article 13(1), alleging arbitrary arrest without disclosure of grounds. The State argued that the actions were part of an ongoing corruption investigation. The Supreme Court held that arrest based on vague or general suspicion does not satisfy constitutional requirements and must be supported by specific and credible information. It further held that arrest cannot be used as a mechanism to gather evidence through subsequent search procedures. The Court emphasized that even if individuals move under police direction, they remain in custody if their liberty is restrained. It found that the failure to communicate a precise reason for arrest constituted a breach of mandatory constitutional safeguards. The Court concluded that the Petitioners were subjected to arbitrary arrest in violation of Article 13(1) and awarded compensation.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Gunasekera v. De Fonseka
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner's husband was arrested late at night by an Assistant Superintendent of Police acting under Emergency Regulations. The arresting officer acted solely on instructions from a superior officer and possessed no personal knowledge or factual basis regarding the alleged offence. The detainee was not informed of the reasons for arrest. A Habeas Corpus application challenged the legality of the arrest and detention, raising principles now reflected in Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning arbitrary arrest and detention. The Court held that the legality of an arrest without warrant depends on the arresting officer personally possessing reasonable grounds for suspicion at the time of arrest. It reasoned that reasonable suspicion is a condition precedent to lawful exercise of arrest powers and cannot be delegated or mechanically adopted from a superior's instructions. The Court further emphasized that a person deprived of liberty has the right to know the grounds of arrest, and an officer unaware of those grounds cannot lawfully communicate them. Since the arresting officer lacked personal suspicion and failed to inform the detainee of the basis for arrest, the detention was held unlawful. Accordingly, the Court allowed the application and declared the arrest and subsequent detention unauthorized in law.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

retrieved_cases.case_name: P. D. A. Panapitiya and Another v. Mangala De Soyza Amarasekara
retrieved_cases.summary: The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

intake.incident_location: Police Narcotics Bureau and Criminal Investigation Department, Colombo
intake.actor_name: Criminal Investigation Department and Sri Lanka Police
intake.what_happened: I am a Sub-Inspector of Police attached to the Police Narcotics Bureau. CID officers took me into custody after allegations that I and other PNB officers were involved in illicit drug trafficking. I say I was kept under arrest at my workplace before being taken by the CID, was not properly told the reason for my arrest, and was later detained under three consecutive detention orders under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, prolonged detention under terrorism-related detention orders, deprivation of liberty, interdiction from police service, impact on occupation and movement, reputational harm, family distress, and seizure of money, bank cards, equipment and vehicles from home.
intake.user_narrative: I am a Sub-Inspector attached to the Police Narcotics Bureau. CID officers took me into custody after a complaint that I and some other PNB officers were involved in drug trafficking. I say I was kept under arrest at my workplace before being taken to the CID and that I was not properly told the reason for my arrest. Later, I was detained under the Prevention of Terrorism Act using several detention orders. CID officers searched my home and seized money, bank cards, a GPS receiver, a satellite phone and several vehicles. I believe my arrest and detention were unfair and affected my liberty, family, reputation and police career.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged that the 2nd petitioner was unlawfully arrested, detained under the PTA and deprived of constitutional rights. The Court held that the petitioners failed to establish that he had been kept under arrest at the Police Narcotics Bureau from 23.06.2020, especially because no relevant PNB officers responsible for the premises were named as respondents. The Court accepted the CID's position that he was summoned to the CID and arrested on 26.06.2020. It found that the complaint by a PNB officer alleging involvement in illicit drug trafficking, together with the materials found during the search of the residence, including cash, bank cards, a GPS receiver, a satellite phone and several vehicles, provided sufficient material for reasonable suspicion under the PTA. The Court also held that non-production before a Magistrate was excused because a detention order was obtained within the statutory PTA period, and that the detention orders signed by the President were valid because the President was also the Minister of Defence. Therefore no fundamental rights infringement was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The petition was dismissed with costs. The Court directed the Inspector General of Police to look into the legality or suitability of allowing the 2nd petitioner to continue employment as a police officer, and directed the Attorney General to examine the relevant facts and consider giving necessary advice to the Inspector General of Police.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation PTA arrest and detention case involving serious allegations against a Police Narcotics Bureau officer. Useful for false-violation control because many articles were granted leave and initially appeared plausible, but the Court rejected all alleged infringements after accepting the legality of the CID arrest, reasonable suspicion and detention orders. No internal corpus case ID was provided, so source_case_id is null and gold_relevant_case_ids is empty.

final_answer:
SECTION 1 — RIGHTS ASSESSMENT:
Based on the structured reasoning chain, the following article(s) appear to remain supported as potentially violated:
- Article 13(1): The petitioner's claim of not being properly informed of the reason for arrest and being kept under arrest at their workplace before being taken to the CID appears to directly engage Article 13(1). Precedent cases like Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others, Seneviratne v. The Attorney-General and Others, and Perera v. The Attorney-General and Others found violations of Article 13(1) where individuals were arrested without proper procedure or without being informed of the reason for arrest.
- Article 13(2): The petitioner's subsequent detention under three consecutive detention orders under the Prevention of Terrorism Act, following an arrest, appears to engage Article 13(2). Precedent cases such as Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others, Seneviratne v. The Attorney-General and Others, and Perera v. The Attorney-General and Others found violations of Article 13(2) for prolonged detention without being produced before a Magistrate or without adequate judicial scrutiny, particularly under the PTA.

Weak or uncertain article(s):
- Article 12(1): While the petitioner alleges unfair arrest and detention, the provided facts do not explicitly describe any differential treatment based on a protected characteristic or a lack of equal protection before the law. The core complaint appears to be about the legality of the arrest and detention procedures rather than a claim of inequality. The selected precedent cases do not directly address Article 12(1) in a similar factual context.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

cases.case_name: Wickramage Stanley Perera v. P.H. Manatunga and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, an Inspector of Police with twenty-six years of service and numerous commendations, alleged that following successful heroin raids he became the target of arbitrary transfers and fabricated disciplinary proceedings initiated by superior officers. Despite an undertaking given by the State to the Supreme Court that the Petitioner would neither be transferred nor deprived of his personal firearm because of threats posed by underworld figures, the weapon was subsequently withdrawn. The Petitioner asserted that he received threats to his life from criminal elements and was followed by associates linked to a senior police officer. Fearing for his safety, he ceased reporting for duty on March 16, 2017, after which a Vacation of Post notice was issued against him. The Petitioner challenged the notice as arbitrary and malicious, alleging a violation of Article 12(1). The Court held that vacation of post required not only physical absence but also animus deserendi, namely an intention to abandon employment permanently. The Court found that the Petitioner's absence arose from a genuine and grave apprehension regarding his personal safety rather than any intention to desert his office. The Court further held that the State and the Inspector General of Police had breached the undertaking previously given to Court concerning the Petitioner's protection, which directly contributed to his absence from work. The conduct of the superior officers in initiating contradictory transfers and fabricated disciplinary measures was held to be mala fide and arbitrary. The Court quashed the Vacation of Post notice, ordered reinstatement with full benefits, and directed individual Respondents to personally pay compensation.

cases.case_name: Peter Leo Fernando v. The Attorney-General and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner's vehicle was intercepted by police on suspicion of smuggling, despite him producing a valid Customs receipt. Police detained him, treated him roughly, and confiscated his passport without legal authority. Instead of following the procedure under the Customs Ordinance requiring production before a Customs officer, the police produced him before a Magistrate at his residence, who then ordered further detention in police custody for four days. The legal issue concerned whether the arrest and subsequent detention complied with Article 13(1) and whether the Magistrate's order insulated the State action from constitutional scrutiny. The Supreme Court held that the police violated Article 13(1) by bypassing the mandatory statutory procedure under the Customs Ordinance, which required expeditious production before Customs authorities. The Court emphasized that deprivation of liberty must strictly follow procedure established by law and cannot be justified by convenience or investigative preference. However, regarding the detention ordered by the Magistrate, the Court held that such act constituted judicial action and therefore fell outside the scope of Article 126 jurisdiction, even if legally erroneous. It clarified that only executive or administrative acts are reviewable under fundamental rights jurisdiction. The Court found no sufficient evidence of collusion to convert the judicial act into executive action. Accordingly, relief was granted only against the police, with costs awarded against the State.

cases.case_name: Sasanasiritissa Thero and Others v. P.A. De Silva and Others
cases.summary: Following a bomb explosion at a public event, the Petitioners, including a Buddhist monk and two associates, were arrested and detained under emergency regulations for 73 days and later subject to continued detention orders. They challenged the legality of arrest and detention under Articles 12(1), 12(2), 13(1), 13(2), and 14(1)(a). The State alleged involvement in conspiracy related to political violence. The Supreme Court found that detention orders were issued mechanically without credible material and for improper political motives. It held that continued detention after clearance of primary allegations constituted mala fide exercise of power and malice in law. The Court also found that arrest of associates solely based on association lacked reasonable justification. It concluded that the State abused emergency powers and violated constitutional safeguards of liberty, equality, and freedom of association. The Petitioners were unlawfully deprived of liberty without proper legal basis. The Court held that Articles 12(1), 12(2), 13(1), 13(2), and 14(1)(a) were violated and awarded compensation.

cases.case_name: Seetha Weerakoon v. Mahendra, OIC, Police Station, Galagedera and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner and her sister were arrested and initially detained under an Emergency Regulations detention order valid for ninety days, which expired on 12 November 1989. Despite expiration of legal authority, the petitioner remained in police custody for approximately one year without being produced before a Magistrate, and only later was remanded to fiscal custody. The State failed to justify continued detention or provide evidence supporting prolonged custody, raising issues under Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning arbitrary arrest and detention and failure to produce a detainee before judicial authority within a reasonable time. The Supreme Court held that once the lawful detention order expired, any continued confinement without fresh valid authority was unconstitutional and amounted to unlawful detention. The Court emphasized that investigative convenience cannot override constitutional safeguards protecting personal liberty, and that prolonged detention without evidence of culpability is impermissible. It further noted that executive officers bear responsibility to ensure strict compliance with legal requirements governing deprivation of liberty. The Court declared the detention illegal, quashed relevant orders, and granted relief including compensation against the State and personal costs against the officer in charge. The decision reaffirmed strict judicial protection against arbitrary executive detention and reinforced the requirement of timely judicial oversight over custodial deprivation of liberty.

retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Wickramage Stanley Perera v. P.H. Manatunga and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner, an Inspector of Police with twenty-six years of service and numerous commendations, alleged that following successful heroin raids he became the target of arbitrary transfers and fabricated disciplinary proceedings initiated by superior officers. Despite an undertaking given by the State to the Supreme Court that the Petitioner would neither be transferred nor deprived of his personal firearm because of threats posed by underworld figures, the weapon was subsequently withdrawn. The Petitioner asserted that he received threats to his life from criminal elements and was followed by associates linked to a senior police officer. Fearing for his safety, he ceased reporting for duty on March 16, 2017, after which a Vacation of Post notice was issued against him. The Petitioner challenged the notice as arbitrary and malicious, alleging a violation of Article 12(1). The Court held that vacation of post required not only physical absence but also animus deserendi, namely an intention to abandon employment permanently. The Court found that the Petitioner's absence arose from a genuine and grave apprehension regarding his personal safety rather than any intention to desert his office. The Court further held that the State and the Inspector General of Police had breached the undertaking previously given to Court concerning the Petitioner's protection, which directly contributed to his absence from work. The conduct of the superior officers in initiating contradictory transfers and fabricated disciplinary measures was held to be mala fide and arbitrary. The Court quashed the Vacation of Post notice, ordered reinstatement with full benefits, and directed individual Respondents to personally pay compensation.

retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner's vehicle was intercepted by police on suspicion of smuggling, despite him producing a valid Customs receipt. The conduct of the superior officers in initiating contradictory transfers and fabricated disciplinary measures was held to be mala fide and arbitrary. The Court quashed the Vacation of Post notice, ordered reinstatement with full benefits, and directed individual Respondents to personally pay compensation.

The Petitioner's vehicle was intercepted by police on suspicion of smuggling, despite him producing a valid Customs receipt. Police detained him, treated him roughly, and confiscated his passport without legal authority. Instead of following the procedure under the Customs Ordinance requiring production before a Customs officer, the police produced him before a Magistrate at his residence, who then ordered further detention in police custody for four days. The legal issue concerned whether the arrest and subsequent detention complied with Article 13(1) and whether the Magistrate's order insulated the State action from constitutional scrutiny. The Supreme Court held that the police violated Article 13(1) by bypassing the mandatory statutory procedure under the Customs Ordinance, which required expeditious production before Customs authorities. The Court emphasized that deprivation of liberty must strictly follow procedure established by law and cannot be justified by convenience or investigative preference. However, regarding the detention ordered by the Magistrate, the Court held that such act constituted judicial action and therefore fell outside the scope of Article 126 jurisdiction, even if legally erroneous. It clarified that only executive or administrative acts are reviewable under fundamental rights jurisdiction. The Court found no sufficient evidence of collusion to convert the judicial act into executive action. Accordingly, relief was granted only against the police, with costs awarded against the State.

retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Existing written law and unwritten law
retrieved_articles.text: Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

cases.case_name: Dhanu Contractors Ltd v Matale Municipal Council
cases.summary: The petitioners, Dhanu Contractors (Pvt) Ltd, challenged the award of a municipal construction tender for the Gongawela Shopping Complex in Matale. Although the petitioners were qualified bidders, the contract was awarded to the eighteenth respondent, Universal Civil Engineering Services, which lacked the mandatory registrations required by the Municipal Council and ICTAD at the time the tender was submitted. Evidence before the Court revealed that the successful bidder had secured the award through deliberate and serious misrepresentation by concealing the absence of the necessary qualifications. The petitioners alleged that the arbitrary award of the contract violated their right to equality and equal protection under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that compliance with tender requirements was mandatory and that a contract awarded to an unqualified bidder was unlawful and void. The Court further found that the Mayor and members of the Municipal Council were directly responsible for the executive and administrative actions that resulted in the infringement of the petitioners' rights. The judgment emphasized that public procurement procedures must be conducted fairly, transparently, and in accordance with established legal standards. Concealment of material facts and manipulation of the competitive bidding process undermined the integrity of public administration and denied equal treatment to qualified bidders. The Court therefore concluded that the petitioners had been subjected to arbitrary and unequal administrative action contrary to Article 12(1). Compensation and costs were awarded against the Council, while the successful bidder and responsible municipal officials were ordered to bear personal liability for their roles in the unlawful tender process.

cases.case_name:
Sunway International (Pvt) Ltd and Another v. Airport & Aviation Services (Sri
Lanka) Limited and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, Sunway International (Pvt) Ltd and another entity, challenged the award of a tender relating to the operation of travel service counters at Bandaranaike International Airport. Although the Technical Evaluation Committee recommended the Petitioners and disqualified the 11th Respondent for lacking financial capability, the Ministerial Procurement Committee waived the mandatory financial eligibility requirement after closure of bids and awarded the tender to the 11th Respondent solely because a higher financial offer had been made. The Petitioners further complained that the Appeal Board hearing their objections consisted of the same officials responsible for the original decision and that they were denied an opportunity to be heard. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they alleged discriminatory and arbitrary treatment. The Court held that Article 12(1) had been violated but rejected the claim under Article 14(1)(g). It reasoned that altering mandatory eligibility conditions after submission of bids amounted to "changing the goal post," thereby depriving other bidders of a fair and equal competitive process. The Court emphasized that State authorities are bound by procurement guidelines and cannot disregard established procedures merely to maximize revenue. It further held that the composition and conduct of the Appeal Board violated principles of natural justice because the same officials effectively adjudicated their own earlier decision without granting the Petitioners a hearing. However, the Court clarified that the constitutional freedom to engage in an occupation does not confer an enforceable right to obtain a particular commercial contract. Compensation was awarded against both the State and the officials personally responsible for the impugned conduct.

cases.case_name:
Target Environmental Services Company (Private) Limited and Another v. Dr.
Ashoka Kahandaliyanage and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner company submitted a tender bid to provide cleaning and maintenance services to several government hospitals. After formally submitting the bid, the Petitioner sent an additional communication offering a special discount on the total bid price. The Technical Evaluation Committee and the Ministry of Healthcare and Nutrition rejected the bid on the basis that the discount offer amounted to an impermissible alteration of price after the deadline and effectively constituted a second bid contrary to the procurement requirements. The Petitioner challenged the rejection under Article 12(1), alleging arbitrary treatment and denial of equal opportunity in the tender process. The Court examined whether the rejection complied with procurement rules designed to ensure fairness and transparency. It held that the tender process depends upon preserving the blind nature of competitive bidding and that permitting bidders to alter prices after submission would undermine fair competition by allowing strategic advantages over competitors. The Court accepted the Respondents' position that the discount communication was a disguised second bid prohibited under the applicable bid conditions. It further observed that the proposed discount unlawfully affected statutory labour cost components fixed by law for worker protection and therefore could not lawfully be reduced to secure a contract. The Court concluded that the rejection was fully consistent with procurement guidelines intended to prevent unfair advantages and maintain transparency in government contracting. The Supreme Court therefore held that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been established and dismissed the application with costs.

cases.case_name: SmithKline Beecham Biologicals S.A. v. State Pharmaceutical Corporation
cases.summary: The State Pharmaceutical Corporation invited worldwide tenders for the supply of Rubella vaccines. The petitioner company submitted the only responsive bid before the deadline and satisfied the mandatory requirement of registration with the Cosmetic Devices and Drugs Authority. Several competing bidders offered lower prices but failed to meet the registration requirement at the relevant time. Although the Cabinet Appointed Tender Board initially decided to award the contract to the petitioner, it later reversed that decision and permitted a non-responsive bidder to submit registration details after the closing date. The petitioners alleged that the altered decision-making process violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution by treating bidders unequally and arbitrarily. The Supreme Court held that the impugned decisions violated the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law. The Court reasoned that public tender procedures require fairness, transparency, and uniform application of mandatory conditions to all participants. A responsive offer must comply with all essential tender requirements at the time the bid is submitted, and permitting non-compliant bidders to cure defects after the deadline while disregarding the only compliant bidder constituted arbitrary discrimination. The Court further emphasized that public interest extends beyond securing the lowest price and includes maintaining integrity and predictability in public procurement processes so that reliable suppliers are not discouraged by unfair treatment. The impugned decisions were quashed and compensation was awarded.

cases.case_name:
Sebastian Benadic and Others v. Kodithuwakku Arachchilage Nihal
Chandrakantha and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Dhanu Contractors Ltd v Matale Municipal Council
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioners, Dhanu Contractors (Pvt) Ltd, challenged the award of a municipal construction tender for the Gongawela Shopping Complex in Matale. Although the petitioners were qualified bidders, the contract was awarded to the eighteenth respondent, Universal Civil Engineering Services, which lacked the mandatory registrations required by the Municipal Council and ICTAD at the time the tender was submitted. Evidence before the Court revealed that the successful bidder had secured the award through deliberate and serious misrepresentation by concealing the absence of the necessary qualifications. The petitioners alleged that the arbitrary award of the contract violated their right to equality and equal protection under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that compliance with tender requirements was mandatory and that a contract awarded to an unqualified bidder was unlawful and void. The Court further found that the Mayor and members of the Municipal Council were directly responsible for the executive and administrative actions that resulted in the infringement of the petitioners' rights. The judgment emphasized that public procurement procedures must be conducted fairly, transparently, and in accordance with established legal standards. Concealment of material facts and manipulation of the competitive bidding process undermined the integrity of public administration and denied equal treatment to qualified bidders. The Court therefore concluded that the petitioners had been subjected to arbitrary and unequal administrative action contrary to Article 12(1). Compensation and costs were awarded against the Council, while the successful bidder and responsible municipal officials were ordered to bear personal liability for their roles in the unlawful tender process.

Lanka) Limited and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioners, Sunway International (Pvt) Ltd and another entity, challenged the award of a tender relating to the operation of travel service counters at Bandaranaike International Airport. Although the Technical Evaluation Committee recommended the Petitioners and disqualified the 11th Respondent for lacking financial capability, the Ministerial Procurement Committee waived the mandatory financial eligibility requirement after closure of bids and awarded the tender to the 11th Respondent solely because a higher financial offer had been made. The Petitioners further complained that the Appeal Board hearing their objections consisted of the same officials responsible for the original decision and that they were denied an opportunity to be heard. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they alleged discriminatory and arbitrary treatment. The Court held that Article 12(1) had been violated but rejected the claim under Article 14(1)(g). It reasoned that altering mandatory eligibility conditions after submission of bids amounted to "changing the goal post," thereby depriving other bidders of a fair and equal competitive process. The Court emphasized that State authorities are bound by procurement guidelines and cannot disregard established procedures merely to maximize revenue. It further held that the composition and conduct of the Appeal Board violated principles of natural justice because the same officials effectively adjudicated their own earlier decision without granting the Petitioners a hearing. However, the Court clarified that the constitutional freedom to engage in an occupation does not confer an enforceable right to obtain a particular commercial contract. Compensation was awarded against both the State and the officials personally responsible for the impugned conduct.

retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner company submitted a tender bid to provide cleaning and maintenance services to several government hospitals. intake.incident_location: Beruwela Police Station and Lanka Fisheries Corporation Beruwela Regional Office
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Beruwela Police Station
intake.what_happened: I was the Regional Manager of the Lanka Fisheries Corporation's Beruwela Regional Office. A purchasing officer with whom I had previous disputes complained to the police alleging financial fraud involving public money. I was asked to come to the Beruwela Police Station, my statement was recorded after several hours, and I was then arrested and produced before the Magistrate with a certificate under the Offences Against Public Property Act. I believe the complaint was false and malicious, that the police did not have a proper basis to arrest me, and that false or exaggerated facts were reported to keep me in remand.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, police custody, remand custody, refusal of bail by the Magistrate, need to seek bail from the High Court, reputational harm, employment-related distress, and failure to obtain action on my earlier complaint against the purchasing officer.
intake.user_narrative: I worked as a Regional Manager at the Beruwela Regional Office of the Lanka Fisheries Corporation. I had problems with a purchasing officer who had earlier been transferred after financial issues, and I had also complained to police that he tried to plant cannabis in my office. Later, he made a complaint against me saying I had committed financial fraud involving public money. The police asked me to come to the Beruwela Police Station. I went in the morning, but my statement was recorded only later in the day, and then I was arrested. The next day I was produced before the Magistrate with a certificate saying the alleged loss was over the public property threshold, so I was remanded and bail was refused. I believe the complaint was malicious, that the police did not properly investigate my side, and that my arrest and detention were unfair.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the arrest was supported by objectively reasonable suspicion based on the complaint and the material in the B Report, including statements about alleged forged supplier bills, cheques issued in a supplier's name, and payments routed through the petitioner. The Court found that the petitioner was arrested at around 2.00 p.m. on 18.02.2016 and produced before the Magistrate at around 3.00 p.m. the next day, which was not unreasonable or unlawful in the circumstances. It also rejected the allegation that false or fabricated facts were reported to deprive the Magistrate of bail jurisdiction under the Offences Against Public Property Act, and found no discriminatory treatment or failure to investigate the petitioner's complaint because the available police records showed that his complaint had been investigated and the 6th respondent warned. Articles 12(1), 13(1) and 13(2) were therefore not infringed.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed. No order was made as to costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation police arrest and remand case involving a public corporation financial-fraud complaint. Useful for false-violation control because Articles 12(1), 13(1) and 13(2) were granted leave and initially appeared plausible, but the Court found reasonable suspicion, timely production before the Magistrate, and no unequal treatment. retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to a fair trial
retrieved_articles.text: Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.
