cases.case_name: Abdul Lathif v. Deputy Inspector General of Police, Nuwara Eliya
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

cases.case_name: Azath Salley v. Colombo Municipal Council and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a former Deputy Mayor and ratepayer of Colombo, challenged the failure of the Colombo Municipal Council to regulate outdoor advertising and enforce municipal by-laws relating to unauthorized hoardings. He alleged that numerous hoardings had been erected unlawfully throughout the city and that approvals were granted selectively and without transparency, causing financial loss to the Council and inconvenience to the public. The Petitioner contended that the arbitrary enforcement of by-laws violated Article 12(1) by denying equal protection of the law. The Supreme Court held that the conduct of the municipal authorities infringed the Petitioner's fundamental rights. The Court emphasized that powers exercised by local authorities are held in trust for the benefit of the public and that failure to enforce established legal standards amounted to a breach of that public trust. It held that equality under Article 12(1) includes the right of citizens to expect authorities to apply laws and procedures consistently and lawfully. Selective enforcement, arbitrary approval of hoardings, and disregard of mandatory by-laws constituted unequal treatment and arbitrary state action. The Court also interpreted Article 126 broadly to permit citizens to challenge executive inaction affecting the wider public interest even where the injury was not unique to a single individual. The Court accordingly directed the Municipal Council to remove unauthorized hoardings and establish transparent regulatory guidelines and procedures governing outdoor advertising within Colombo.

cases.case_name:
JPC Trade Company Ltd and R. Lahiru Rakshitha v. Jagath P. Wijeweera and
Others
cases.summary: The 1st Petitioner, a Japanese vehicle exporting company, and its Country Manager were investigated by Sri Lanka Customs on allegations of undervaluing imported vehicles in order to reduce customs duties payable to the State. Investigations disclosed that undervalued pro-forma invoices had been issued to local importers while the remaining balance of the vehicle prices was collected through a local agent and transferred unlawfully to Japan. Following an inquiry conducted under the Customs Ordinance, the 2nd Petitioner was ordered to pay a mitigated forfeiture amounting to Rs. 6,000,000. The Petitioners alleged that their rights under Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 13(4) had been violated because the importer involved in the transactions had not been similarly punished. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that Article 12 guarantees equality only in the lawful exercise of executive power and does not entitle a party to claim "equal violation of the law." The Court observed that the Petitioners sought to rely upon the alleged failure to prosecute another party in order to avoid lawful consequences arising from their own misconduct. The Court further noted that the Petitioners had deliberately suppressed material facts because the 2nd Petitioner had already admitted involvement in the undervaluation scheme during the Customs investigation despite later claiming otherwise before Court. The Court held that Customs officials were legally bound to act upon the findings of the inquiry under the Customs Ordinance and that the allegations of arbitrary punishment lacked merit. The application was dismissed with costs.

cases.case_name:
K.H.G. Kushan Indika v. Christy Leonard Ranjan Wijesekera, OIC Pitigala and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, employed as a driver for the Sri Lanka State Plantation Corporation, was waiting at a bus halt on April 2, 2007 when a police jeep arrived and the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Pitigala Police Station, questioned him. Although the Petitioner produced his driving licence as identification, the 1st Respondent assaulted him by slapping him repeatedly and compelled him to load a heavy motorbike into a truck. When the Petitioner requested assistance, the 1st Respondent assaulted him with a club several times. The Petitioner was then taken to the police station, detained in a cell for nearly two hours, and released without any statement being recorded or charges being filed. The Respondent attempted to justify the arrest on the basis of suspicious conduct. The Court held that no reasonable suspicion existed to support the arrest and clarified that a driving licence constituted valid identification. The Court determined that the public assault, forced labour, and unlawful detention subjected the Petitioner to degrading treatment within the meaning of Article 11, notwithstanding the non-grievous nature of the injuries. The Court further held that the failure to provide reasons for arrest or record a statement constituted a serious procedural lapse. The Supreme Court concluded that Articles 11 and 13(1) had been violated and directed the 1st Respondent to personally compensate the Petitioner.

cases.case_name: K.P.K.L.P. Maduwanthi v. S.M.G.K. Perera and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a senior officer of the Sri Lanka Administrative Service, challenged her transfer to the Ministry pool after an earlier approved transfer to Dambulla was deferred due to allegations of conflict of interest involving her husband's alleged acquisition of state land through irregular transactions. She alleged violation of Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g), claiming arbitrariness and infringement of legitimate expectation. The Supreme Court held that the transfer was justified under Public Service Commission rules permitting reassignment during investigations into misconduct. It found that the Petitioner had made material misrepresentations regarding her husband's business interests, thereby attracting the clean hands doctrine and disentitling her from relief in equity. The Court further held that placement in the pool was necessary to prevent interference with ongoing investigations and to ensure administrative integrity. It also concluded that no legitimate expectation can arise where the expected outcome would facilitate a conflict of interest or improper conduct. Additionally, the Court directed referral of the matter for corruption investigation. Accordingly, it held that there was no violation of fundamental rights and dismissed the application.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Velmurugu v Attorney-General and Another
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner, a member of the District Development Council, was arrested by army personnel on 9 August 1981 during communal disturbances under the orders of the 2nd respondent, an Assistant Superintendent of Police. He alleged that after the arrest the 2nd respondent instructed the army personnel to "do as they like with him," following which he was brutally assaulted inside an army truck, kicked with booted feet, had his beard burnt, and sustained a fractured jaw. The petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13 of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest by State officers. The respondents denied responsibility for the alleged torture and disputed that any constitutional violation had occurred. The Supreme Court, by a majority of three to two, dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established. The Court applied a high degree of probability because of the gravity of allegations involving torture by State authorities. It emphasized that the petitioner failed to complain before the Magistrate, medical officer, or police at the earliest opportunity. The Court further reasoned that State liability arises only where wrongful acts are committed under colour of office or pursuant to administrative practice. The alleged conduct was characterized as a private criminal aberration rather than official executive action attributable to the State.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Velmurugu v Attorney-General and Another
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, a member of the District Development Council, was arrested by army personnel on 9 August 1981 during communal disturbances under the orders of the 2nd respondent, an Assistant Superintendent of Police. He alleged that after the arrest the 2nd respondent instructed the army personnel to "do as they like with him," following which he was brutally assaulted inside an army truck, kicked with booted feet, had his beard burnt, and sustained a fractured jaw. The petitioner invoked Articles 11 and 13 of the Constitution, alleging torture and unlawful arrest by State officers. The respondents denied responsibility for the alleged torture and disputed that any constitutional violation had occurred. The Supreme Court, by a majority of three to two, dismissed the application and held that no infringement of fundamental rights had been established. The Court applied a high degree of probability because of the gravity of allegations involving torture by State authorities. It emphasized that the petitioner failed to complain before the Magistrate, medical officer, or police at the earliest opportunity. The Court further reasoned that State liability arises only where wrongful acts are committed under colour of office or pursuant to administrative practice. The alleged conduct was characterized as a private criminal aberration rather than official executive action attributable to the State.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Abdul Lathif v. Deputy Inspector General of Police, Nuwara Eliya
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

K.H.G. Kushan Indika v. Christy Leonard Ranjan Wijesekera, OIC Pitigala and
Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner, employed as a driver for the Sri Lanka State Plantation Corporation, was waiting at a bus halt on April 2, 2007 when a police jeep arrived and the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Pitigala Police Station, questioned him. Although the Petitioner produced his driving licence as identification, the 1st Respondent assaulted him by slapping him repeatedly and compelled him to load a heavy motorbike into a truck. When the Petitioner requested assistance, the 1st Respondent assaulted him with a club several times. The Petitioner was then taken to the police station, detained in a cell for nearly two hours, and released without any statement being recorded or charges being filed. The Court further held that the failure to provide reasons for arrest or record a statement constituted a serious procedural lapse. The Supreme Court concluded that Articles 11 and 13(1) had been violated and directed the 1st Respondent to personally compensate the Petitioner.

The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

The Petitioner, employed as a driver for the Sri Lanka State Plantation Corporation, was waiting at a bus halt on April 2, 2007 when a police jeep arrived and the 1st Respondent, the Officer-in-Charge of Pitigala Police Station, questioned him. Although the Petitioner produced his driving licence as identification, the 1st Respondent assaulted him by slapping him repeatedly and compelled him to load a heavy motorbike into a truck. When the Petitioner requested assistance, the 1st Respondent assaulted him with a club several times. The Petitioner was then taken to the police station, detained in a cell for nearly two hours, and released without any statement being recorded or charges being filed. The Respondent attempted to justify the arrest on the basis of suspicious conduct. The Court held that no reasonable suspicion existed to support the arrest and clarified that a driving licence constituted valid identification. The Court determined that the public assault, forced labour, and unlawful detention subjected the Petitioner to degrading treatment within the meaning of Article 11, notwithstanding the non-grievous nature of the injuries. The Court further held that the failure to provide reasons for arrest or record a statement constituted a serious procedural lapse. The Supreme Court concluded that Articles 11 and 13(1) had been violated and directed the 1st Respondent to personally compensate the Petitioner.

Later, a public administration circular and new scheme of recruitment placed our post on the MN-1 salary scale. We believe this is unfair because many of us are graduates, our service standards have been lowered, the supra grade was removed, promotion opportunities were restricted, and we are placed below or close to clerical staff who work under us. We asked the authorities to place us on a higher salary scale, but they refused, saying the post does not strictly require a degree and the same scale should apply across provinces.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners challenged the categorisation and salary scale of Revenue Inspectors under Public Administration Circular No. 06/2006 and the 2015 Scheme of Recruitment, alleging violations of equality, non-discrimination and occupational freedom. The Court held that the salary placement was part of a structured and consistent salary policy verified by the National Salaries and Cadre Commission, not an arbitrary or discriminatory act. Because the Revenue Inspector post did not strictly require a degree, and because assigning different salary scales to the same post based on different recruitment routes could itself create unequal treatment, the decision to place the post on MN-1 had a reasonable basis. The petitioners failed to show differential treatment from similarly circumstanced persons without reasonable basis, and Article 14(1)(g) was also not infringed.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed.

No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to form and join trade unions
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to form and join trade unions. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to form and join a trade union.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

cases.case_name:
Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Others v. R.B. Premadasa, DG
Rubber Development Dept and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, comprising the Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Rubber Development Officers, challenged a new Scheme of Recruitment approved by the Public Service Commission on 14 November 2014. The revised scheme classified them as Supervisory Management Assistant - Technical officers under salary code MN 3 and removed the degree qualification previously associated with recruitment. The Petitioners contended that their actual duties and status warranted classification as Field or Office Based Officers under salary code MN 5. They further alleged that the changes adversely affected their professional standing and opportunities within the service. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they argued that the scheme was discriminatory and unlawfully interfered with their occupational rights. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application had been filed outside the constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2). Documentary evidence demonstrated that the Petitioners had participated in a meeting on 25 November 2014 specifically discussing amendments to the already approved Scheme of Recruitment, thereby proving prior knowledge of the impugned decision. The Court dismissed the application in limine without examining the substantive merits. It held that the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2) is mandatory and begins from the date the alleged infringement becomes known to the Petitioners. The Court rejected the claim that awareness arose only upon publication of a later job advertisement and found that no exceptional circumstances had prevented earlier invocation of the Court's jurisdiction.

cases.case_name:
Padma Maithrilatha Akarawita and Others v. Dr. Nanda Wickramasinghe and
Others (Supra Grade Librarians Case)
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Supra Grade Librarians in the public service, challenged the salary structure introduced through Public Administration Circular No. 6/2006 revising public service salaries. They contended that Supra Grade Librarians had historically enjoyed salary parity with officers in the Sri Lanka Administrative Service Class II Grade II and alleged that the revised circular created discrimination by granting SLAS officers a more favourable salary conversion. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) of the Constitution, asserting unequal treatment and arbitrary discrimination. The Court examined whether the Petitioners and SLAS officers constituted similarly situated categories capable of comparison for constitutional equality purposes. It held that the two services belonged to entirely distinct categories within the public service and therefore could not automatically be treated as equals for salary determination. The Court further considered evidence demonstrating that, following recommendations by the National Salaries and Cadre Commission, the Petitioners had in fact been placed on a salary step enabling them to draw higher remuneration than the SLAS officers with whom they compared themselves. In light of this evidence, the Court found no actual financial disadvantage or discriminatory treatment suffered by the Petitioners. It further held that the salary revisions formed part of a broader policy decision concerning restructuring of the public service and that there was no evidence of arbitrariness or irrationality in the implementation of the circular. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

cases.case_name:
R.D.M.K.K. Wimalachandra and Others v. Mahinda Yapa Abeywardena and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, consisting of twenty-two Agriculture Monitoring Officers and their trade union, challenged the introduction of a new Service Minute and Circular No. 10/2012 establishing the Programme Officers' Service under the Ministry of Agriculture. They alleged that the restructuring arbitrarily altered their designations and potentially excluded them from a limited competitive examination relevant to promotions. The Petitioners further claimed discriminatory treatment because Economic Assistants, who were Arts graduates recruited through a competitive process, were placed on a higher salary scale than the Petitioners, although both groups had entered public service under graduate employment schemes. The Respondents maintained that absorption into the new service was optional and that officers who declined absorption would remain in their existing posts. Relying on Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), the Petitioners contended that the scheme violated equality and occupational rights. The Court dismissed the application and held that no arbitrary or discriminatory conduct had been established. It reasoned that arbitrariness required capricious or irrational executive action and that the optional nature of the scheme demonstrated reasonableness rather than compulsion. The Court further held that Economic Assistants and the Petitioners did not belong to the same class because they had been recruited through materially different procedures. The Court additionally held that the Petitioners were estopped from relitigating the salary issue because a previous application seeking similar relief had already been refused. The Respondents' assurance that a future promotion scheme would be introduced was also accepted.

cases.case_name: Wickramasinghe and Others v. Attorney General
cases.summary: The petitioners, public sector technical officers, challenged a decision altering their salary placement after appointment. Although initial recruitment documents guaranteed higher salary steps to preserve prior seniority and pay, the respondents later unilaterally placed them at lower initial salary levels. The petitioners alleged violation of Article 12(1), arguing breach of legitimate expectation and unfair administrative action. The respondents contended that revised administrative decisions justified the salary adjustment. The Supreme Court held that the salary terms formed part of binding employment conditions and could not be altered unilaterally after acceptance of appointment. It found that the respondents acted arbitrarily and contrary to principles of fairness and consistency in administrative law. The Court further held that legitimate expectation arising from official appointment letters must be honoured unless a rational basis exists for deviation. It concluded that failure to implement agreed salary steps constituted unequal and unreasonable treatment under Article 12(1). Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and directed restoration of the originally promised salary structure.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

intake.incident_location: Sri Lanka Police Department, Colombo
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Ministry of Law and Order, Public Service Commission and National Police Commission
intake.actor_role: police promotion authorities and public service officials
intake.what_happened: We were Inspectors in the Police Reserve Force and voluntarily joined the Regular Police Force in 1999 at the lower rank of Sub-Inspector under an absorption scheme. Later we were promoted to Inspector in the Regular Force. When applications were called for promotion to Chief Inspector, we were told we had not completed the required eight years as Inspectors in the Regular Force. We believe our earlier service as Inspectors in the Reserve Force should also be counted, especially because officers absorbed later from the Reserve Force were allowed to count their Reserve Force service for promotion.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of opportunity to be considered for promotion to Chief Inspector of Police, seniority disadvantage, career progression delay, and unequal treatment compared with officers absorbed from the Reserve Force in 2006.
intake.user_narrative: We were Inspectors in the Police Reserve Force before we applied to join the Regular Police Force under a special absorption scheme. When we joined in 1999, we had to accept the lower rank of Sub-Inspector and continued serving in the Regular Force. Later, after earlier legal proceedings and administrative relief, we were promoted to Inspector from 2006. In 2013, when applications were called for promotion to Chief Inspector, the authorities said we did not have the required eight years of service as Inspectors. We believe this is unfair because we had already served as Inspectors in the Reserve Force before joining the Regular Force, and officers who stayed in the Reserve Force and joined the Regular Force later were allowed to count their Reserve Force service for promotion.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the petitioners, who voluntarily entered the Regular Force in 1999 at the lower rank of Sub-Inspector, could not add their earlier Reserve Force service as Inspectors when calculating eligibility for promotion to Chief Inspector in 2013. Their Reserve Force service had already been taken into account when they were promoted to Inspector with effect from 01.02.2006, and allowing the same past service to be repeatedly used for later promotions would be impermissible. The Court also held that officers absorbed in 1999 and officers absorbed in 2006 were distinct categories governed by different conditions, and the petitioners failed to include the officers already promoted in 2013 as necessary parties. The Article 12(1) claim was therefore rejected.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation police promotion and seniority case. Useful for false-violation control because unequal treatment initially appears plausible, but the Court found a rational distinction between officers absorbed into the Regular Force in 1999 and those absorbed in 2006, and also found a fatal procedural defect due to non-joinder of promoted officers. cases.case_name:
M.P.A.C. Pieris and 27 Others v. N.K. Illangakoon, Inspector General of Police
and Others
cases.summary: SC/F.R/348/2013 concerned 28 Sub-Inspectors who challenged the failure of the Inspector General of Police to backdate their promotions to Inspector effective from 1 January 2003. Although Circular No. 1737/2003 provided for filling 629 vacancies and 471 officers were promoted, 158 vacancies remained unfilled and the petitioners were promoted only in 2006, resulting in loss of seniority and subsequent career disadvantages, including loss of eligibility for higher ranks. The Supreme Court examined whether Article 12(1) had been violated through unequal treatment in promotions. The Court found that multiple official recommendations, including those of successive Inspectors General and the Nawaratne Committee, had created a legitimate expectation that promotions would be backdated. The Court held that failure to implement these recommendations resulted in arbitrary deprivation of seniority and allowed junior officers to supersede the petitioners. It characterized this as a continuing violation affecting career progression. The Court emphasized that public service promotions must adhere to fairness, rationality, and consistency to uphold equality before the law. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were infringed and ordered backdating of promotions to restore seniority and rectify the constitutional breach.

cases.case_name: Gunawardana v. National Police Commission
cases.summary: The petitioners, Police Inspectors, challenged the cancellation of a completed recruitment process for promotion to Assistant Superintendent of Police, despite having successfully passed examinations and being placed on a merit list. The National Police Commission and Inspector General of Police cancelled the process based on a Cabinet decision to restructure the police service. The petitioners alleged violations of Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g), claiming deprivation of earned promotional rights. The Supreme Court held that once a competitive recruitment process is completed and a merit list is finalized, candidates acquire a legitimate expectation of promotion. It found that the retrospective cancellation of a valid selection process was arbitrary and irrational. The Court further held that while restructuring of public services is permissible, it cannot be used to nullify completed lawful processes without justification. It emphasized that administrative discretion must be exercised consistently with the rule of law and fairness. Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and quashed the impugned cancellation decisions.

cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name:
Balachandra Arachchige Don Nuwan Chathuranga Padmasiri and Others v. C.
D. Wickramaratne and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, Sub-Inspectors of Police, challenged a 2020 Scheme of Recruitment governing promotion to Inspector of Police, alleging that it introduced arbitrary criteria by reducing the weightage of seniority, assigning marks for "good entries" favouring certain categories of officers, and introducing a discretionary "Special Promotion" category based on the Inspector General's opinion and trust. They contended that these provisions violated Article 12(1) and Article 14(1)(g) by undermining equality and fair professional advancement. The Supreme Court held that the Special Promotion provision conferred unfettered discretion without objective standards, rendering it arbitrary and unconstitutional. It found that such open-ended authority created a risk of subjective and unequal decision-making inconsistent with the rule of law. Applying severability, the Court struck down only the impugned discretionary promotion clause while preserving the remainder of the scheme. The Court also rejected a preliminary time-bar objection, holding that limitation runs from the date of actual knowledge of the impugned scheme. It further held that arbitrary denial of fair promotional consideration directly impairs effective engagement in lawful occupation within public service. Accordingly, the Special Promotion category was declared void and the Petitioners' rights were held to be violated.

cases.case_name: N.C. Gajaweera v. National Police Commission
cases.summary: The petitioners, Chief Inspectors of the Special Task Force, challenged the National Police Commission's decision to promote certain officers to Assistant Superintendent of Police without following the established competitive procedure. They alleged that senior and more qualified officers were bypassed in violation of merit-based selection and Article 12(1). The respondents argued administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that once a formal recruitment and promotion scheme with marking criteria is established, it cannot be arbitrarily abandoned. It found that appointments made through letters rather than competitive evaluation were unlawful and inconsistent with administrative fairness. The Court recognized the petitioners' legitimate expectation that promotions would be based on published criteria. It further held that failure to provide rational justification for deviation from procedure constituted arbitrariness. The Court declared the impugned appointments null and void and ordered adherence to proper selection processes. It concluded that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated due to unequal and non-transparent treatment in public service recruitment.

retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on presumption of innocence and retrospective penalties. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 13(5) and 13(6) shall be subject only to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national security. For the purposes of this paragraph law includes regulations made under the law for the time being relating to public security.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination

The Supreme Court held that once a competitive recruitment process is completed and a merit list is finalized, candidates acquire a legitimate expectation of promotion. It found that the retrospective cancellation of a valid selection process was arbitrary and irrational. The Court further held that while restructuring of public services is permissible, it cannot be used to nullify completed lawful processes without justification. It emphasized that administrative discretion must be exercised consistently with the rule of law and fairness. Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and quashed the impugned cancellation decisions.

The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. cases.case_name: W. M. K. De Silva v. Chairman, Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation and Others
cases.summary: In SC Application No. 69/88, the petitioner, a clerical employee of the Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation, challenged her termination through a "vacation of post" notice issued without inquiry. She alleged that she was physically present at work but was denied duties and that the termination was politically motivated following a change in management. She further claimed psychological distress and reputational harm resulting from the abrupt dismissal. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 11 and 14(1)(g). It held that use of disciplinary mechanisms such as "vacation of post" in the absence of factual basis or fair inquiry constituted an abuse of administrative power. The Court found that the termination was arbitrary, lacked procedural fairness, and effectively deprived the petitioner of her lawful occupation. It further held that humiliating removal of an employee without due process amounted to degrading treatment under Article 11. The Court emphasized that public authorities must act as model employers and cannot use administrative discretion to settle personal or political scores. It concluded that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered reinstatement with back wages and costs.

cases.case_name: Jayakody v. Sri Lanka Insurance and Robinson Hotel Co. Ltd
cases.summary: The petitioner, an employee of Robinson Club Bentota Ltd., was suspended following allegations of fraud by management officials. The company operated as a joint venture involving Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation and a foreign corporation. A preliminary objection was raised that the suspension constituted a private employment matter and did not amount to executive or administrative action capable of founding a fundamental rights claim under Article 126. The case involved Article 12(1) concerning equality before the law. The Supreme Court examined the relationship between the State and the corporate entities involved. It held that Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation was effectively a State agency because its shares were held by the Treasury and its directors were state-appointed. The Court further reasoned that the second respondent company functioned as an agent of the State entity, and disciplinary actions carried out through that corporate structure retained the character of executive or administrative action. Distinguishing earlier restrictive decisions concerning statutory corporations, the Court expanded the scope of constitutional jurisdiction where effective state control existed over the entity concerned. Accordingly, the preliminary objection was overruled and the matter was permitted to proceed on its merits within the Supreme Court's fundamental rights jurisdiction.

cases.case_name: Batuwana Dewage Lionel Hemakumara v. Ruwan Gunasekara and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a Reserve Sub-Inspector of Police, was suspended from service in 1999 following his arrest on a murder charge. Although he was acquitted in 2011, disciplinary proceedings continued for several years until he was reinstated on August 19, 2016, subject to the condition that he would not receive back wages for the seventeen-year suspension period. The Petitioner challenged the refusal to pay back wages as arbitrary and discriminatory, alleging a violation of Article 12(1). The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application was filed outside the one-month constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2), as the reinstatement letter containing the impugned condition had been issued in August 2016 while the application was filed only in December 2016. The Court upheld the preliminary objection and held that the filing of an administrative appeal did not suspend or renew the constitutional limitation period. The Court further held that reserve police officers were governed by distinct circulars and conditions of service from the regular police force and were entitled to remuneration only for periods during which they actually performed duties. Since the Petitioner had not worked during the suspension period, he possessed no legal entitlement to back wages. The Court also rejected the allegation of discrimination because the Petitioner failed to establish differential treatment compared to similarly situated reservists. The application was accordingly dismissed for being time-barred and lacking substantive merit.

cases.case_name: M.D.S.A. Perera v. Dharmasena Dissanayake and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a senior accountant in the public service, challenged disciplinary proceedings initiated shortly before retirement, alleging violation of Article 12(1) due to arbitrary administrative action. The dispute arose after he used official stamp in Right to Information applications relating to a public incident, initially attracting a recommendation for a warning only. The Public Service Commission later escalated the matter into formal disciplinary charges and compelled retirement under statutory provisions allowing retirement pending inquiry. The Supreme Court examined whether the escalation from a warning to formal charges was supported by a prima facie case. It held that the preliminary investigation had not established misconduct and that initiation of charges lacked evidentiary foundation. The Court found that the Commission acted contrary to procedural safeguards under the Establishments Code and ignored recommendations of subordinate authorities without justification. It further held that the timing and circumstances of the proceedings indicated arbitrariness and misuse of disciplinary powers. The Court concluded that the actions of the Public Service Commission amounted to unequal and arbitrary treatment in violation of Article 12(1). It held the petitioner's rights were infringed and awarded costs against the State.

cases.case_name: Wickramasinghe and Others v. Attorney General
cases.summary: The petitioners, public sector technical officers, challenged a decision altering their salary placement after appointment. Although initial recruitment documents guaranteed higher salary steps to preserve prior seniority and pay, the respondents later unilaterally placed them at lower initial salary levels. The petitioners alleged violation of Article 12(1), arguing breach of legitimate expectation and unfair administrative action. The respondents contended that revised administrative decisions justified the salary adjustment. The Supreme Court held that the salary terms formed part of binding employment conditions and could not be altered unilaterally after acceptance of appointment. It found that the respondents acted arbitrarily and contrary to principles of fairness and consistency in administrative law. The Court further held that legitimate expectation arising from official appointment letters must be honoured unless a rational basis exists for deviation. It concluded that failure to implement agreed salary steps constituted unequal and unreasonable treatment under Article 12(1). Accordingly, the Court found that the petitioners' fundamental rights were violated and directed restoration of the originally promised salary structure.

retrieved_cases.case_name: W. M. K. De Silva v. Chairman, Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: In SC Application No. 69/88, the petitioner, a clerical employee of the Ceylon Fertilizer Corporation, challenged her termination through a "vacation of post" notice issued without inquiry. She alleged that she was physically present at work but was denied duties and that the termination was politically motivated following a change in management. She further claimed psychological distress and reputational harm resulting from the abrupt dismissal. The Supreme Court examined violations of Articles 11 and 14(1)(g). It held that use of disciplinary mechanisms such as "vacation of post" in the absence of factual basis or fair inquiry constituted an abuse of administrative power. The Court found that the termination was arbitrary, lacked procedural fairness, and effectively deprived the petitioner of her lawful occupation. It further held that humiliating removal of an employee without due process amounted to degrading treatment under Article 11. The Court emphasized that public authorities must act as model employers and cannot use administrative discretion to settle personal or political scores. It concluded that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and ordered reinstatement with back wages and costs.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Jayakody v. Sri Lanka Insurance and Robinson Hotel Co. Ltd
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, an employee of Robinson Club Bentota Ltd., was suspended following allegations of fraud by management officials. The company operated as a joint venture involving Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation and a foreign corporation. A preliminary objection was raised that the suspension constituted a private employment matter and did not amount to executive or administrative action capable of founding a fundamental rights claim under Article 126. The case involved Article 12(1) concerning equality before the law. The Supreme Court examined the relationship between the State and the corporate entities involved. It held that Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation was effectively a State agency because its shares were held by the Treasury and its directors were state-appointed. The Court further reasoned that the second respondent company functioned as an agent of the State entity, and disciplinary actions carried out through that corporate structure retained the character of executive or administrative action. Distinguishing earlier restrictive decisions concerning statutory corporations, the Court expanded the scope of constitutional jurisdiction where effective state control existed over the entity concerned. Accordingly, the preliminary objection was overruled and the matter was permitted to proceed on its merits within the Supreme Court's fundamental rights jurisdiction.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Batuwana Dewage Lionel Hemakumara v. Ruwan Gunasekara and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a Reserve Sub-Inspector of Police, was suspended from service in 1999 following his arrest on a murder charge. Although he was acquitted in 2011, disciplinary proceedings continued for several years until he was reinstated on August 19, 2016, subject to the condition that he would not receive back wages for the seventeen-year suspension period. The Petitioner challenged the refusal to pay back wages as arbitrary and discriminatory, alleging a violation of Article 12(1). The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application was filed outside the one-month constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2), as the reinstatement letter containing the impugned condition had been issued in August 2016 while the application was filed only in December 2016. The Court upheld the preliminary objection and held that the filing of an administrative appeal did not suspend or renew the constitutional limitation period. The Court further held that reserve police officers were governed by distinct circulars and conditions of service from the regular police force and were entitled to remuneration only for periods during which they actually performed duties. Since the Petitioner had not worked during the suspension period, he possessed no legal entitlement to back wages. The Court also rejected the allegation of discrimination because the Petitioner failed to establish differential treatment compared to similarly situated reservists. The application was accordingly dismissed for being time-barred and lacking substantive merit.

intake.incident_location: Saranankara Housing Project, Kalubowila, Dehiwala
intake.actor_name: Dehiwala Mount Lavinia Municipal Council and Urban Development Authority
intake.actor_role: municipal council officials and urban development authorities
intake.what_happened: I live in a housing scheme and built a small additional structure in front of my house because of lack of space. The Municipal Commissioner later sent me a letter saying the construction was unauthorized and asking me to remove it. A few days later, municipal officers came to the premises and I say they removed the spiral staircase connected to the structure without first obtaining a court order.
intake.harm_suffered: Threatened demolition of part of the house, alleged removal of access to the upper floor, distress, humiliation, disruption to home life, and fear of losing part of the residence.
intake.user_narrative: I live in a house in the Saranankara Housing Project in Kalubowila. Because my family did not have enough space, I first put up a small temporary structure in front of the house and later made it into a permanent two-storey structure of the same size. The Municipal Commissioner sent me a letter saying the construction was unauthorized and directing me to remove it. Soon after, municipal officers came to the property and I say they removed the spiral staircase without giving me proper notice or first getting a court order. I believe the officials acted unfairly and that my home and family were affected.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that municipal authorities unlawfully required her to demolish an unauthorized structure and removed a spiral staircase, violating Articles 11, 12(1) and 14(1)(h), with leave granted on Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(h). The Court held that the Urban Development Authority had validly delegated planning-related powers to local authority officers, including powers connected with enforcement against unauthorized development. The Court also found that the petitioner admitted building a permanent structure without prior approval, that the structure encroached on a common roadway and drain affecting other residents, and that the evidence did not prove that municipal officers removed the spiral staircase or fence. The petitioner therefore failed to establish any infringement of Article 12(1) or 14(1)(h), and the Article 11 allegation was not accepted.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed with no order as to costs. The respondents were directed to demolish the unauthorized construction forthwith in terms of the law and procedure.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation municipal unauthorized-construction case. Useful for false-violation control because the petitioner alleged arbitrary demolition-related action and home interference, but the Court found valid delegated authority, insufficient proof of the alleged removal, and unlawful encroachment by the petitioner onto roadway and drainage space. No internal corpus case ID was provided, so source_case_id is null and gold_relevant_case_ids is empty.

cases.case_name:
Don Piyasena Karunaratne and Others v. Anuradhapura Municipal Council and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, former occupants of Municipal Council staff quarters, sought transfer of ownership of the houses they had occupied for several decades, relying on a rent-purchase claim and a ministerial direction asserting a long-term expectation of ownership. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) due to unequal treatment in denial of property transfer. The Respondents argued that the premises were staff quarters not eligible for conversion and that statutory provisions under the housing legislation restricted ownership transfer based on rent thresholds, which the Petitioners exceeded. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were legally ineligible under the governing statutory framework, particularly Section 5(A), which imposed strict eligibility conditions. It further found that the agreements constituted tenancy arrangements rather than enforceable rent-purchase contracts capable of creating ownership rights. The Court also held that no legitimate expectation arose because the Council had made no binding promise but only indicated discretionary future consideration. Accordingly, it concluded that there was no arbitrary or unequal treatment and dismissed the application for failure to establish a constitutional violation.

cases.case_name: Ernest Fernando v. Municipal Council of Moratuwa and Others
cases.summary: In SC(FR) Application No. 278/2021, the petitioner challenged the Moratuwa Municipal Council's handling of a housing estate title transfer policy. The Council had introduced a scheme to transfer deeds to long-term occupants at a nominal value, yet the petitioner alleged unequal treatment, claiming that others received deeds while his long-standing occupation was ignored. His claim was complicated by a prior Court of Appeal determination that his purchase agreement was void under the Registration of Title Act. The Supreme Court examined whether there was a violation of Article 12(1) based on alleged unequal application of the policy. The Court found that at the time of filing, no final administrative refusal had been made and the process was still ongoing, rendering the application premature. However, it observed that public authorities must apply policies consistently and fairly, and that long-term possession, including predecessor occupation, could be relevant in assessing entitlement. It emphasized that arbitrary deviation from declared policy may infringe equality guarantees. Despite dismissing the application on procedural grounds, the Court directed the Council to consider the petitioner's eligibility fairly and make a reasoned determination. A dissenting view held that reliance on a void agreement could not establish lawful possession for benefit under the policy.

cases.case_name:
Daya Chandrasiri Jayanetti and Others v. Urban Development Authority (UDA)
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, residents of Chapel Lane, Nugegoda, challenged the operation of Royal Institute and the construction of unauthorized high-rise buildings within a Mixed Development Zone where educational institutions were prohibited under the applicable Development Plan. They alleged that the Urban Development Authority and Kotte Municipal Council unlawfully permitted construction contrary to zoning regulations, including erecting a building with five upper floors on a site below the minimum land extent and situated on a road only six meters wide instead of the required twelve meters. The Petitioners further complained that no Certificate of Conformity had been issued for one building despite occupation by approximately 1,900 students, causing traffic congestion, noise, and restrictions on movement. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(h), they argued that the authorities had granted preferential treatment to the school while disregarding the rights of residents. The Court held that the Respondents had violated the Petitioners' fundamental rights by failing to enforce zoning laws and building regulations. It emphasized that occupation without a Certificate of Conformity directly contravened statutory regulations and created serious public safety risks. The Court found the approval of a high-rise building on a narrow road to be an intentional violation of legal requirements and ordered the demolition of the illegal constructions and cancellation of permits within three months.

cases.case_name: Subadra v. Kotikawatte Mulleriyawa Pradeshiya Sabha
cases.summary: The petitioner alleged that officers of the Pradeshiya Sabha forcibly entered her property and demolished a boundary wall without prior notice, claiming it was done to harass her and benefit a neighbour. The respondents contended that the wall was an unauthorised structure on a reservation and that it collapsed accidentally during lawful drainage maintenance work. The petitioner alleged violation of Article 12(1). The Supreme Court dismissed the application, accepting the respondents' explanation that the damage occurred incidentally during lawful public works and was not a targeted demolition. The Court further held that the structure was illegal and therefore no compensable right arose from its damage. It emphasized that state authorities performing lawful duties cannot be held liable for incidental damage to unlawful constructions unless mala fides are proven. The Court found no evidence of malice, discrimination, or selective targeting against the petitioner. It concluded that the petitioner failed to discharge the burden of proof required to establish unequal treatment or arbitrary state action, and accordingly held that no fundamental rights violation was established.

cases.case_name: Roberts and Another v. Ratnayake and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners held municipal tenancies and leases for business stalls which were terminated by the Kandy Municipal Council on grounds of unauthorized structural alterations and residential use of commercial premises. They alleged unequal treatment compared to other stallholders who committed similar by-law breaches but were not terminated, invoking Article 12(1) on equality and equal protection. The State contended that termination was lawful due to contractual breaches and municipal by-laws. The Supreme Court held that the Petitioners were not similarly circumstanced to the other tenants as they had committed both by-law violations and breaches of tenancy agreements. It further held that enforcement of contractual terms does not automatically amount to infringement of fundamental rights unless constitutional arbitrariness is established. The Court found that lawful termination of tenancy under contractual and statutory authority could not be challenged as discriminatory absent proof of identical circumstances and irrational differentiation. It concluded that the Petitioners failed to discharge the burden of proving unequal treatment under Article 12(1), and therefore no fundamental rights violation was established. The application was dismissed.

intake.actor_name: Airport and Aviation Services (Sri Lanka) (Private) Limited
intake.actor_role: public aviation company officials and board members
intake.what_happened: We are engineers, senior technical officers and technical officers employed by Airport and Aviation Services. We obtained postgraduate qualifications such as MBAs because professional allowances had previously been paid more broadly, but after a revision to the professional allowance scheme, we were excluded because we did not fall within the specified engineering professional qualification category or divisional-head category.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of professional allowance, reduced employment benefits, financial loss, disappointment after pursuing postgraduate studies, and alleged unequal treatment in salary-related benefits.
intake.user_narrative: We work at Airport and Aviation Services as engineers, senior technical officers and technical officers. Many of us pursued postgraduate studies such as MBAs because we believed these qualifications would help us qualify for professional allowances. Earlier, the allowance had been paid more broadly, but after the scheme was revised, we were excluded because the company said our qualifications did not fall within the required professional category for engineering staff. We believe this is unfair because we invested time and money in higher studies expecting to receive the allowance, and we feel we were treated unequally compared with others who receive it.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged that the revised professional allowance scheme violated Article 12(1) because they had obtained postgraduate business qualifications and had expected to qualify for the allowance. The Court held that the petitioners were employed in the engineering field but did not possess the relevant professional engineering qualifications required under the revised scheme, and therefore were not similarly circumstanced with engineers who qualified for the allowance. The Court also noted that the petitioners had been warned that the postgraduate business studies they pursued were not relevant for the classification they sought. In addition, the application was filed well outside the one-month period after the revision was communicated, making it time-barred. No infringement of Article 12(1) was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed without costs.

intake.incident_location: Kalukele junction on the Polonnaruwa-Mahiyanganaya main road and Aralaganwila Police Station
intake.actor_name: Sri Lanka Police, Aralaganwila Police Station
intake.what_happened: We took part in a village protest at Kalukele junction because wild elephants were repeatedly entering our village and paddy fields, damaging crops and property and causing fear among villagers. The protest blocked the main road for some time. Police later said a Magistrate had issued orders relating to the protest, but those orders were not addressed to us. Several days later, we were summoned to Aralaganwila Police Station, arrested in relation to the protest, produced before the Magistrate and remanded.
intake.harm_suffered: Arrest, police custody, remand custody for about 14 days, disruption to farming during the Yala cultivation season, alleged loss to paddy fields due to inability to attend to them, distress, restriction of liberty, and fear that the arrest was punishment for joining a protest.
intake.user_narrative: We are villagers from Kalukele. For a long time wild elephants had been entering our village and paddy fields, damaging crops and houses and even causing deaths. Because the authorities had not properly solved the problem, many villagers joined a protest at Kalukele junction to draw attention to our situation. The protest blocked the Polonnaruwa-Mahiyanganaya main road. Police came and later said there were court orders about stopping the protest, but those orders were not addressed to us and we were not personally served with them. We attended a meeting at the police station the next day about the elephant issue. Several days later, we were told to come to the Aralaganwila Police Station, where we were arrested and later remanded. We believe the police unfairly used the criminal process against us for taking part in the protest.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The Court held that the protest at Kalukele junction, though arising from genuine grievances about the human-elephant conflict, unlawfully blocked the Polonnaruwa-Mahiyanganaya main road and amounted to offences including public nuisance, obstruction and wrongful restraint. Therefore the arrest of the petitioners for being members of an unlawful assembly and causing wrongful restraint was not unlawful, and Article 13(1) was not infringed. The Court also declined to find violations of Articles 12(1), 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b) because of the unlawful character of the protest, and no final relief was granted on the other pleaded Article 14 claims. However, the 1st respondent's B Report did not comply with the law and his request to remand the petitioners was based on arbitrary and insufficient reasons. This caused the petitioners to be detained in remand custody for 14 days, infringing Article 13(2).
gold.gold_remedy: The application was partly allowed. The Court declared that the 1st respondent infringed the petitioners' rights under Article 13(2) and ordered him to pay Rs. 30,000 as compensation from his personal funds to the two petitioners. The Court also directed the Attorney General to convey observations on the human-elephant conflict to relevant executive authorities and file a report within six months, directed the Inspector General of Police to issue a Police Order on protest-related policing principles and file a report within six months, and directed the Registrar to forward copies of the judgment to specified officials.
gold.evaluation_notes: Partial-violation protest and remand case. retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of access to public places and worship
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of peaceful assembly
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of peaceful assembly. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to form and join trade unions
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to form and join trade unions. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to form and join a trade union.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
