The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of access to public places and worship
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. The alleged violation appears to be **(a) A DIRECT act by a state authority acting in official capacity**.

Here's the reasoning:

1.  **The role of the actor involved:** The actors involved are identified as "police officers" from the "Sri Lanka Police, Aralaganwila Police Station." The police are a state institution responsible for law enforcement.
2.  **Whether they were acting in official capacity:** The facts state that the individuals were "summoned to Aralaganwila Police Station, arrested in relation to the protest, produced before the Magistrate and remanded." These actions—summoning, arrest, production before a Magistrate, and remand—are official functions and powers exercised by police officers and the judiciary within the framework of the criminal justice system. They are not actions that can be undertaken by private individuals.
3.  **The relevant constitutional provisions regarding state action:** While the provided constitutional articles do not explicitly define "state action," provisions like Article 13(1) ("No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law") and Article 13(2) ("Every person held in custody... shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court...") describe actions (arrest, detention, production before a judge) that are inherently carried out by state authorities (police, courts) in their official capacity. The alleged violation directly concerns these types of actions.
4.  **Any distinction between personal conduct and official conduct:** The actions described (arrest, production before a Magistrate, remand) are specific powers and duties conferred upon law enforcement and judicial officers by the state. They are clearly distinct from personal conduct and fall squarely within the scope of official duties.

We found 3 similar case(s) in our database: Bernard Soysa v Attorney-General; Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others; Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector

cases.case_name: Bernard Soysa v Attorney-General
cases.summary: On 11 January 1991 the petitioners, who were members of political parties, organized a Satyagraha protest at the Maha Maluwa of the Dalada Maligawa in Kandy to demonstrate against the Gulf War. Police officers intervened, seized posters and placards, and dispersed the gathering. The petitioners maintained that the protest was peaceful and alleged violations of Articles 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b) of the Constitution relating to freedom of speech, expression, and peaceful assembly. The police contended that the demonstrators were shouting slogans, carrying placards, obstructing access to a sacred religious site, and disturbing public order during a period of civil unrest. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been infringed. The Court reasoned that the Maha Maluwa was primarily a place associated with worship and religious observance rather than a public forum intended for political demonstrations. It emphasized that no implied right existed to conduct political protests at such a location without obtaining permission from the relevant religious authorities. The Court further found that the gathering could not be regarded as entirely peaceful because the shouting of slogans and display of placards disrupted the religious atmosphere surrounding the temple premises. Since the freedoms guaranteed under Article 14 are subject to restrictions in the interests of public order, the police were entitled to act under existing legal powers to disperse an assembly perceived as threatening security and order at a sensitive religious location.

cases.case_name: Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

cases.case_name:
Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector
Channa Abeyratne and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector Channa Abeyratne and Others arose from a land dispute involving allegations of encroachment by a Buddhist priest. The petitioner claimed that on 7 June 2010 he was forcibly arrested at his residence and detained at Maho Police Station until midnight, during which he was allegedly threatened by the Headquarters Inspector. The respondents denied any arrest, stating that the petitioner voluntarily attended the station upon request to resolve the complaint. Police records indicated the officer-in-charge was away on duty, and an affidavit from the petitioner's uncle confirmed that the petitioner went to the station on his own and left without complaint. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 12(1) and 13(1), asserting arbitrary arrest and unequal treatment. The Supreme Court emphasised that in fundamental rights proceedings alleging police misconduct, the burden lies on the petitioner to establish facts with a high degree of probability. It found significant inconsistencies between the petitioner's version and contemporaneous documentary and testimonial evidence. The Court held that there was no credible proof of arrest within the meaning of law and that the petitioner's attendance at the police station was voluntary. Accordingly, the Court concluded that no infringement of constitutional rights had been established and dismissed the application in its entirety for failure of proof.

cases.case_name:
Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and
Others
cases.summary: The petitioner in Gurusinghe Senevirathnage Tharindu Priyan Akalanka v. Wijesinghe and Others concerned allegations of custodial torture and illegal detention following an arrest on 20 September 2017 by Anuradhapura police officers. The petitioner alleged that he was arrested without explanation, taken to a secluded teak forest near Thisa Wewa, suspended from a tree, and brutally assaulted for two hours before being detained at the police station for four days without medical care or production before a Magistrate. The respondents claimed that he was a drug user who sustained injuries while attempting to flee during questioning related to a stolen motorcycle. Medical evidence, however, confirmed six grievous injuries including a brachial plexus rupture consistent with forceful suspension. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2). The Supreme Court found the respondents' explanation wholly implausible and held that the injuries could only have resulted from deliberate custodial violence. It further held that failure to maintain proper arrest records and failure to produce the petitioner before a Magistrate constituted unlawful detention. The Court concluded that both torture and arbitrary detention were established and held the responsible officers personally liable, awarding compensation and costs from their personal funds.

cases.case_name:
Ven. Aturupalayagama Pragna Surinda Thero and Another v. Officer-in-Charge,
Police Station, Minneriya and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, Buddhist monks, alleged that police officers unlawfully deprived them of possession of a temple and facilitated rival claimants in violation of Article 12(1). The dispute arose after competing claims over occupation of temple premises led to potential public disorder, prompting police intervention and a Magistrate's order directing custody to be vested with the Divisional Secretary. The respondents argued that police acted to maintain public order and prevent escalation of conflict between rival groups. The Supreme Court examined whether police conduct was arbitrary or discriminatory. It found that the petitioners had suppressed material facts, including their initial unlawful occupation of state land and lack of formal monastic status at the time of dispute. The Court held that police acted lawfully under judicial direction and took necessary steps to prevent breach of peace. It further found that property custody was managed by the lawful civil authority pursuant to court order, not by arbitrary police action. The Court concluded that the petitioners failed to establish bad faith or unequal treatment and that the application lacked credibility. Accordingly, it held that Article 12(1) was not violated and dismissed the application with costs.

Here's an analysis of each case:

**Case 1: Bernard Soysa v Attorney-General (S.C. APPLICATION NO. 2/91) [1991]**

1.  **KEY SIMILAR FACTS**:
    *   Both situations involve a public protest where police intervened.
    *   In both, there was an alleged disruption: the current situation involved blocking a main road, while Bernard Soysa involved shouting slogans, displaying placards, obstructing access to a sacred site, and disturbing public order.

2.  **COURT DECISION**:
    *   The court found no violation of fundamental rights and dismissed the application.

3.  **RATIO DECIDENDI**:
    *   The core legal reasoning was that the location of the protest (Maha Maluwa) was primarily for worship, not political demonstrations, and no implied right existed to protest there without permission.
    *   The court also reasoned that the gathering was not entirely peaceful due to shouting slogans and disrupting the religious atmosphere.
    *   It emphasized that freedoms under Article 14 are subject to restrictions in the interests of public order, justifying police action to disperse an assembly perceived as threatening security and order.

4.  **RELEVANCE TO CURRENT SITUATION**:
    *   This precedent suggests that the right to protest is not absolute and can be restricted if it disrupts public order.
    *   A court might consider whether blocking a main road, as in the current situation, constitutes a disruption to public order that could justify police intervention, similar to how disrupting a sacred site was viewed in Bernard Soysa.
    *   However, the specific context of a sacred religious site in Bernard Soysa differs from a public road, which might lead to different considerations regarding the reasonableness of restrictions.

**Case 2: Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others (SC FR 253/2020) [2020]**

1.  **KEY SIMILAR FACTS**:
    *   Both situations involve an arrest by the police.
    *   In both, there are allegations of police acting improperly or unfairly using the criminal process (settling a civil dispute in Abeynayake, and allegedly punishing for protest in the current situation).
    *   In both, the police claimed their actions were lawful (based on a cognizable offence in Abeynayake, and based on court orders and public order in the current situation).

2.  **COURT DECISION**:
    *   The court found no violation of fundamental rights and dismissed the petition.

3.  **RATIO DECIDENDI**:
    *   The core legal reasoning was that the police intervention and arrest were lawful because they were based on a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence

step_10.answer:
SECTION 1 — RIGHTS ASSESSMENT:
Based on the structured reasoning chain, the following article(s) appear to remain supported as potentially violated:
- Article 13(1): The facts suggest a potential violation of Article 13(1) as the villagers were arrested 'several days later' after the protest, after being summoned to the police station, and they believe the police 'unfairly used the criminal process' against them for protesting. The claim that court orders were not addressed to them or personally served further suggests a potential lack of procedure established by law for their arrest. Precedent in W.M.K. Wijesuriya (ID 113) and S.C. (FR) Application No. 20/2009 (ID 324) supports claims of unlawful arrest where proper procedure is not followed or where arrest is for exercising fundamental rights without lawful justification.

Weak or uncertain article(s):
- Article 13(2): While the petitioners were arrested, the provided facts do not explicitly state that they were not informed of the reasons for their arrest at the time of arrest. The narrative focuses on the unfairness of the process and the lack of service of court orders, rather than a failure to communicate the immediate reasons for arrest. W.M.K. Wijesuriya (ID 113) supports this article if reasons were not given, but the facts are not explicit on this point.
- Article 13(4): The facts state that the villagers were 'arrested and later remanded,' which implies they were produced before a Magistrate, as remand requires a judicial order. The core complaint appears to be about the lawfulness of the arrest and the subsequent remand itself, rather than a failure to be brought before a judge without unreasonable delay or an unlawful detention prior to judicial production. While W.M.K. Wijesuriya (ID 113) addresses the right to be brought before a judge, the facts do not clearly indicate a violation of this specific procedural aspect.
- Article 12(1): The petitioners state they believe the police 'unfairly used the criminal process against us for taking part in the protest,' which could imply unequal treatment. However, the provided facts do not offer specific details or comparative evidence to demonstrate that they were treated differently from others in similar circumstances or that the law was applied discriminatorily based on a protected ground. The claim is a general assertion of unfairness.
- Article 14(1)(b): While the villagers participated in a protest to draw attention to their situation, which is an exercise of the freedom of peaceful assembly, the facts state that 'The protest blocked the Polonnaruwa-Mahiyanganaya main road.' This action could be considered a disruption to public order, which may fall under permissible restrictions on fundamental rights. Bernard Soysa (ID 17) serves as a cautionary precedent, indicating that protests causing public disruption or not being entirely peaceful may justify police intervention. S.C. (FR) Application No. 20/2009 (ID 324) supports the right to peaceful assembly, but the 'blocking of a main road' introduces a significant factual challenge to the 'peaceful' aspect of the assembly.

SECTION 2 — PRECEDENT:
The precedent alignment was classified as: supports.

SECTION 3 — STRENGTHS OF THE CASE:
- The alleged act involves direct action by a state authority (police officers) in their official capacity, which is a prerequisite for a fundamental rights claim.
- The petitioners explicitly state their belief that the police 'unfairly used the criminal process against us for taking part in the protest,' suggesting a direct link between their protest activity and the subsequent arrest and remand.
- The claim that court orders regarding the protest were not addressed to the villagers or personally served suggests potential procedural irregularities in the arrest, directly supporting a claim under Article 13(1).
- The petitioners suffered actual, tangible harm including arrest, police custody, and remand custody, which constitutes a restriction of liberty.
- Precedent from W.M.K. Wijesuriya (ID 113) and S.C. (FR) Application No. 20/2009 (ID 324) directly supports claims of unlawful arrest under Article 13(1) where proper procedure is not followed or where arrest is for exercising fundamental rights without lawful justification.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of access to public places and worship
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of access to public places and worship. No person shall, on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex or any one of such grounds, be subject to any disability, liability, restriction or condition with regard to access to shops, public restaurants, hotels, places of public entertainment and places of public worship of his own religion.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from arbitrary arrest
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Punishment only by order of a competent court
retrieved_articles.text: Punishment only by order of a competent court. No person shall be punished with death or imprisonment except by order of a competent court, made in accordance with procedure established by law. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, pending investigation or trial, shall not constitute punishment.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of peaceful assembly
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of peaceful assembly. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of peaceful assembly.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Bernard Soysa v Attorney-General
retrieved_cases.summary: On 11 January 1991 the petitioners, who were members of political parties, organized a Satyagraha protest at the Maha Maluwa of the Dalada Maligawa in Kandy to demonstrate against the Gulf War. Police officers intervened, seized posters and placards, and dispersed the gathering. The petitioners maintained that the protest was peaceful and alleged violations of Articles 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b) of the Constitution relating to freedom of speech, expression, and peaceful assembly. The police contended that the demonstrators were shouting slogans, carrying placards, obstructing access to a sacred religious site, and disturbing public order during a period of civil unrest. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been infringed. The Court reasoned that the Maha Maluwa was primarily a place associated with worship and religious observance rather than a public forum intended for political demonstrations. It emphasized that no implied right existed to conduct political protests at such a location without obtaining permission from the relevant religious authorities. The Court further found that the gathering could not be regarded as entirely peaceful because the shouting of slogans and display of placards disrupted the religious atmosphere surrounding the temple premises. Since the freedoms guaranteed under Article 14 are subject to restrictions in the interests of public order, the police were entitled to act under existing legal powers to disperse an assembly perceived as threatening security and order at a sensitive religious location.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Abeynayake and Others v. Sanjeewa and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioners were involved in a long-standing property dispute concerning use of a private roadway, during which the 12th respondent lodged multiple complaints alleging obstruction and damage to property. Based on one such complaint, the 1st petitioner was arrested by police in Moragahahena for alleged criminal damage. The petitioners alleged that the police acted with bias and used arrest powers to settle a private civil dispute, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 13(1). The respondents maintained that the arrest followed a legitimate complaint of a cognizable offence and was necessary for maintaining public order. The Supreme Court dismissed the petition, holding that police intervention was lawful and based on valid criminal allegations. It found no evidence of collusion or mala fide conduct between the police and the complainant. The Court further held that investigating breaches of peace and property damage falls within the lawful duties of the police. It concluded that the arrest was not arbitrary but grounded in a specific complaint supported by reasonable cause. Accordingly, no violation of fundamental rights was established.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector
Channa Abeyratne and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner in Herath Mudiyanselage Wasantha Anura Kumara v. Headquarters Inspector Channa Abeyratne and Others arose from a land dispute involving allegations of encroachment by a Buddhist priest. The petitioner claimed that on 7 June 2010 he was forcibly arrested at his residence and detained at Maho Police Station until midnight, during which he was allegedly threatened by the Headquarters Inspector. The respondents denied any arrest, stating that the petitioner voluntarily attended the station upon request to resolve the complaint. Police records indicated the officer-in-charge was away on duty, and an affidavit from the petitioner's uncle confirmed that the petitioner went to the station on his own and left without complaint. The petitioner alleged violations of Articles 12(1) and 13(1), asserting arbitrary arrest and unequal treatment. The Supreme Court emphasised that in fundamental rights proceedings alleging police misconduct, the burden lies on the petitioner to establish facts with a high degree of probability. It found significant inconsistencies between the petitioner's version and contemporaneous documentary and testimonial evidence. The Court held that there was no credible proof of arrest within the meaning of law and that the petitioner's attendance at the police station was voluntary. Accordingly, the Court concluded that no infringement of constitutional rights had been established and dismissed the application in its entirety for failure of proof.

intake.what_happened: We produced and directed a 60-episode television drama at our own expense and submitted it to Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation for telecasting. The drama was approved after preview and later scheduled and advertised for telecast. After some delay and after we signed a commercial agreement, the corporation began airing it, but later terminated the telecast before all episodes were shown, saying it was not generating expected ratings and revenue.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of opportunity to fully telecast the teledrama, alleged financial loss after spending personal savings and borrowings on production, loss of commercial opportunity with other channels, disappointment among viewers, and alleged harm to creative and professional work.
intake.user_narrative: We produced a teledrama called La Sanda Pamula after spending our own savings, borrowing money and even mortgaging property. We submitted it to Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation, paid the preview fee, and were told that it had been approved. The corporation later advertised that the drama would be telecast and eventually started airing it after we signed an agreement. However, before all episodes were shown, the corporation sent a notice terminating the telecast. We believe this was unfair because we had invested heavily in the production, the trailer and telecast on Rupavahini affected our ability to offer it to other channels, and viewers were also disappointed by the sudden cancellation.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioners alleged that Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation unlawfully terminated the telecast of their teledrama and thereby violated constitutional rights including equality, expression, occupation and information-related rights, with leave granted on Articles 12(1), 14(1)(a) and 14(1)(b). The Court held that the dispute arose from a commercial agreement under which the corporation had purchased rights to transmit, retransmit and simulcast the teledrama. The corporation produced viewing ratings and internal reports showing low ratings and insufficient revenue, and the Court accepted that termination was a business decision taken under the agreement. The Court emphasized that every contractual dispute, commercial decision or breach of ordinary rights does not amount to a fundamental rights violation, even where the corporation is amenable to fundamental rights jurisdiction. No fundamental rights violation was established.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed.

cases.case_name: Bennet Rathnayake v Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation
cases.summary: The petitioner produced a telefilm titled "Makara Vijithaya" at considerable expense and repeatedly requested the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation to telecast it during prime time broadcasting hours. The Corporation rejected the request on three occasions through different review boards without disclosing the identities of board members, the criteria applied, the procedures followed, or the reasons for refusal. The petitioner alleged that the conduct of the respondents violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution by denying equal treatment and subjecting him to arbitrary administrative action. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed and awarded substantial compensation and costs, including personal liability against several respondents. The Court reasoned that statutory powers exercised by the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation are held in trust for the public and therefore must be exercised fairly, transparently, and reasonably. It found that the absence of objective standards and the failure to provide reasons or procedural safeguards rendered the decision-making process arbitrary. The Court further emphasized that broadcasting frequencies constitute public property and cannot be controlled capriciously by State authorities. By denying access without rational justification or disclosed standards, the respondents failed to ensure equitable treatment and abused the discretionary powers entrusted to them. The Court concluded that administrative opacity and arbitrary exclusion from public broadcasting violated constitutional guarantees of equality and fair treatment under Article 12(1).

cases.case_name: Vasudeva Nanayakkara v. Choksy and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners sought enforcement of a prior Supreme Court judgment relating to the annulment of the privatization of the Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation, claiming entitlement to profits earned during a transitional period prior to restoration of state ownership. They alleged violation of Article 12(1) in relation to executive implementation of the earlier judgment. The respondents argued that no profits existed and that the claim was inconsistent with final judicial determinations. The Supreme Court rejected the application, relying on audited financial statements showing that the company had incurred losses during the relevant period. It held that there was no factual or legal basis for claiming interim profits. The Court further emphasized the principle of finality of judgments, stating that court orders cannot be reopened or altered through collateral motions. It held that restitution had already been achieved through restoration of ownership and that no further obligations remained. Accordingly, the application was dismissed and no violation of fundamental rights was found.

cases.case_name:
JPC Trade Company Ltd and R. Lahiru Rakshitha v. Jagath P. Wijeweera and
Others
cases.summary: The 1st Petitioner, a Japanese vehicle exporting company, and its Country Manager were investigated by Sri Lanka Customs on allegations of undervaluing imported vehicles in order to reduce customs duties payable to the State. Investigations disclosed that undervalued pro-forma invoices had been issued to local importers while the remaining balance of the vehicle prices was collected through a local agent and transferred unlawfully to Japan. Following an inquiry conducted under the Customs Ordinance, the 2nd Petitioner was ordered to pay a mitigated forfeiture amounting to Rs. 6,000,000. The Petitioners alleged that their rights under Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 13(4) had been violated because the importer involved in the transactions had not been similarly punished. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that Article 12 guarantees equality only in the lawful exercise of executive power and does not entitle a party to claim "equal violation of the law." The Court observed that the Petitioners sought to rely upon the alleged failure to prosecute another party in order to avoid lawful consequences arising from their own misconduct. The Court further noted that the Petitioners had deliberately suppressed material facts because the 2nd Petitioner had already admitted involvement in the undervaluation scheme during the Customs investigation despite later claiming otherwise before Court. The Court held that Customs officials were legally bound to act upon the findings of the inquiry under the Customs Ordinance and that the allegations of arbitrary punishment lacked merit. The application was dismissed with costs.

Muthukumarana and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners in Rajaye Thakserukaruwange Sangamaya and Others v. P. P. D. S. Muthukumarana and Others, a trade union and five government valuers, challenged administrative actions affecting salary increments, seniority deductions, and a revised promotional marking scheme issued in July 2021. They alleged that these measures were retaliatory following trade union activities and discriminated against union members, violating Articles 12(1), 14(1)(d) and 14(1)(g). The State raised a preliminary objection that the application was filed beyond the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2). The Supreme Court examined whether the alleged infringement was continuous and whether a pending Human Rights Commission inquiry could suspend time limits under Section 13(1) of the HRC Act. It held that the publication of the revised marking scheme constituted the last operative act, and therefore the limitation period commenced from that date. The Court further found that the petitioners failed to produce evidence of an ongoing HRC inquiry sufficient to suspend the statutory deadline. Emphasising the mandatory nature of the constitutional time bar, the Court held that bare assertions were insufficient to extend jurisdiction. It concluded that the application was time-barred and dismissed it in limine without examining the substantive merits of the alleged infringement.

cases.case_name: Silva v. Bank of Ceylon
cases.summary: The petitioner challenged the Bank of Ceylon's sale of mortgaged property and its refusal to disclose resale details and remit surplus proceeds after recovery of a loan. The bank had purchased the property at auction and later resold it at a significantly higher price, retaining the excess. The petitioner claimed entitlement to the surplus under statutory and constitutional principles, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The respondents relied on a restrictive interpretation of the Bank of Ceylon Ordinance, arguing no obligation to disclose resale proceeds or pay excess. The Supreme Court held that Section 27 of the Ordinance imposes a statutory duty to return surplus proceeds to the mortgagor after settlement of debt. It further held that refusal to disclose financial details necessary to assert this right was arbitrary and contrary to fairness. The Court emphasized that state-linked financial institutions must act transparently and cannot retain windfall profits beyond lawful entitlement. It found that withholding surplus funds constituted unequal application of law and breach of public trust principles. The petitioner's rights were therefore violated and the bank was directed to disclose, compute, and remit the excess with interest.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Bennet Rathnayake v Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner produced a telefilm titled "Makara Vijithaya" at considerable expense and repeatedly requested the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation to telecast it during prime time broadcasting hours. The Corporation rejected the request on three occasions through different review boards without disclosing the identities of board members, the criteria applied, the procedures followed, or the reasons for refusal. The petitioner alleged that the conduct of the respondents violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution by denying equal treatment and subjecting him to arbitrary administrative action. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed and awarded substantial compensation and costs, including personal liability against several respondents. The Court reasoned that statutory powers exercised by the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation are held in trust for the public and therefore must be exercised fairly, transparently, and reasonably. It found that the absence of objective standards and the failure to provide reasons or procedural safeguards rendered the decision-making process arbitrary. The Court further emphasized that broadcasting frequencies constitute public property and cannot be controlled capriciously by State authorities. By denying access without rational justification or disclosed standards, the respondents failed to ensure equitable treatment and abused the discretionary powers entrusted to them. The Court concluded that administrative opacity and arbitrary exclusion from public broadcasting violated constitutional guarantees of equality and fair treatment under Article 12(1).

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to a fair trial
retrieved_articles.text: Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Bennet Rathnayake v Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner produced a telefilm titled "Makara Vijithaya" at considerable expense and repeatedly requested the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation to telecast it during prime time broadcasting hours. The Corporation rejected the request on three occasions through different review boards without disclosing the identities of board members, the criteria applied, the procedures followed, or the reasons for refusal. The petitioner alleged that the conduct of the respondents violated Article 12(1) of the Constitution by denying equal treatment and subjecting him to arbitrary administrative action. The Supreme Court held that the petitioner's right to equality and equal protection of the law had been infringed and awarded substantial compensation and costs, including personal liability against several respondents. The Court reasoned that statutory powers exercised by the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation are held in trust for the public and therefore must be exercised fairly, transparently, and reasonably. It found that the absence of objective standards and the failure to provide reasons or procedural safeguards rendered the decision-making process arbitrary. The Court further emphasized that broadcasting frequencies constitute public property and cannot be controlled capriciously by State authorities. By denying access without rational justification or disclosed standards, the respondents failed to ensure equitable treatment and abused the discretionary powers entrusted to them. The Court concluded that administrative opacity and arbitrary exclusion from public broadcasting violated constitutional guarantees of equality and fair treatment under Article 12(1).

retrieved_cases.case_name: Silva v. Bank of Ceylon
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner challenged the Bank of Ceylon's sale of mortgaged property and its refusal to disclose resale details and remit surplus proceeds after recovery of a loan. The bank had purchased the property at auction and later resold it at a significantly higher price, retaining the excess. The petitioner claimed entitlement to the surplus under statutory and constitutional principles, alleging violation of Article 12(1). The respondents relied on a restrictive interpretation of the Bank of Ceylon Ordinance, arguing no obligation to disclose resale proceeds or pay excess. The Supreme Court held that Section 27 of the Ordinance imposes a statutory duty to return surplus proceeds to the mortgagor after settlement of debt. It further held that refusal to disclose financial details necessary to assert this right was arbitrary and contrary to fairness. The Court emphasized that state-linked financial institutions must act transparently and cannot retain windfall profits beyond lawful entitlement. It found that withholding surplus funds constituted unequal application of law and breach of public trust principles. The petitioner's rights were therefore violated and the bank was directed to disclose, compute, and remit the excess with interest.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.

Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

source_case_name: Sumith Aluthkorala v. Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority and Others

intake.incident_location: Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority, Colombo
intake.actor_name: Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority
intake.actor_role: provincial public road development authority officials
intake.what_happened: I was appointed as a Road Development Officer on a six-month contract basis by the Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority, and the contract was repeatedly extended for several years. After the last contract period ended, I continued reporting to work expecting the usual renewal letter and arrears of salary, but my salary was stopped and I later received a letter saying my services had been terminated with effect from the earlier expiry date.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of employment, non-payment of salary from August 2008, financial hardship, career uncertainty, and alleged retaliatory termination after involvement in a public land and environmental dispute.
intake.user_narrative: I was appointed as a Road Development Officer for the Colombo District on a six-month contract by the Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority. My contract was repeatedly extended for six months at a time, and in the past I would continue working after the expiry date while the formal renewal letter and salary arrears came later. After my last contract period ended, I continued reporting to duty as usual, but my salary was not paid. Later, I received a letter saying my services had been terminated with effect from the earlier expiry date. I believe this was unfair, especially because I had been involved in opposing the use of a state land called Galgoda Kele for a garbage disposal project and had filed a case about that issue.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that termination of his contract appointment as Road Development Officer violated Article 12(1). The Court held that before claiming relief for termination, the petitioner had to establish that his appointment was lawful. The Western Province Provincial Road Development Authority was established by statute, and the power to appoint staff was vested in the Provincial Public Service Commission. The documents relied on by the petitioner showed appointment or extension by the Chairman or General Manager, who had no statutory power to make such appointments. The appointment was therefore devoid of legal effect and null and void, and the Court could not grant relief that would perpetuate an unlawful appointment. Article 12(1) was not infringed.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed with no order as to costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation public authority employment termination case. Useful for false-violation control because the petitioner alleged unlawful and retaliatory termination after repeated contract extensions, but the Court rejected the Article 12(1) claim because the underlying appointment itself was legally invalid. cases.case_name:
Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Others v. R.B. Premadasa, DG
Rubber Development Dept and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, comprising the Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Rubber Development Officers, challenged a new Scheme of Recruitment approved by the Public Service Commission on 14 November 2014. The revised scheme classified them as Supervisory Management Assistant - Technical officers under salary code MN 3 and removed the degree qualification previously associated with recruitment. The Petitioners contended that their actual duties and status warranted classification as Field or Office Based Officers under salary code MN 5. They further alleged that the changes adversely affected their professional standing and opportunities within the service. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they argued that the scheme was discriminatory and unlawfully interfered with their occupational rights. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application had been filed outside the constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2). Documentary evidence demonstrated that the Petitioners had participated in a meeting on 25 November 2014 specifically discussing amendments to the already approved Scheme of Recruitment, thereby proving prior knowledge of the impugned decision. The Court dismissed the application in limine without examining the substantive merits. It held that the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2) is mandatory and begins from the date the alleged infringement becomes known to the Petitioners. The Court rejected the claim that awareness arose only upon publication of a later job advertisement and found that no exceptional circumstances had prevented earlier invocation of the Court's jurisdiction.

cases.case_name:
Abdul Razak Mohamed Hussain v. M.M.N.D. Bandara, Secretary, Ministry of
Education and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a retired Principal of a Government School, challenged the calculation of his pension and salary-related benefits under Public Administration Circular No. 9/2004, which introduced a revised salary structure for public officers. The dispute concerned whether the Petitioner fell within Clause 10.1, applicable to pensioners retiring on or before December 1, 2004, or Clause 10.2, applicable to officers who worked on December 1, 2004 and retired thereafter. The Petitioner argued that because he had worked on his final day of service, he should receive the more advantageous benefits available under Clause 10.2. The Respondents maintained that the Petitioner's retirement legally took effect on December 1, 2004 and therefore fell squarely within Clause 10.1. The Court relied on prior judicial precedent establishing that where an officer's retirement becomes effective from a specified date, the officer is deemed to have retired on that date itself. Applying this interpretation, the Court held that the Petitioner retired on December 1, 2004 and therefore did not qualify for benefits reserved for officers retiring after that date. The Court further emphasized the necessity of strictly construing the language of administrative circulars governing pension entitlements and held that the Petitioner had received all benefits applicable to his proper category. Since the classification was based on objective criteria applicable uniformly to all similarly situated officers, the Court found no arbitrariness or unequal treatment. The Supreme Court therefore concluded that no violation of Article 12(1) had been established and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Sathkumara Pathirannehelage Sisira Senanayake v. Land Reform Commission
and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner applied for the post of Director Finance at the Land Reform Commission and was selected as the most suitable candidate. By letter dated April 22, 2016, the Commission formally appointed him to the position with effect from May 15, 2016. Acting in reliance on the appointment, the Petitioner resigned from his previous employment. However, on April 28, 2016, the Chairman of the Commission issued a further letter temporarily suspending the appointment without providing any reasons. The Respondents justified the suspension by referring to a Ministry directive ordering an investigation into an appointment. The Petitioner contended that the directive related to the position of Accountant and not to the Director Finance post for which he had been selected. Alleging violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), the Petitioner challenged the legality of the suspension. The Supreme Court held that the Chairman lacked authority to suspend the appointment on the basis of a directive that clearly referred to a different post. The Court further held that suspending a valid appointment without lawful cause, particularly after the Petitioner had resigned from his former employment in reliance upon it, constituted arbitrary and unreasonable executive action. The Court concluded that the Respondents had violated the Petitioner's constitutional rights to equality and lawful occupation. The suspension letter was declared null and void, and directions were issued requiring the Commission to implement the original appointment within one month.

cases.case_name: D.B.D Rajapakshe v. Director General of Irrigation and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner served as a contract Management Assistant in the Irrigation Department from 2008 and was appointed in November 2014 to the permanent and pensionable post of clerk with effect from October 2014 under Circular No. 25/2014. In August 2015, the Director General of Irrigation cancelled her permanent appointment and subsequently prevented her from reporting for duty. The State contended that the appointment had been issued mistakenly because the relevant circular applied only to employees on salary scale MN1, whereas the Petitioner had been receiving remuneration under the slightly higher MN2 scale. The Petitioner alleged that the cancellation of her permanent appointment violated Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Court held that even if the appointment had resulted from an administrative error, the mistake was attributable to the Government and not to any misconduct by the Petitioner. Applying the principle that no person should benefit from his own wrong, the Court reasoned that the State could not penalize a citizen for an error committed by its own officials. The Court further held that the issuance of the appointment letter and payment of salary over an eight-month period created a legitimate expectation that the Petitioner would continue in the permanent cadre until retirement. The cancellation of the appointment solely because she earned a slightly higher salary than the minimum threshold was held to be arbitrary and capricious. The Court therefore found violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), quashed the cancellation letters, ordered reinstatement with back wages, and awarded compensation against the State.

cases.case_name:
Sebastian Benadic and Others v. Kodithuwakku Arachchilage Nihal
Chandrakantha and Others
cases.summary: The petitioners, relatives of victims of a fatal bus accident, alleged that the Road Development Authority failed to maintain road safety by not removing a landslide boulder obstructing a mountainous road, thereby violating Article 12(1). The respondents contended that the road was under contractor supervision, that expert advice recommended careful removal methods due to monsoon risks, and that warning measures had been implemented. The Supreme Court considered whether there was a failure of administrative duty amounting to unequal or arbitrary state action. It found that the authority had taken reasonable steps including partial clearance, installation of warning signs, and engagement of expert consultation for safe removal through chemical blasting. The Court further held that the accident was significantly contributed to by driver negligence, including excessive speed on a hazardous route, and that public authorities are not insurers against all accidents involving negligent conduct by road users. It emphasized that administrative responsibility must be assessed in context of environmental conditions and operational constraints. The Court concluded that the respondents had not acted arbitrarily or in breach of their duty under Article 12(1) and dismissed the application.

step_8.answer:
Here's an analysis of each case:

**Case 1: D.B.D Rajapakshe v. Director General of Irrigation and Others (SC. FR Application No. 418/2015) [2015]**

1.  **KEY SIMILAR FACTS:**
    *   The Petitioner in this case was initially a contract employee whose services were later made permanent, and then her permanent appointment was cancelled. The user was a contract employee whose contract was repeatedly extended, and then their services were terminated.
    *   The cancellation of the Petitioner's appointment was attributed to an administrative error by the Government, not the Petitioner's fault. The user's termination, after a pattern of extensions and continued work, might also involve an administrative decision or oversight.
    *   The Petitioner had a legitimate expectation of continued employment due to the issuance of a permanent appointment letter and payment of salary over an eight-month period. The user, having had their contract repeatedly extended and continuing to report to duty after the last expiry date, also appears to have had an expectation of renewal.
    *   The termination in *Rajapakshe* was deemed arbitrary and capricious. The user's termination, effective from an earlier expiry date after they had continued working, could similarly be argued as arbitrary.

2.  **COURT DECISION:**
    *   The court found a violation of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g).
    *   The outcome was that the cancellation letters were quashed, the Petitioner was reinstated with back wages, and compensation was awarded against the State.

3.  **RATIO DECIDENDI:**
    *   The core legal reasoning was that the State cannot penalize a citizen for an error committed by its own officials, applying the principle that no person should benefit from his own wrong.
    *   The court also held that the issuance of an appointment letter and payment of salary over a period created a legitimate expectation of continued employment until retirement.
    *   The cancellation of an appointment solely due to an administrative error attributable to the State, especially when it affects a legitimate expectation, was considered arbitrary and capricious.

4.  **RELEVANCE TO CURRENT SITUATION:**
    *   This precedent suggests that if the user's termination was due to an administrative decision or error, and the user had a legitimate expectation of continued employment based on the repeated extensions of their contract and the practice of continuing to work after expiry, a court might view the termination as arbitrary and a violation of fundamental rights.

stage_b_cases.case_name: D.B.D Rajapakshe v. Director General of Irrigation and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner served as a contract Management Assistant in the Irrigation Department from 2008 and was appointed in November 2014 to the permanent and pensionable post of clerk with effect from October 2014 under Circular No. 25/2014. In August 2015, the Director General of Irrigation cancelled her permanent appointment and subsequently prevented her from reporting for duty. The State contended that the appointment had been issued mistakenly because the relevant circular applied only to employees on salary scale MN1, whereas the Petitioner had been receiving remuneration under the slightly higher MN2 scale. The Petitioner alleged that the cancellation of her permanent appointment violated Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Court held that even if the appointment had resulted from an administrative error, the mistake was attributable to the Government and not to any misconduct by the Petitioner. Applying the principle that no person should benefit from his own wrong, the Court reasoned that the State could not penalize a citizen for an error committed by its own officials. The Court further held that the issuance of the appointment letter and payment of salary over an eight-month period created a legitimate expectation that the Petitioner would continue in the permanent cadre until retirement. The cancellation of the appointment solely because she earned a slightly higher salary than the minimum threshold was held to be arbitrary and capricious. The Court therefore found violations of Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), quashed the cancellation letters, ordered reinstatement with back wages, and awarded compensation against the State.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Others v. R.B. Premadasa, DG
Rubber Development Dept and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioners, comprising the Sri Lanka Nidahas Rubber Inspectors' Union and Rubber Development Officers, challenged a new Scheme of Recruitment approved by the Public Service Commission on 14 November 2014. The revised scheme classified them as Supervisory Management Assistant - Technical officers under salary code MN 3 and removed the degree qualification previously associated with recruitment. The Petitioners contended that their actual duties and status warranted classification as Field or Office Based Officers under salary code MN 5. They further alleged that the changes adversely affected their professional standing and opportunities within the service. Invoking Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g), they argued that the scheme was discriminatory and unlawfully interfered with their occupational rights. The Respondents raised a preliminary objection that the application had been filed outside the constitutional time limit prescribed by Article 126(2). Documentary evidence demonstrated that the Petitioners had participated in a meeting on 25 November 2014 specifically discussing amendments to the already approved Scheme of Recruitment, thereby proving prior knowledge of the impugned decision. The Court dismissed the application in limine without examining the substantive merits. It held that the one-month limitation period under Article 126(2) is mandatory and begins from the date the alleged infringement becomes known to the Petitioners. The Court rejected the claim that awareness arose only upon publication of a later job advertisement and found that no exceptional circumstances had prevented earlier invocation of the Court's jurisdiction.

stage_b_cases.case_name:
Abdul Razak Mohamed Hussain v. M.M.N.D. Bandara, Secretary, Ministry of
Education and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a retired Principal of a Government School, challenged the calculation of his pension and salary-related benefits under Public Administration Circular No. 9/2004, which introduced a revised salary structure for public officers. The dispute concerned whether the Petitioner fell within Clause 10.1, applicable to pensioners retiring on or before December 1, 2004, or Clause 10.2, applicable to officers who worked on December 1, 2004 and retired thereafter. The Petitioner argued that because he had worked on his final day of service, he should receive the more advantageous benefits available under Clause 10.2. The Respondents maintained that the Petitioner's retirement legally took effect on December 1, 2004 and therefore fell squarely within Clause 10.1. The Court relied on prior judicial precedent establishing that where an officer's retirement becomes effective from a specified date, the officer is deemed to have retired on that date itself. Applying this interpretation, the Court held that the Petitioner retired on December 1, 2004 and therefore did not qualify for benefits reserved for officers retiring after that date. The Court further emphasized the necessity of strictly construing the language of administrative circulars governing pension entitlements and held that the Petitioner had received all benefits applicable to his proper category. Since the classification was based on objective criteria applicable uniformly to all similarly situated officers, the Court found no arbitrariness or unequal treatment.
