retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Existing written law and unwritten law
retrieved_articles.text: Existing written law and unwritten law. All existing written law and unwritten law shall be valid and operative notwithstanding any inconsistency with the preceding provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Removal or deportation orders
retrieved_articles.text: Removal or deportation orders. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Jurisdiction of Supreme Court in respect of fundamental rights. The Supreme Court shall have sole and exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine any question relating to the infringement or imminent infringement by executive or administrative action of any fundamental right or language right declared and recognised by Chapter III or Chapter IV. Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right of access to information
retrieved_articles.text: Right of access to information. Every citizen shall have the right of access to any information as provided for by law, being information that is required for the exercise or protection of a citizen's right held by: (a) the State, a Ministry or any Government Department or any statutory body established or created by or under any law; (b) any Ministry of a Minister of the Board of Ministers of a Province or any Department or any statutory body established or created by a statute of a Provincial Council; (c) any local authority; and (d) any other person, who is in possession of such information relating to any institution referred to in sub-paragraphs (a), (b) or (c) of this paragraph.

A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

Where any person alleges that any such fundamental right or language right relating to such person has been infringed or is about to be infringed by executive or administrative action, he may himself or by an attorney-at-law on his behalf, within one month thereof, in accordance with such rules of court as may be in force, apply to the Supreme Court by way of petition in writing addressed to such Court praying for relief or redress in respect of such infringement. Such application shall be heard by three Judges of the Supreme Court and may be supported by affidavit.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

intake.user_narrative: I run a business in Kattankudy and I am involved in local political work. A woman I knew called me saying two men claiming to be CID officers had come to her house and demanded money to release her husband, who had been arrested in a cannabis case. I went there with some friends, questioned the two men, realized they were not police officers, and called 119. Later I found out that the police had filed a report saying I had assaulted those men and had disappeared from the area. I believe this report was false and was meant to interfere with my involvement in an upcoming political rally. A few days later, police officers arrested me near the Kattankudy Police Station. I say I was not properly told the reason at the time and that the arrest was politically motivated.

cases.case_name: P. D. A. Panapitiya and Another v. Mangala De Soyza Amarasekara
cases.summary: The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

cases.case_name:
H. M. Punchimenike and Another v. D. M. Bandula Saman Dissanayake and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, a mother and daughter, alleged that Excise Department officers used excessive force during an arrest relating to suspected illicit alcohol possession, including physical assault, humiliation in public, and forced transportation. The Respondents contended that only minimum force was used following resistance and abusive conduct by the Petitioners. The Petitioner alleged violation of Article 11, with leave granted only in respect of the second Petitioner. The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture and degrading treatment require a high standard of proof and corroborative evidence of maltreatment of a serious nature. It found that medical records did not support claims of physical assault consistent with the alleged violence, and no injuries were documented. It further held that video evidence submitted failed to substantiate the allegations. The Court also considered inconsistencies in contemporaneous complaints and prior conduct of the Petitioners, affecting credibility. Accordingly, it concluded that the burden of proof had not been discharged and held that no violation of Article 11 was established.

cases.case_name: Abdul Lathif v. Deputy Inspector General of Police, Nuwara Eliya
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

cases.case_name: Ganeshan Samson Roy v. M.M. Janaka Marasinghe and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested and remanded following allegations of financial fraud arising from a complaint by a private individual regarding a disputed transaction involving bank account use and alleged vehicle import fraud. Despite the existence of exculpatory evidence, including recorded communications negating involvement in the alleged scheme, CID officers proceeded with arrest and prosecution. The Petitioner invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2), alleging arbitrary arrest, unequal treatment, and procedural violations. The Supreme Court held that the CID acted mechanically on an unverified complaint without conducting independent assessment of credibility or examining available exculpatory material. It found that the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion and was therefore arbitrary and unconstitutional. The Court further held that failure to communicate specific grounds of arrest violated constitutional safeguards under Article 13(1). It also imposed liability on the private complainant for instigating wrongful executive action through false allegations. However, it found no violation of Article 13(2) as the requirement of production before a Magistrate was satisfied. Accordingly, the Court held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights under Articles 12(1) and 13(1) had been violated.

cases.case_name: Dodampe Gamage Asantha Aravinda v. Atapattu and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner alleged that he was unlawfully arrested following a dispute and subjected to custodial assault and fabricated drug charges by police officers. He further claimed he was detained without proper legal justification and produced before court on false evidence. The case raised issues under Articles 11, 13(1), and 13(2). The Court found credible evidence supporting allegations of physical assault and fabrication of charges, including inconsistencies in police accounts and lack of lawful justification for arrest. It held that the conduct of police officers amounted to cruel, inhuman, and degrading treatment under Article 11. The Court further found that failure to inform the Petitioner of reasons for arrest and delay in judicial production violated constitutional safeguards governing personal liberty. It emphasized that Article 13 protections are fundamental checks against abuse of police power. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's rights were violated and ordered compensation, including State liability for the conduct of its officers.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Abdul Lathif v. Deputy Inspector General of Police, Nuwara Eliya
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

retrieved_cases.case_name: P. D. A. Panapitiya and Another v. Mangala De Soyza Amarasekara
retrieved_cases.summary: The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

retrieved_cases.case_name:
H. M. Punchimenike and Another v. D. M. Bandula Saman Dissanayake and
Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioners, a mother and daughter, alleged that Excise Department officers used excessive force during an arrest relating to suspected illicit alcohol possession, including physical assault, humiliation in public, and forced transportation. The Respondents contended that only minimum force was used following resistance and abusive conduct by the Petitioners. The Petitioner alleged violation of Article 11, with leave granted only in respect of the second Petitioner. The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture and degrading treatment require a high standard of proof and corroborative evidence of maltreatment of a serious nature. It found that medical records did not support claims of physical assault consistent with the alleged violence, and no injuries were documented. It further held that video evidence submitted failed to substantiate the allegations. The Court also considered inconsistencies in contemporaneous complaints and prior conduct of the Petitioners, affecting credibility. Accordingly, it concluded that the burden of proof had not been discharged and held that no violation of Article 11 was established.

Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.
Freedom from torture, cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment. No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The Petitioner, a factory chairman, initially sought police protection due to industrial unrest but was instead arrested on a cheating allegation relating to a settled civil debt. Police ignored information from the complainant and legal counsel confirming settlement of the dispute. Officers misled the Magistrate by falsely claiming the Petitioner was absconding and produced him at a Magistrate's residence at night to obtain a remand order. The constitutional issue concerned Articles 13(1) and 13(2), particularly whether the arrest and subsequent detention were supported by reasonable suspicion and lawful procedure. The Supreme Court held that no objective basis existed for a criminal arrest since the underlying debt was settled, and thus the arrest lacked reasonable suspicion as required by law. It further held that the conduct of the police amounted to mala fide action, involving deliberate deception of the judicial officer and circumvention of legal safeguards. The Court emphasized that obtaining a remand order through misrepresentation vitiates the legality of detention. It concluded that both arrest and detention were arbitrary and unconstitutional, and imposed personal liability on the officers due to their deliberate misconduct, ordering compensation against them and costs against the State.

The first petitioner, a police constable, alleged that his superior officers fabricated allegations of heroin consumption against him because he had refused to release suspected drug traffickers. After being accused at the police station, the petitioner fled fearing a conspiracy. The police subsequently arrested and detained his wife and their nine-month-old child for several hours in an attempt to pressure him into surrendering and giving statements favorable to the respondents. The petitioner later surrendered and obtained negative urine, Judicial Medical Officer, and Government Analyst reports disproving the allegations. Despite this, he was interdicted and faced a second allegedly malicious case accusing him of threatening witnesses after he indicated his intention to seek legal remedies. The petitioners invoked Articles 12(1), 13(1), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that the actions of the respondents were arbitrary, malicious, and constituted an abuse of executive power. The Court reasoned that the medical and analyst reports demonstrated that the drug allegations were fabricated to satisfy personal animosity. The Court further held that arresting and detaining family members, including an infant, in order to pressure a suspect was wholly unlawful and incompatible with constitutional protections against arbitrary arrest. Interdicting the petitioner before lawful inquiry or prosecution was viewed as a calculated attempt to destroy his career and therefore violated equality and occupational rights.

The Petitioners, a mother and daughter, alleged that Excise Department officers used excessive force during an arrest relating to suspected illicit alcohol possession, including physical assault, humiliation in public, and forced transportation. The Respondents contended that only minimum force was used following resistance and abusive conduct by the Petitioners. The Petitioner alleged violation of Article 11, with leave granted only in respect of the second Petitioner. The Supreme Court held that allegations of torture and degrading treatment require a high standard of proof and corroborative evidence of maltreatment of a serious nature. It found that medical records did not support claims of physical assault consistent with the alleged violence, and no injuries were documented. It further held that video evidence submitted failed to substantiate the allegations. The Court also considered inconsistencies in contemporaneous complaints and prior conduct of the Petitioners, affecting credibility. Accordingly, it concluded that the burden of proof had not been discharged and held that no violation of Article 11 was established.

cases.case_name: Veeradas v. Controller of Immigration and Emigration and Others
cases.summary: In SC Application No. 221/88, the petitioner was stopped at an airport boarding gate while attempting to travel abroad to address Amnesty International. An Air Lanka security officer suspected irregularities in the petitioner's passport and detained him, subsequently handing him over to police who produced him before a Magistrate. He was later exonerated when authorities confirmed the passport was genuine. The petitioner alleged that the arrest and detention were politically motivated to prevent him from speaking internationally, violating Articles 11, 13(1), 13(2), 14(1)(a), and 14(1)(h). The Supreme Court examined whether the officer's actions were lawful and justified. It held that the arrest was made in good faith based on reasonable suspicion arising from perceived irregularities in the travel document. The Court found statutory protection applicable where a person acts under a bona fide mistake of fact and believes their conduct is justified by law. It further held that the petitioner failed to prove mala fide intent or political suppression. The arrest and detention were therefore not arbitrary or unlawful. The Court concluded that no violation of fundamental rights had occurred and dismissed the application.

cases.case_name:
Kandegedara Priyawansa v. Gotabhaya Rajapakse, Secretary, Ministry of
Defence and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a former soldier, was arrested on February 27, 2010, by officers of the Terrorist Investigation Division in connection with the murder investigation of journalist Lasantha Wickramatunga. The arrest was based on information that SIM cards allegedly used by the perpetrators had been purchased using the National Identity Card of one Pitchchai Jesudasan, who claimed that he lost his identity card after consuming liquor with the Petitioner. Following his arrest, the Petitioner was detained under a detention order and later remanded in custody. In August 2013, the Magistrate discharged the Petitioner upon the advice of the Attorney General due to absence of evidence. The Petitioner alleged that he had not been informed of the reasons for his arrest and that the arrest and detention violated Articles 12(1) and 13(1) of the Constitution. The Supreme Court held that mere suspicion or association with a person who lost an identity card could not amount to reasonable grounds for arrest in relation to a serious offence such as murder. The Court further noted the absence of arrest notes and the failure of the arresting officer to submit an affidavit justifying the arrest. It held that lawful arrest requires objective material supporting reasonable suspicion rather than conjecture or speculation. Since the initial arrest lacked legal foundation, the detention order issued thereafter was also unsupported by sufficient material. The Court concluded that the Petitioner's constitutional rights had been violated.

cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

cases.case_name:
Major Wengappuli Arachchige Samantha v. Inspector Ranjan Samarasinghe and
Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner, a Major in the Sri Lanka Army, was arrested following a fatal road traffic accident involving an army vehicle in which a child died and several passengers were injured. Although the Petitioner was a passenger, he was arrested and remanded on suspicion of aiding and abetting the driver. The police justified the arrest on alleged breaches of motor traffic law and concerns of public unrest. The Petitioner invoked Articles 12(1) and 13(1), alleging arbitrary arrest and unequal treatment under law. The Supreme Court held that there was no legal or evidentiary basis for imputing abetment, as mere presence in a vehicle does not constitute participation in a criminal act. It further found that the provisions relied upon by police were misapplied to the facts of the case. The Court rejected the justification of protective custody, holding that arrest cannot be effected for the alleged safety of the person detained. It also found a complete absence of reasonable suspicion, rendering the arrest arbitrary and unconstitutional. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioner's fundamental rights had been violated.

cases.case_name: Edward Sivalingam v. Sub Inspector Jayasekera and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested on August 4, 2006 at a lodge in Vavuniya while in possession of a National Identity Card, a Methodist Church identification card, and an LTTE travel pass. Following the discovery of a large cache of explosives in a lorry on the previous day, the authorities suspected the Petitioner of involvement in unlawful activities. The Petitioner alleged that officers attached to the Criminal Investigation Department assaulted him with clubs in order to obtain a confession, causing injuries to his arm, head, and back. He was detained for eight months at CID Headquarters and for a further four months at the Boossa Detention Camp pursuant to successive Detention Orders issued under Emergency Regulations. A confession was recorded in Sinhala, and the Petitioner later asserted that he did not understand the language. The Court examined multiple Medico-Legal Reports from doctors in Colombo and Galle, all of which disclosed no injuries or signs of dislocation, thereby contradicting the allegations of torture. The Court further held that the Petitioner's possession of an LTTE travel pass, coupled with the surrounding circumstances relating to the explosives discovery, provided reasonable suspicion justifying arrest and investigation. The Court also found that the Petitioner had deliberately misled the Court regarding his fluency in Sinhala, noting evidence that he had conducted sermons in Sinhala and originated from a Sinhala-speaking area. The detention was held to be lawful under Emergency Regulations, and the Supreme Court concluded that no violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), or 13(2) had been established.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Abeywardena v Inspector General of Police
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner owned and operated "Jackpot Machines" imported under valid licenses and installed in public establishments. In June 1991 the Police seized the machines pursuant to Emergency Regulations introduced by the President prohibiting private jackpot operations. The petitioner challenged the regulations, contending that they discriminated against private operators while exempting lotteries conducted by the State or public corporations. He alleged violations of Articles 12(1), 12(2), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution and argued that the restrictions were unconstitutional despite Article 15(7). The respondents maintained that the regulations were necessary in the interests of public order and national security. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been violated. The Court reasoned that the distinction between private gaming establishments and State lotteries constituted a valid classification because private jackpot centers had been associated with narcotics, prostitution, and terrorism. It held that Article 12 does not require perfect legislative symmetry and that the State may selectively eliminate perceived threats to public order. The Court further observed that Article 14(1)(g) protects only lawful occupations, and once the regulations rendered jackpot operations unlawful, constitutional protection ceased. The President's subjective satisfaction regarding the necessity of Emergency Regulations could not be reviewed absent proof of mala fides. The Court also emphasized that equitable relief requires clean hands and cannot legitimize illegal conduct.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Abeywardena v Inspector General of Police
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner owned and operated "Jackpot Machines" imported under valid licenses and installed in public establishments. In June 1991 the Police seized the machines pursuant to Emergency Regulations introduced by the President prohibiting private jackpot operations. The petitioner challenged the regulations, contending that they discriminated against private operators while exempting lotteries conducted by the State or public corporations. He alleged violations of Articles 12(1), 12(2), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution and argued that the restrictions were unconstitutional despite Article 15(7). The respondents maintained that the regulations were necessary in the interests of public order and national security. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been violated. The Court reasoned that the distinction between private gaming establishments and State lotteries constituted a valid classification because private jackpot centers had been associated with narcotics, prostitution, and terrorism. It held that Article 12 does not require perfect legislative symmetry and that the State may selectively eliminate perceived threats to public order. The Court further observed that Article 14(1)(g) protects only lawful occupations, and once the regulations rendered jackpot operations unlawful, constitutional protection ceased. The President's subjective satisfaction regarding the necessity of Emergency Regulations could not be reviewed absent proof of mala fides. The Court also emphasized that equitable relief requires clean hands and cannot legitimize illegal conduct.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

stage_b_cases.case_name: Edward Sivalingam v. Sub Inspector Jayasekera and Others
stage_b_cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested on August 4, 2006 at a lodge in Vavuniya while in possession of a National Identity Card, a Methodist Church identification card, and an LTTE travel pass. Following the discovery of a large cache of explosives in a lorry on the previous day, the authorities suspected the Petitioner of involvement in unlawful activities. The Petitioner alleged that officers attached to the Criminal Investigation Department assaulted him with clubs in order to obtain a confession, causing injuries to his arm, head, and back. He was detained for eight months at CID Headquarters and for a further four months at the Boossa Detention Camp pursuant to successive Detention Orders issued under Emergency Regulations. A confession was recorded in Sinhala, and the Petitioner later asserted that he did not understand the language. The Court examined multiple Medico-Legal Reports from doctors in Colombo and Galle, all of which disclosed no injuries or signs of dislocation, thereby contradicting the allegations of torture. The Court further held that the Petitioner's possession of an LTTE travel pass, coupled with the surrounding circumstances relating to the explosives discovery, provided reasonable suspicion justifying arrest and investigation. The Court also found that the Petitioner had deliberately misled the Court regarding his fluency in Sinhala, noting evidence that he had conducted sermons in Sinhala and originated from a Sinhala-speaking area. The detention was held to be lawful under Emergency Regulations, and the Supreme Court concluded that no violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), or 13(2) had been established.

The arrest, holding in custody, detention or other deprivation of personal liberty of a person, by reason of a removal order or a deportation order made under the provisions of the Immigrants and Emigrants Act or the Indo-Ceylon Agreement (Implementation) Act, No. 14 of 1967, or such other law as may be enacted in substitution therefor, shall not be a contravention of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom of movement and choice of residence
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to be produced before a judge
retrieved_articles.text: Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Abeywardena v Inspector General of Police
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner owned and operated "Jackpot Machines" imported under valid licenses and installed in public establishments. In June 1991 the Police seized the machines pursuant to Emergency Regulations introduced by the President prohibiting private jackpot operations. The petitioner challenged the regulations, contending that they discriminated against private operators while exempting lotteries conducted by the State or public corporations. He alleged violations of Articles 12(1), 12(2), and 14(1)(g) of the Constitution and argued that the restrictions were unconstitutional despite Article 15(7). The respondents maintained that the regulations were necessary in the interests of public order and national security. The Supreme Court dismissed the application and held that no fundamental rights had been violated. The Court reasoned that the distinction between private gaming establishments and State lotteries constituted a valid classification because private jackpot centers had been associated with narcotics, prostitution, and terrorism. It held that Article 12 does not require perfect legislative symmetry and that the State may selectively eliminate perceived threats to public order. The Court further observed that Article 14(1)(g) protects only lawful occupations, and once the regulations rendered jackpot operations unlawful, constitutional protection ceased. The President's subjective satisfaction regarding the necessity of Emergency Regulations could not be reviewed absent proof of mala fides. The Court also emphasized that equitable relief requires clean hands and cannot legitimize illegal conduct.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Weerawansa v. The Attorney-General and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The petitioner, a Customs officer, was arrested under the Prevention of Terrorism Act on suspicion of involvement in smuggling weapons and aircraft parts for an insurgent organization. He challenged the legality of his arrest and prolonged detention, arguing there was no credible or objective material linking him to unlawful activity. He was detained for several months and later remanded by a Magistrate without adequate judicial scrutiny of jurisdiction or the legality of prior executive detention. The case involved Articles 13(1) and 13(2) of the Constitution concerning freedom from arbitrary arrest and detention. The Supreme Court held that arrest under anti-terror legislation must be supported by objective grounds of suspicion and cannot rely on vague or unverified intelligence. It further held that judicial remand must be an independent judicial act, requiring consideration of legality and authority under which a person is already detained. The Court found that the remand process in this case was defective and amounted to administrative continuation of executive custody rather than genuine judicial oversight. As a result, the prolonged detention was characterized as unconstitutional executive action. The Court held that the petitioner's fundamental rights were violated and imposed compensation on State officials responsible for the unlawful arrest and detention.

retrieved_cases.case_name: Edward Sivalingam v. Sub Inspector Jayasekera and Others
retrieved_cases.summary: The Petitioner was arrested on August 4, 2006 at a lodge in Vavuniya while in possession of a National Identity Card, a Methodist Church identification card, and an LTTE travel pass. Following the discovery of a large cache of explosives in a lorry on the previous day, the authorities suspected the Petitioner of involvement in unlawful activities. The Petitioner alleged that officers attached to the Criminal Investigation Department assaulted him with clubs in order to obtain a confession, causing injuries to his arm, head, and back. He was detained for eight months at CID Headquarters and for a further four months at the Boossa Detention Camp pursuant to successive Detention Orders issued under Emergency Regulations. A confession was recorded in Sinhala, and the Petitioner later asserted that he did not understand the language. The Court examined multiple Medico-Legal Reports from doctors in Colombo and Galle, all of which disclosed no injuries or signs of dislocation, thereby contradicting the allegations of torture. The Court further held that the Petitioner's possession of an LTTE travel pass, coupled with the surrounding circumstances relating to the explosives discovery, provided reasonable suspicion justifying arrest and investigation. The Court also found that the Petitioner had deliberately misled the Court regarding his fluency in Sinhala, noting evidence that he had conducted sermons in Sinhala and originated from a Sinhala-speaking area. The detention was held to be lawful under Emergency Regulations, and the Supreme Court concluded that no violations of Articles 11, 12(1), 13(1), or 13(2) had been established.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.
Freedom of movement and choice of residence. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom of movement and of choosing his residence within Sri Lanka.
Freedom to return to Sri Lanka. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to return to Sri Lanka.

Right to be produced before a judge. Every person held in custody, detained or otherwise deprived of personal liberty shall be brought before the judge of the nearest competent court according to procedure established by law and shall not be further held in custody, detained or deprived of personal liberty except upon and in terms of the order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.
Freedom from arbitrary arrest. No person shall be arrested except according to procedure established by law. Any person arrested shall be informed of the reason for his arrest.
Right to a fair trial. Any person charged with an offence shall be entitled to be heard, in person or by an Attorney-at-Law, at a fair trial by a competent court.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

intake.actor_name: Ceylon Petroleum Corporation
intake.actor_role: public corporation officials and human resources authorities
intake.what_happened: I am an employee of the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation and applied for internal promotion to the post of Officer (Audit) Grade A7. After applications were called, the marking scheme used at the interview was different from the marking scheme in the notice. I was not selected, while several other employees were promoted. I believe I should have received marks for my Chartered Accountancy Executive Level qualification and that the change in the marking scheme unfairly affected my chance of promotion.
intake.harm_suffered: Loss of promotion opportunity, career progression delay, alleged unfair selection process, lower marks for qualifications, and disadvantage compared with selected candidates.
intake.user_narrative: I have worked at the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation for many years, first as an Accounts Clerk and later in audit-related roles. When applications were called for the Officer (Audit) Grade A7 post, I applied because I believed I had the required qualifications. I later found out that the marking scheme used at the interview was different from the one stated when applications were called. I also believe my Chartered Accountancy Executive Level qualification should have been treated as equivalent to a diploma and given more marks. Several others were selected while I was not. I feel the process was unfair and that I lost a promotion I should have received.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner challenged her non-selection for promotion to Officer (Audit) Grade A7, arguing that the marking scheme was changed after applications were called and that she was denied marks for an ICASL Executive Level qualification. The Court accepted that changing a marking scheme without informing applicants can create a prima facie equality issue and that transparency is required in promotion processes. However, the Court found that the change to the marking scheme was introduced in good faith as part of a broader restructuring, that the petitioner benefited from the increased marks for seniority, and that the decisive issue was whether she possessed the relevant ICASL certificate at the required time. Although she had completed the components, she was certified only after applications closed and after the interview. Therefore, even if the original marking scheme had applied, she was not entitled to the additional marks, no prejudice was caused, and Article 12(1) was not infringed.
gold.gold_remedy: The application was dismissed without costs.
gold.evaluation_notes: Clear no-violation public corporation promotion case with an initially plausible procedural fairness issue. Useful for false-violation and weak-article control because the Court recognized a prima facie concern about changing promotion criteria, but rejected the Article 12(1) claim after finding no prejudice and no entitlement to the claimed qualification marks. cases.case_name: Jayasundara v. Pathmasiri and Others
cases.summary: The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

cases.case_name: Hewa Kulasuriyage Anura Nimal v. Commissioner General of Excise
cases.summary: The petitioner, an excise inspector, challenged a promotion decision alleging incorrect allocation of marks for seniority and merit, resulting in exclusion from the final list. The respondents contended that the selection process followed the established Scheme of Recruitment and that marks were awarded consistently across all candidates. The Supreme Court held that promotion assessments fall within the lawful administrative discretion of relevant authorities, particularly where structured evaluation criteria exist. It found no evidence of mala fides, bias, or deviation from prescribed marking procedures. The Court further held that dissatisfaction with scoring outcomes alone does not constitute a constitutional violation unless supported by proof of arbitrariness or unequal application of rules. It concluded that the petitioner was evaluated under the same framework as other candidates and that no differential or discriminatory treatment occurred. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, affirming that equality under Article 12(1) requires demonstrable departure from legal standards rather than subjective disagreement with administrative scoring.

cases.case_name: K. L. I. Amarasekera and Others v. Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

cases.case_name:
W.K.B. Seneviratne and 5 Others v. Justice P.R.P. Perera, Chairman, Public
Service Commission and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, who served as Class II Jailors in the Department of Prisons, challenged the promotion of the 15th to 23rd Respondents to the rank of Class I Jailors. The promotions were conducted under a 2004 marking scheme allocating marks for seniority, experience, performance, and presentation at an interview. The Petitioners alleged that the promotions violated Article 12(1) because several selected officers were junior to them in service and because the marking scheme introduced subjectivity. They also contended that an inquiry was pending against the 17th Respondent, making that promotion improper. The Respondents maintained that the governing recruitment scheme lawfully permitted promotions based on both seniority and merit. The Court held that seniority alone was not the exclusive criterion in public service promotions and that the applicable recruitment framework authorized the consideration of efficiency and performance. Although the Court acknowledged that interview presentation marks introduced some degree of subjectivity, it found this acceptable because such marks represented only a limited portion of the total evaluation and were assessed by a balanced panel. The Court further determined that the Petitioners had failed to provide any specific evidence regarding the alleged inquiry against the 17th Respondent. The Supreme Court concluded that the marking scheme constituted an objective method of appraisal ensuring fairness among eligible candidates and held that the Petitioners failed to establish any infringement of the right to equality and equal protection of the law.

cases.case_name:
Weerathunga Arachchige Michael Padmasiri and Others v. The Governor –
Southern Province and Others
cases.summary: The Petitioners, officers of the Co-operative Development Department, challenged revised Schemes of Recruitment introduced in 2015 and implemented through 2016 selection processes, which introduced new marking criteria based on higher educational qualifications and professional training. They alleged that the new criteria were arbitrary and disadvantaged existing officers, thereby violating Articles 12(1) and 14(1)(g). The Supreme Court dismissed the application on the preliminary ground of limitation under Article 126(2). It held that the Petitioners had knowledge of the impugned scheme once official vacancy notices were published in March 2016 and participated in the selection process without objection. The Court found that such participation constituted acquiescence, preventing them from later challenging the legality of the process after failing to secure selection. It further held that the application was filed beyond the mandatory one-month period and therefore was jurisdictionally barred. The Court did not proceed to examine the substantive fairness of the recruitment criteria. Accordingly, the application was dismissed as time-barred without a finding on the merits.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of occupation. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

retrieved_articles.heading: Affirmative action for advancement
retrieved_articles.text: Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from discrimination
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

retrieved_articles.heading: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights
retrieved_articles.text: Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

retrieved_articles.heading: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces
retrieved_articles.text: Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

retrieved_articles.heading: Rights of certain permanent residents
retrieved_articles.text: Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.

retrieved_articles.heading: Right to equality before the law
retrieved_articles.text: Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

retrieved_articles.heading: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation
retrieved_articles.text: Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(g) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of national economy or in relation to: (a) the professional, technical, academic, financial and other qualifications necessary for practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, trade, business or enterprise and the licensing and disciplinary control of the person entitled to such fundamental right; and (b) the carrying on by the State, a State agency or a public corporation of any trade, business, industry, service or enterprise whether to the exclusion, complete or partial, of citizens or otherwise.

Affirmative action for advancement. Nothing in this Article shall prevent special provision being made, by law, subordinate legislation or executive action, for the advancement of women, children or disabled persons.

Freedom from discrimination. No citizen shall be discriminated against on the grounds of race, religion, language, caste, sex, political opinion, place of birth or any one of such grounds. Provided that it shall be lawful to require a person to acquire within a reasonable time sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any employment or office in the Public, Judicial or Local Government Service or in the service of any Public Corporation, where such knowledge is reasonably necessary for the discharge of the duties of such employment or office. Provided further that it shall be lawful to require a person to have a sufficient knowledge of any language as a qualification for any such employment or office where no function of that employment or office can be discharged otherwise than with a knowledge of that language.

Remedy for infringement of fundamental rights. Every person shall be entitled to apply to the Supreme Court, as provided by Article 126, in respect of the infringement or imminent infringement, by executive or administrative action, of a fundamental right to which such person is entitled under the provisions of this Chapter.

Freedom from retrospective penal legislation. No person shall be held guilty of an offence on account of any act or omission which did not, at the time of such act or omission, constitute such an offence and no penalty shall be imposed for any offence more severe than the penalty in force at the time such offence was committed. Nothing in this Article shall prejudice the trial and punishment of any person for any act or omission which, at the time when it was committed, was criminal according to the general principles of law recognized by the community of nations. It shall not be contravention of this Article to require the imposition of a minimum penalty for an offence provided that such penalty does not exceed the maximum penalty prescribed for such offence at the time such offence was committed.

Restrictions on freedom of speech and expression. The exercise and operation of the fundamental right declared and recognized by Article 14(1)(a) shall be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of racial and religious harmony or in relation to parliamentary privilege, contempt of court, defamation or incitement to an offence.

Restrictions applicable to Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces. The exercise and operation of the fundamental rights declared and recognized by Articles 12(1), 13 and 14 shall, in their application to the members of the Armed Forces, Police Force and other Forces charged with the maintenance of public order, be subject to such restrictions as may be prescribed by law in the interests of the proper discharge of their duties and the maintenance of discipline among them.

Rights of certain permanent residents. A person who, not being a citizen of any other country, has been permanently and legally resident in Sri Lanka immediately prior to the commencement of the Constitution and continues to be so resident shall be entitled, for a period of ten years from the commencement of the Constitution, to the rights declared and recognized by paragraph (1) of this Article.
Right to equality before the law. All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

Freedom to engage in lawful occupation. Every citizen is entitled to the freedom to engage by himself or in association with others in any lawful occupation, profession, trade, business or enterprise.

The petitioner, a Senior Superintendent of Police, challenged promotion decisions whereby junior or lower-scoring officers were promoted to Assistant DIG positions despite his higher merit ranking. He alleged that the National Police Commission altered marking schemes and applied subjective criteria, violating Article 12(1). The respondents relied on administrative discretion in promotions. The Supreme Court held that promotion criteria must be transparent, consistent, and applied uniformly to all eligible officers. It found that altering marking schemes during the selection process to favour certain candidates was arbitrary and violated equality principles. The Court further held that seniority and merit cannot be disregarded without a rational basis, and doing so constitutes abuse of executive power. It emphasized that public service bodies must act as model employers ensuring fairness and objectivity in promotions. The Court concluded that the petitioner was unfairly bypassed and held that his fundamental rights were violated. Relief including retrospective consideration for promotion and compensation was granted.

The petitioner, an excise inspector, challenged a promotion decision alleging incorrect allocation of marks for seniority and merit, resulting in exclusion from the final list. The respondents contended that the selection process followed the established Scheme of Recruitment and that marks were awarded consistently across all candidates. The Supreme Court held that promotion assessments fall within the lawful administrative discretion of relevant authorities, particularly where structured evaluation criteria exist. It found no evidence of mala fides, bias, or deviation from prescribed marking procedures. The Court further held that dissatisfaction with scoring outcomes alone does not constitute a constitutional violation unless supported by proof of arbitrariness or unequal application of rules. It concluded that the petitioner was evaluated under the same framework as other candidates and that no differential or discriminatory treatment occurred. Accordingly, the application was dismissed, affirming that equality under Article 12(1) requires demonstrable departure from legal standards rather than subjective disagreement with administrative scoring.

The Petitioners, senior officers of the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, challenged the denial of promotion under a recruitment framework that retained an outdated circular reserving a percentage of vacancies for officers over 50 years of age to be assessed solely on interview performance. Although initially instructed to sit a written examination "nominally," they were later denied promotion despite satisfying interview requirements, while junior officers were selected. The Respondents relied on a purported new recruitment scheme, but the Supreme Court found that the original circular had never been lawfully rescinded by the competent authority. The Petitioners invoked Article 12(1) and alleged unequal treatment and violation of legitimate expectation. The Court held that administrative circulars remain valid until properly revoked and that internal communications cannot override binding directives. It further held that the Petitioners had a legitimate expectation arising from both established practice and explicit assurances that interview-based selection would apply. The Court also affirmed that arbitrary deviation from published criteria constitutes violation of equal protection even absent discrimination in intent. Accordingly, it held that the Petitioners' fundamental rights had been violated and ordered retrospective promotion with back wages.

intake.user_narrative: I own a property in Galle. A nearby lot in the original plan had been reserved for a common well, but the well was later abandoned and filled. Authorities then started building a two-storey community hall on that lot. I was already worried because the land near my house has a slope with rocks and drainage problems, and I had complained before about water and soil movement from the neighbouring property. When I saw excavation and construction starting, I complained to the police, the Municipal Council, the Divisional Secretary, the Urban Development Authority and the National Building Research Organization because I feared the construction would make the land unstable and endanger my family and property. I believe the authorities ignored my safety concerns and allowed the building to continue unfairly.

gold.gold_reasoning_summary: The petitioner alleged that construction of a community hall on Lot 9, previously reserved for a common well, violated Article 12(1) because it was unsafe, contrary to Urban Development Authority regulations, inconsistent with National Building Research Organization recommendations, and inadequately investigated. The Court rejected the time-bar objection because the construction and complaints could be treated as a continuing issue. On the merits, the Court held that the authorities could relax the relevant site extent and width requirements under Regulation 17(3), and that the construction was not outlawed. The Court also found that the NBRO recommendations relied on by the petitioner concerned the eastern boundary between the petitioner's property and the 9th respondent's land, not the community hall site, and that NBRO material relating to the community hall did not show danger. There was no material establishing arbitrary, discriminatory or unequal treatment, so Article 12(1) was not infringed.
